subareas.name: Conference proceedings and collections of articles

page.hook: What is a proof, and how does mathematics organize, explain and share what it knows?
about: This class collects writing about mathematics as a whole instead of one branch. It covers general surveys, books for nonspecialists, problem books, recreational mathematics, popular exposition, dictionaries and formula collections, the philosophy and methodology of mathematics, and conference proceedings. It also covers general questions of mathematical modeling, such as dimensional analysis, and the links between mathematics and music, art, architecture and literature.

There is no single method here. What unites the material is a view from above: how proofs work, how definitions are chosen, how a model is matched to the world, and how results are explained to wider audiences. Many ideas that every mathematician uses, such as induction, proof by contradiction and counting arguments, are met first in books that belong to this class.

example.title: Units decide the answer
example.text: How does the period \(T\) of a pendulum depend on its length \(\ell\), its mass \(m\) and gravity \(g\)? Length is in meters, \(g\) in meters per second squared, mass in kilograms. The only combination with units of seconds is \(\sqrt{\ell/g}\). So \(T=C\sqrt{\ell/g}\), where the pure number \(C\) may depend on the swing angle. Mass cannot matter, and at the same angle a pendulum four times as long takes twice as long.

objects.gloss: A finite chain of logical steps that establishes a statement from accepted assumptions.
A statement taken as a starting point without proof.
A precise agreement on what a term means, on which all later reasoning depends.
A statement believed to be true for which no proof is known.
A mathematical description of a real system, used to explain or predict its behavior.
Reasoning about physical formulas from the units of the quantities involved.
Writing that explains known mathematics to students, other specialists or the public.

theorems.name: Principle of mathematical induction
theorems.statement: Let \(P(n)\) be a statement about natural numbers. If \(P(0)\) holds and \(P(n)\) implies \(P(n+1)\) for every \(n\), then \(P(n)\) holds for every natural number \(n\).

theorems.name: Pigeonhole principle
theorems.statement: If \(n+1\) objects are placed in \(n\) boxes, then some box contains at least two objects.

theorems.name: Irrationality of the square root of 2
theorems.statement: There are no positive integers \(p\) and \(q\) with \(p^2=2q^2\). Hence \(\sqrt2\) is not a ratio of whole numbers.

theorems.name: Euler's theorem on the Königsberg bridges
theorems.statement: A connected finite graph, possibly with several edges between two vertices, has a closed walk that uses every edge exactly once if and only if every vertex has even degree. Euler showed that the condition is necessary, which settles the Königsberg bridge puzzle; sufficiency was proved later.

theorems.name: Buckingham pi theorem
theorems.statement: Suppose a physical law relates \(n\) quantities, and the matrix of exponents expressing their units in terms of base units has rank \(k\). If the law holds in every system of units, it can be rewritten as a relation among \(n-k\) dimensionless products of the quantities.

page.hook: Who first found the theorems we learn in school, and how did they think about them?
about: The history of mathematics studies how mathematical ideas arose, changed and spread, from the clay tablets of Mesopotamia and the papyri of Egypt through Greek, Chinese, Indian and Islamic mathematics to the present. It also covers the lives of mathematicians, the schools and institutions they worked in, and the editing of their collected works and correspondence.

Its methods are those of the historian: close reading of primary sources in their original language and notation, dating and comparing manuscripts, and placing the work in its culture. A recurring caution is not to read modern concepts into old texts. The field touches every branch of mathematics, since each has a past, and it connects to the history of science and to mathematics education.

example.title: A Babylonian square root
example.text: The clay tablet YBC 7289, written in Mesopotamia between about 1800 and 1600 BCE, shows a square with its diagonals and the number 1;24,51,10 in base 60. That is \(1+\frac{24}{60}+\frac{51}{60^2}+\frac{10}{60^3}\approx 1.4142130\), while \(\sqrt2\approx 1.4142136\). The scribe had the ratio of diagonal to side correct to better than one part in a million, more than a thousand years before Euclid.

objects.gloss: An original document, such as a tablet, manuscript, letter or first printed edition.
Greek treatise from about 300 BCE that set the pattern of definitions, postulates and proofs.
Clay tablet with wedge-shaped writing; the main source for Mesopotamian mathematics.
Base 60 place-value notation of Mesopotamia, still used for minutes and seconds.
The symbols used to write mathematics, which changed greatly over time and shaped what was easy to do.
The study of how the history of mathematics itself has been written and interpreted.
An account of a mathematician's life, work and surroundings.

theorems.name: Pythagorean theorem
theorems.statement: In a right triangle with legs \(a\), \(b\) and hypotenuse \(c\), \(a^2+b^2=c^2\). The relation was used in Old Babylonian mathematics, and a proof appears as Proposition I.47 of Euclid's Elements.

theorems.name: Euclid's theorem on primes
theorems.statement: There are infinitely many prime numbers. Proposition IX.20 of Euclid's Elements shows that any finite list of primes omits at least one prime.

theorems.name: Archimedes' quadrature of the parabola
theorems.statement: The area of a segment of a parabola cut off by a chord is \(\tfrac43\) of the area of the triangle with the chord as base and third vertex at the point of the arc where the tangent is parallel to the chord.

theorems.name: Cardano's formula for the cubic
theorems.statement: For real numbers \(p>0\) and \(q\), the equation \(x^3+px=q\) has the real root \(x=\sqrt[3]{\tfrac q2+\sqrt{D}}+\sqrt[3]{\tfrac q2-\sqrt{D}}\) with \(D=\tfrac{q^2}{4}+\tfrac{p^3}{27}\). The rule was published in Cardano's Ars Magna, which credits del Ferro and Tartaglia.

theorems.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus
theorems.statement: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(F'=f\) there, then \(\int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a)\). Newton and Leibniz, working independently in the late seventeenth century, made this link between tangents and areas the basis of a general calculus.

theorems.name: Independence of the parallel postulate
theorems.statement: Hyperbolic geometry satisfies Euclid's postulates except the parallel postulate, so that postulate cannot be proved from the others. Lobachevsky and Bolyai published such geometries around 1830, and in 1868 Beltrami gave a model of hyperbolic geometry inside Euclidean geometry.

open.name: Purpose of Plimpton 322
open.gloss: How this Old Babylonian table of numbers related to right triangles was computed, and what it was used for, is still debated.

open.name: Transmission between ancient traditions
open.gloss: How far Mesopotamian, Greek, Indian and Chinese mathematics influenced one another is only partly documented.

subareas.name: Philosophical aspects of logic and foundations

page.hook: Can every true statement about whole numbers be proved, and what can no computer ever decide?
about: Mathematical logic studies mathematical reasoning itself. It asks what a proof is, which statements follow from which axioms, what it means for a statement to be true in a structure, and what can be computed by a mechanical procedure. Its main branches are model theory, computability theory, set theory and proof theory.

The method is to treat statements and proofs as precise finite objects and then prove theorems about them. Set theory supplies a common foundation for the rest of mathematics, and model theory has produced results in algebra and number theory. Computability theory is the starting point of theoretical computer science, and proof theory compares the strength of axiom systems.

example.title: A number beyond all numbers
example.text: Take all true first-order statements about the natural numbers and add a new symbol \(c\) with the axioms \(c>0\), \(c>1\), \(c>2\), and so on. Any finite set of these axioms holds in the ordinary natural numbers if \(c\) is read as a large enough number. By the compactness theorem, all of them hold together in some structure. It obeys every first-order truth of arithmetic, yet it contains an element above every ordinary number.

objects.gloss: A statement built from variables, relations and functions using and, or, not, for all and there exists.
A set with chosen relations and functions, in which formulas are true or false.
A finite sequence of formulas, each an axiom or obtained from earlier ones by a fixed rule.
A function on natural numbers whose values a Turing machine can calculate.
The Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms for sets with the axiom of choice, the usual foundation of mathematics.
Numbers that extend counting to the order type and the size of infinite sets.
A technique for building new models of set theory, used to prove independence results.

theorems.name: Gödel's completeness theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(T\) be a set of first-order sentences and \(\varphi\) a sentence. Then \(\varphi\) is true in every model of \(T\) if and only if there is a formal proof of \(\varphi\) from \(T\).

theorems.name: Compactness theorem
theorems.statement: A set of first-order sentences has a model if every finite subset of it has a model.

theorems.name: Löwenheim-Skolem theorem
theorems.statement: If a first-order theory in a countable language has an infinite model, then it has a model of every infinite cardinality.

theorems.name: Gödel's first incompleteness theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(T\) be a consistent theory whose axioms can be listed by an algorithm and which contains Robinson arithmetic. Then there is a sentence of arithmetic that \(T\) neither proves nor refutes. Gödel assumed slightly more than consistency; Rosser removed the extra assumption in 1936.

theorems.name: Undecidability of the halting problem
theorems.statement: There is no algorithm that decides, for every Turing machine \(M\) and input \(w\), whether \(M\) eventually halts on \(w\).

theorems.name: Independence of the continuum hypothesis
theorems.statement: The continuum hypothesis says that every infinite set of real numbers is either countable or of the same cardinality as \(\mathbb{R}\). If ZFC is consistent, it neither proves nor refutes this. Gödel showed in 1938 that it cannot be refuted, and Cohen showed in 1963 that it cannot be proved.

open.name: Vaught's conjecture
open.gloss: A complete first-order theory in a countable language has, up to isomorphism, either countably many countable models or as many as there are real numbers.

open.name: Inner models for large cardinals
open.gloss: Whether there is a canonical model of set theory, similar to Gödel's constructible universe, that contains a supercompact cardinal.

open.name: P versus NP
open.gloss: Whether every problem whose solutions can be checked in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time.

page.hook: How many ways can it be done, and must some pattern appear once a structure is large enough?
about: Combinatorics studies finite and discrete structures: arrangements, selections, graphs, families of sets, designs and partitions. It asks whether a structure with prescribed properties exists, how many such structures there are, how large or small one can be, and how to build one. Graph theory, the study of networks of points joined by edges, is its largest branch.

Its tools include bijections, recurrences and generating functions for counting, and extremal and probabilistic arguments for existence. Linear algebra, group representations and topology are used as well. The area supplies the mathematics of algorithms and networks in computer science, and it exchanges problems and methods with number theory, probability, algebra, geometry and statistical physics.

example.title: Six people at a party
example.text: Among any six people there are three who all know each other or three who are mutual strangers. Pick one person. Of the other five, at least three are her acquaintances or at least three are strangers to her; say three are acquaintances. If two of those know each other, they form a trio with her. Otherwise those three are mutual strangers. Five people are not enough: seat them in a circle where each knows only the two neighbors.

objects.gloss: A set of vertices with a set of edges, each joining two vertices.
An arrangement of the elements of a finite set in some order.
A way of writing a positive integer as a sum of positive integers, ignoring order.
A power series whose coefficients are the terms of a counting sequence.
A family of subsets of a finite set in which elements meet in a balanced, prescribed way.
An abstraction of linear independence that applies to vectors, graphs and more.
A filling of a staircase-like array of boxes by numbers that increase along rows and columns.

theorems.name: Cayley's formula
theorems.statement: The number of trees on \(n\) labeled vertices is \(n^{n-2}\).

theorems.name: Ramsey's theorem
theorems.statement: For all positive integers \(r\) and \(s\) there is an \(N\) such that, whenever each edge of the complete graph on \(N\) vertices is colored red or blue, there are \(r\) vertices with all edges among them red or \(s\) vertices with all edges among them blue.

theorems.name: Hall's marriage theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(G\) be a finite bipartite graph with parts \(X\) and \(Y\). There is a matching that covers every vertex of \(X\) if and only if every subset \(S\) of \(X\) has at least \(|S|\) neighbors in \(Y\).

theorems.name: Turán's theorem
theorems.statement: A graph on \(n\) vertices that contains no complete subgraph on \(r+1\) vertices has at most \(\left(1-\tfrac1r\right)\tfrac{n^2}{2}\) edges.

theorems.name: Szemerédi's theorem
theorems.statement: Every set of positive integers with positive upper density contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length.

theorems.name: Four color theorem
theorems.statement: The vertices of every planar graph without loops can be colored with four colors so that adjacent vertices receive different colors. The proof relies on a computer check of a large number of cases.

open.name: Ramsey number of five
open.gloss: The least number of vertices that forces five vertices with all edges of one color, in every red and blue coloring of a complete graph, is not known exactly.

open.name: Hadwiger's conjecture
open.gloss: Every graph with no \(K_t\) minor can be properly colored with \(t-1\) colors; this is open for \(t\ge 7\).

open.name: Union-closed sets conjecture
open.gloss: If a finite family of sets is closed under unions and contains a nonempty set, some element lies in at least half of the sets.

page.hook: What can be said when things are only partly ranked, like tasks where some must come before others?
about: Order theory studies sets with a relation of comparison, such as the divisors of a number ordered by divisibility or the subsets of a set ordered by inclusion. A lattice is an ordered set in which any two elements have a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound. The area also treats Boolean algebras and groups, rings and other algebraic structures that carry a compatible order.

Arguments combine algebra with pictures. Finite ordered sets are drawn as Hasse diagrams, and a lattice can be described either by its order or by its operations of join and meet. Representation theorems realize abstract lattices as families of sets or of open sets in a space. The area supplies basic tools to logic, universal algebra, combinatorics, topology and computer science.

example.title: The divisors of 12
example.text: Order the divisors of 12, namely 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12, by divisibility. The numbers 4 and 6 are incomparable, since neither divides the other. Their greatest lower bound is their greatest common divisor 2, and their least upper bound is their least common multiple 12. Every pair has both bounds, so this is a lattice. No three divisors are pairwise incomparable, and two chains cover all six: \(1,2,4,12\) and \(3,6\).

objects.gloss: A set with a relation that is reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive.
A subset in which every two elements are comparable, or in which no two are.
An ordered set in which every two elements have a join and a meet.
A lattice in which join and meet distribute over each other, as union and intersection do.
A distributive lattice with least and greatest elements in which every element has a complement.
An ordered set in which every subset has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound.
Maps \(f\) and \(g\) between ordered sets with \(f(x)\le y\) exactly when \(x\le g(y)\).

theorems.name: Zorn's lemma
theorems.statement: If every chain in a nonempty partially ordered set \(P\) has an upper bound in \(P\), then \(P\) has a maximal element. Over the Zermelo-Fraenkel axioms this statement is equivalent to the axiom of choice.

theorems.name: Stone's representation theorem
theorems.statement: Every Boolean algebra is isomorphic to the algebra of all sets that are both open and closed in some compact, Hausdorff, totally disconnected space.

theorems.name: Birkhoff's representation theorem
theorems.statement: Every finite distributive lattice is isomorphic to the lattice of down-sets of the ordered set of its join-irreducible elements, with union and intersection as join and meet.

theorems.name: Dilworth's theorem
theorems.statement: In a finite partially ordered set, the largest size of an antichain equals the smallest number of chains whose union is the whole set.

theorems.name: Knaster-Tarski fixed point theorem
theorems.statement: Every order-preserving map from a complete lattice to itself has a fixed point. Moreover, its fixed points form a complete lattice, so there is a least and a greatest fixed point.

theorems.name: Forbidden sublattice theorems
theorems.statement: A lattice is modular if and only if it has no sublattice isomorphic to the five-element pentagon \(N_5\) (Dedekind). It is distributive if and only if it has no sublattice isomorphic to \(N_5\) or to the five-element diamond \(M_3\) (Birkhoff).

open.name: 1/3-2/3 conjecture
open.gloss: In every finite partially ordered set that is not a chain there are elements \(x,y\) such that \(x\) precedes \(y\) in between one third and two thirds of all linear extensions.

open.name: Dedekind numbers
open.gloss: The number of antichains in the lattice of subsets of an \(n\)-element set is known exactly only for \(n\le 9\), and no closed formula is known.

page.hook: What is true of every system of operations and equations, whether it is arithmetic or something stranger?
about: Universal algebra studies algebraic structures in general: a set together with any collection of operations, such as the multiplication of a group or the join and meet of a lattice. Instead of treating groups, rings and lattices one kind at a time, it asks what holds for all such structures and how classes of them defined by equations behave.

The basic constructions are subalgebras, homomorphic images, products, and quotients by congruences. A central theme is that properties of the congruence lattices of all algebras in a class correspond to the existence of terms satisfying certain identities. The area overlaps with logic, lattice theory and category theory, and it now supplies the main tools for classifying the complexity of constraint satisfaction problems.

example.title: Groups by equations, fields not
example.text: A group can be described as a set with a binary product, a unary inverse and a constant \(e\) satisfying the identities \(x(yz)=(xy)z\), \(xe=x\) and \(xx^{-1}=e\). Because only identities are used, subgroups, quotients and products of groups are again groups. Fields cannot be described this way, whatever operations are chosen: the product \(\mathbb{Q}\times\mathbb{Q}\) is not a field, since \((1,0)\cdot(0,1)=(0,0)\) although neither factor is zero.

objects.gloss: A list of operation symbols, each with a fixed number of arguments.
A set together with one operation for each symbol of a signature.
A map between algebras of the same signature that respects every operation.
An equivalence relation compatible with all operations, so that the quotient is again an algebra.
The class of all algebras of a signature that satisfy a given set of identities.
The most general algebra in a variety on a given set of generators.
A set of operations on a set that contains the projections and is closed under composition.

theorems.name: Homomorphism theorem
theorems.statement: If \(f\colon A\to B\) is a surjective homomorphism of algebras, then \(\theta=\{(a,a') : f(a)=f(a')\}\) is a congruence of \(A\), and the quotient \(A/\theta\) is isomorphic to \(B\).

theorems.name: Birkhoff's variety theorem
theorems.statement: A class of algebras of one signature is the class of all models of some set of identities if and only if it is closed under homomorphic images, subalgebras and arbitrary direct products.

theorems.name: Completeness of equational logic
theorems.statement: An identity holds in every algebra satisfying a set \(\Sigma\) of identities if and only if it can be derived from \(\Sigma\) by reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity, substitution of terms for variables, and replacement of equal subterms.

theorems.name: Birkhoff's subdirect representation theorem
theorems.statement: Every algebra is isomorphic to a subdirect product of subdirectly irreducible algebras.

theorems.name: Maltsev's theorem
theorems.statement: In a variety \(V\), the congruences of every algebra commute under composition if and only if there is a ternary term \(p\) for which the identities \(p(x,y,y)=x\) and \(p(x,x,y)=y\) hold in \(V\).

theorems.name: Jónsson's lemma
theorems.statement: Let \(V\) be the variety generated by a class \(K\) of algebras, and suppose every algebra in \(V\) has a distributive congruence lattice. Then every subdirectly irreducible algebra in \(V\) is a homomorphic image of a subalgebra of an ultraproduct of members of \(K\).

open.name: Finite lattice representation problem
open.gloss: Is every finite lattice isomorphic to the lattice of congruences of some finite algebra?

open.name: Infinite-domain constraint satisfaction
open.gloss: Whether the split of constraint satisfaction problems into polynomial-time and NP-complete ones, proved for finite templates, extends to a natural class of infinite templates.

Finite fields and commutative rings (number-theoretic aspects)
Connections of number theory and logic

page.hook: Which whole numbers are sums of two squares, and why do primes thin out the way they do?
about: Number theory studies the whole numbers and the questions that grow out of them: how the primes are distributed, which equations have solutions in integers or in fractions, and how well irrational numbers can be approximated by fractions. Its problems are often easy to state and hard to solve, and some stood for centuries before a proof was found.

The methods come from all over mathematics. Analytic number theory uses complex analysis, through the zeta function and its relatives, to count primes. Algebraic number theory enlarges the integers to rings of algebraic numbers. Arithmetic geometry treats equations as curves and higher-dimensional shapes. Modular forms and the Langlands program tie these strands together, and computation with large primes underlies modern cryptography.

example.title: Sums of two squares
example.text: Try to write primes as a sum of two squares: \(5=1+4\), \(13=4+9\), \(17=1+16\), \(29=4+25\), \(37=1+36\). But \(3\), \(7\), \(11\), \(19\) and \(23\) cannot be written this way. The pattern: an odd prime is a sum of two squares exactly when it leaves remainder 1 on division by 4. One direction is easy, since a square leaves remainder 0 or 1. The other was stated by Fermat and first proved by Euler.

objects.gloss: A whole number above 1 divisible only by 1 and itself.
Two integers are congruent modulo \(n\) when their difference is divisible by \(n\).
A polynomial equation for which integer or rational solutions are sought.
Functions of a complex variable that encode primes and other arithmetic data.
A field obtained from the rationals by adjoining a root of a polynomial with rational coefficients.
A smooth cubic curve such as \(y^2=x^3+ax+b\), whose points form an abelian group.
A highly symmetric analytic function on the upper half-plane whose coefficients carry arithmetic information.

theorems.name: Lagrange's four-square theorem
theorems.statement: Every nonnegative integer is a sum of four squares of integers.

theorems.name: Quadratic reciprocity
theorems.statement: For distinct odd primes \(p\) and \(q\), \(\left(\frac{p}{q}\right)\left(\frac{q}{p}\right)=(-1)^{\frac{p-1}{2}\cdot\frac{q-1}{2}}\). Here \(\left(\frac{a}{p}\right)\), for \(a\) not divisible by \(p\), is \(1\) if \(a\) is a square modulo \(p\) and \(-1\) otherwise.

theorems.name: Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progressions
theorems.statement: If \(a\) and \(m\) are positive integers with no common factor above 1, then infinitely many primes are congruent to \(a\) modulo \(m\).

theorems.name: Prime number theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(\pi(x)\) be the number of primes not exceeding \(x\). Then \(\pi(x)\log x/x\) tends to \(1\) as \(x\) tends to infinity.

theorems.name: Mordell's theorem
theorems.statement: The rational points of an elliptic curve defined over \(\mathbb{Q}\) form a finitely generated abelian group.

theorems.name: Fermat's Last Theorem
theorems.statement: For every integer \(n>2\) there are no positive integers \(x\), \(y\), \(z\) with \(x^n+y^n=z^n\).

open.name: Riemann hypothesis
open.gloss: Every zero of the Riemann zeta function with real part strictly between 0 and 1 has real part \(\tfrac12\).

open.name: Twin prime conjecture
open.gloss: There are infinitely many primes \(p\) such that \(p+2\) is also prime.

open.name: Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture
open.gloss: The rank of the group of rational points of an elliptic curve over \(\mathbb{Q}\) equals the order of vanishing of its L-function at \(s=1\).

subareas.name: Connections between field theory and logic

page.hook: Why is there a formula for the roots of a quadratic equation but none for the general equation of degree five?
about: Field theory studies number systems in which one can add, subtract, multiply and divide, such as the rational, real and complex numbers and the finite fields used in coding. It asks how a field can be enlarged by adjoining roots of polynomials, and what the symmetries of such an enlargement reveal about the polynomial.

Galois theory is the core method. It translates questions about the roots of a polynomial into questions about a finite group of permutations of those roots. This explains why equations of degree five have no general solution by radicals and which constructions are possible with ruler and compass. The area also covers ordered and real closed fields, valued fields, differential fields, and the location of roots of polynomials.

example.title: Adjoining a square root
example.text: The numbers \(a+b\sqrt2\) with \(a,b\) rational form a field \(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)\). Sums and products stay of this form, and so do inverses: \(1/(a+b\sqrt2)=(a-b\sqrt2)/(a^2-2b^2)\), where the denominator is not zero because \(\sqrt2\) is irrational. The map sending \(a+b\sqrt2\) to \(a-b\sqrt2\) respects addition and multiplication. Together with the identity map it forms the Galois group of this field over \(\mathbb{Q}\), a group with two elements.

objects.gloss: A set with addition and multiplication obeying the usual rules, in which nonzero elements have inverses.
A field containing a given smaller field; its degree is its dimension over the smaller field.
The monic polynomial of least degree over a field that has a given element as a root.
The smallest extension over which a given polynomial factors into linear factors.
The group of automorphisms of an extension field that fix every element of the base field.
An algebraic extension in which every nonconstant polynomial has a root.
A field with finitely many elements, such as the integers modulo a prime \(p\).

theorems.name: Fundamental theorem of algebra
theorems.statement: Every nonconstant polynomial with complex coefficients has a complex root.

theorems.name: Fundamental theorem of Galois theory
theorems.statement: Let \(L/K\) be a finite Galois extension with group \(G\). Sending a subgroup \(H\) to its fixed field \(L^H\) is an inclusion-reversing bijection between the subgroups of \(G\) and the fields between \(K\) and \(L\). The field \(L^H\) is Galois over \(K\) exactly when \(H\) is normal in \(G\).

theorems.name: Abel-Ruffini theorem
theorems.statement: For each \(n\ge 5\) there is no formula that expresses the roots of the general polynomial of degree \(n\) in terms of its coefficients using only field operations and extraction of roots. For example, the roots of \(x^5-x-1\) cannot be expressed in this way starting from rational numbers.

theorems.name: Galois's solvability criterion
theorems.statement: A polynomial over a field \(K\) of characteristic 0 is solvable by radicals if and only if the Galois group of its splitting field over \(K\) is a solvable group.

theorems.name: Classification of finite fields
theorems.statement: The number of elements of a finite field is \(p^n\) for some prime \(p\) and integer \(n\ge 1\). For each such prime power there is, up to isomorphism, exactly one field with that many elements, and its nonzero elements form a cyclic group under multiplication.

theorems.name: Artin's solution of Hilbert's seventeenth problem
theorems.statement: A polynomial in \(n\) variables with real coefficients that takes no negative value on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is a sum of squares of rational functions with real coefficients.

open.name: Inverse Galois problem
open.gloss: Is every finite group the Galois group of some Galois extension of \(\mathbb{Q}\)?

open.name: Shafarevich's conjecture
open.gloss: The absolute Galois group of the maximal abelian extension of \(\mathbb{Q}\) is a free profinite group of countable rank.

Theory of modules and ideals in commutative rings
Homological methods in commutative ring theory
Chain conditions, finiteness conditions in commutative ring theory
Arithmetic rings and other special commutative rings
Applications of logic to commutative algebra
Computational aspects and applications of commutative rings

page.hook: Whole numbers factor into primes; what is the analog for polynomials in several variables?
about: Commutative algebra studies commutative rings, their ideals, and the modules over them. The model examples are the integers and the rings of polynomials in several variables over a field, together with rings built from these by taking quotients, fractions and completions. Ideals generalize the notion of divisibility, and prime ideals play the role that prime numbers play among the integers.

It is the local algebra behind algebraic geometry and algebraic number theory. A system of polynomial equations corresponds to an ideal, and the geometry of its solution set is read off from the quotient ring. Typical techniques are localization at a prime, completion, dimension theory, and homological methods such as free resolutions and depth. Gröbner bases make many of the constructions computable.

example.title: A line with a thickened point
example.text: In the polynomial ring \(k[x,y]\) over a field, take the ideal \(I=(x^2,xy)\). Its zero set in the plane is the line \(x=0\). But \(I\) is smaller than the ideal \((x)\) of that line: one checks that \(I=(x)\cap(x,y)^2\). The second piece lives at the origin only. So the algebra sees the line together with an extra infinitesimal thickening at one point, information that the bare zero set forgets.

objects.gloss: A set with addition and multiplication obeying the usual rules, including \(ab=ba\).
A subset closed under addition and under multiplication by every element of the ring.
A proper ideal \(P\) such that \(ab\in P\) implies \(a\in P\) or \(b\in P\).
The analog of a vector space with scalars taken from a ring instead of a field.
A ring of fractions formed by allowing chosen elements as denominators.
A ring in which every ideal is generated by finitely many elements.
The largest length of a chain of prime ideals, matching the geometric dimension.

theorems.name: Hilbert's basis theorem
theorems.statement: If \(R\) is a Noetherian commutative ring, then so is the polynomial ring \(R[x]\). In particular, every ideal of \(k[x_1,\dots,x_n]\) with \(k\) a field is finitely generated.

theorems.name: Hilbert's Nullstellensatz
theorems.statement: Let \(k\) be an algebraically closed field and \(I\) an ideal of \(k[x_1,\dots,x_n]\). If a polynomial \(f\) vanishes at every common zero of \(I\) in \(k^n\), then some power of \(f\) lies in \(I\).

theorems.name: Lasker-Noether theorem
theorems.statement: In a Noetherian commutative ring, every ideal is an intersection of finitely many primary ideals.

theorems.name: Krull's principal ideal theorem
theorems.statement: In a Noetherian commutative ring, every prime ideal that is minimal among the primes containing a given principal ideal has height at most 1.

theorems.name: Nakayama's lemma
theorems.statement: Let \(M\) be a finitely generated module over a commutative ring \(R\), and let \(I\) be an ideal contained in the Jacobson radical of \(R\). If \(IM=M\), then \(M=0\).

theorems.name: Quillen-Suslin theorem
theorems.statement: Every finitely generated projective module over a polynomial ring \(k[x_1,\dots,x_n]\) over a field \(k\) is free.

open.name: Serre's positivity conjecture
open.gloss: Whether Serre's intersection multiplicity of two modules over a regular local ring is positive when their dimensions add up to the dimension of the ring; open in mixed characteristic.

open.name: Small Cohen-Macaulay modules
open.gloss: Whether every complete Noetherian local domain has a finitely generated module whose depth equals the dimension of the ring; open from dimension 3 on.

subareas.name: Arithmetic problems in algebraic geometry; Diophantine geometry

page.hook: What shapes do the solutions of polynomial equations trace out, and how do two such shapes meet?
about: Algebraic geometry studies the sets of solutions of systems of polynomial equations, such as lines, conics, cubic curves and surfaces, and their higher-dimensional analogs, called varieties. It asks what shapes these sets have, how they intersect, how they vary in families, and when two of them are essentially the same.

The subject translates geometry into commutative algebra and back: a variety corresponds to a ring of functions on it. Schemes, sheaves and cohomology extend this dictionary so that it works over any field or ring, including the integers, which joins the subject to number theory. Over the complex numbers it meets complex analysis, topology and differential geometry, and it has close ties to theoretical physics.

example.title: Rational points on the circle
example.text: Draw the line through \((-1,0)\) with slope \(t\). It meets the circle \(x^2+y^2=1\) in one further point, \(\left(\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2},\frac{2t}{1+t^2}\right)\). For \(t=\tfrac12\) this is \(\left(\tfrac35,\tfrac45\right)\), which gives the triple \(3^2+4^2=5^2\). Every rational slope gives a point with rational coordinates, and every such point except \((-1,0)\) arises this way. So the circle is parametrized by a line, and every Pythagorean triple arises, up to scaling, from such a point.

objects.gloss: The set of common zeros of a collection of polynomials in several variables.
Ordinary space completed by points at infinity, so that parallel lines meet.
A space built by gluing spectra of commutative rings; the general object of the subject.
A map between varieties given locally by polynomials or quotients of polynomials.
A rule assigning data, such as functions, to open sets in a way compatible with restriction and gluing.
A formal integer combination of subvarieties of codimension one, such as zeros and poles of a function.
A variety or scheme whose points classify geometric objects of a given kind.

theorems.name: Bézout's theorem
theorems.statement: Two projective plane curves of degrees \(d\) and \(e\) over an algebraically closed field, with no common component, meet in exactly \(de\) points when points are counted with intersection multiplicity.

theorems.name: Cayley-Salmon theorem
theorems.statement: Every smooth cubic surface in projective 3-space over an algebraically closed field contains exactly 27 lines.

theorems.name: Riemann-Roch theorem for curves
theorems.statement: Let \(D\) be a divisor on a smooth projective curve of genus \(g\) over an algebraically closed field, and \(K\) a canonical divisor. Then \(\ell(D)-\ell(K-D)=\deg D+1-g\), where \(\ell(D)\) is the dimension of the space of rational functions \(f\) with \(\operatorname{div}(f)+D\ge 0\), together with zero.

theorems.name: Hironaka's resolution of singularities
theorems.statement: For every variety \(X\) over a field of characteristic 0 there are a smooth variety \(Y\) and a proper birational morphism \(Y\to X\).

theorems.name: Weil conjectures
theorems.statement: Let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety over a field with \(q\) elements. Its zeta function, which counts the points of \(X\) over all finite extensions, is a rational function of \(q^{-s}\), satisfies a functional equation, and has all zeros and poles of absolute value \(q^{-i/2}\) for integers \(i\) with \(0\le i\le 2\dim X\). The last statement was proved in 1974.

theorems.name: Faltings's theorem
theorems.statement: A smooth projective curve of genus at least 2 defined over a number field has only finitely many points with coordinates in that field.

open.name: Hodge conjecture
open.gloss: On a smooth complex projective variety, every rational cohomology class of type \((p,p)\) is a rational combination of classes of algebraic subvarieties.

open.name: Resolution of singularities in characteristic p
open.gloss: Whether every variety over a field of positive characteristic has a resolution of singularities; open in dimension 4 and above.

open.name: Jacobian conjecture
open.gloss: A polynomial map from \(\mathbb{C}^n\) to itself whose Jacobian determinant is a nonzero constant has a polynomial inverse; open for every \(n\ge 2\).

name: Linear and multilinear algebra; matrix theory

page.hook: How do you solve a thousand linear equations at once, and what does a matrix do to space?
about: Linear algebra studies vector spaces and the linear maps between them, together with the matrices that represent those maps. Its starting point is the solution of systems of linear equations. From there it moves to determinants, eigenvalues, canonical forms of matrices, inner products, and bilinear and multilinear forms, including tensors.

Nearly every part of mathematics reduces some of its problems to linear ones, so the area serves as a common language. The basic theory over a field is classical. Current work concerns special classes of matrices, matrix inequalities, tensors and matrices over rings. Computation with large matrices is central to science, engineering, statistics and machine learning.

example.title: Fibonacci numbers from a matrix
example.text: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\). Then \(A^2=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(A^3=\begin{pmatrix}3&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}\): the entries of \(A^n\) are consecutive Fibonacci numbers \(1,1,2,3,5,8,\dots\) The eigenvalues of \(A\) are the roots \(\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\) and \(\psi=\frac{1-\sqrt5}{2}\) of \(\lambda^2=\lambda+1\). Diagonalizing \(A\) gives the formula \(F_n=(\varphi^n-\psi^n)/\sqrt5\) for the \(n\)th Fibonacci number, with \(F_1=F_2=1\).

objects.gloss: A set of vectors that can be added together and multiplied by scalars from a field.
A map between vector spaces that respects addition and scalar multiplication.
A rectangular array of numbers that represents a linear map in chosen bases.
A number attached to a square matrix; it is nonzero exactly when the matrix is invertible.
A scalar \(\lambda\) and nonzero vector \(v\) with \(Av=\lambda v\).
A scalar-valued function of two vectors that is linear in each; inner products are examples.
The vector space through which every bilinear map on a pair of spaces factors uniquely.

theorems.name: Rank-nullity theorem
theorems.statement: If \(T\colon V\to W\) is a linear map and \(V\) is finite-dimensional, then \(\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T=\dim V\).

theorems.name: Cayley-Hamilton theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(A\) be a square matrix over a commutative ring and \(p(t)=\det(tI-A)\) its characteristic polynomial. Then \(p(A)=0\). Cayley stated the theorem in 1858 and verified small cases; Frobenius gave a general proof in 1878.

theorems.name: Spectral theorem
theorems.statement: Every real symmetric matrix \(A\) can be written \(A=Q\Lambda Q^{T}\) with \(Q\) orthogonal and \(\Lambda\) real diagonal. Likewise every complex Hermitian matrix is diagonalized by a unitary matrix and has real eigenvalues.

theorems.name: Jordan normal form
theorems.statement: Every square matrix over an algebraically closed field is similar to a block diagonal matrix of Jordan blocks, and the blocks are unique up to their order.

theorems.name: Singular value decomposition
theorems.statement: Every real \(m\times n\) matrix \(A\) can be written \(A=U\Sigma V^{T}\), with \(U\) and \(V\) orthogonal and \(\Sigma\) an \(m\times n\) matrix that is zero off the diagonal and has nonnegative diagonal entries. Those entries are determined by \(A\) up to order.

theorems.name: Perron's theorem
theorems.statement: A square real matrix with all entries positive has a positive eigenvalue \(r\) that is a simple root of the characteristic polynomial and exceeds the absolute value of every other eigenvalue. It has an eigenvector for \(r\) with all entries positive.

open.name: Exponent of matrix multiplication
open.gloss: Can two \(n\times n\) matrices be multiplied using about \(n^2\) arithmetic operations, up to a factor \(n^{\varepsilon}\)? The best known exponent is below 2.38.

open.name: Hadamard conjecture
open.gloss: For every multiple \(n\) of 4 there is an \(n\times n\) matrix with entries \(\pm1\) whose rows are pairwise orthogonal.

open.name: Crouzeix's conjecture
open.gloss: For every complex square matrix \(A\) and polynomial \(p\), the spectral norm of \(p(A)\) is at most twice the maximum of \(|p|\) on the numerical range of \(A\).

subareas.name: Modules, bimodules and ideals in associative algebras
Representation theory of associative rings and algebras
Division rings and semisimple Artin rings
Radicals and radical properties of associative rings
Chain conditions, growth conditions, and other forms of finiteness for associative rings and algebras
Associative rings and algebras arising under various constructions
Hopf algebras, quantum groups and related topics
Associative rings and algebras with additional structure

page.hook: What changes in algebra when \(ab\) and \(ba\) are allowed to differ, as they do for matrices?
about: This area studies rings in which multiplication is associative but need not be commutative. The basic examples are rings of square matrices, the quaternions, group algebras, and rings of differential operators. A ring is understood largely through its modules, the objects on which it acts, in the way a group is understood through its representations.

Structure theory splits a ring into a radical and a semisimple part and classifies the simple pieces. Homological methods and Morita theory compare rings through their categories of modules. The area includes representations of finite-dimensional algebras by quivers, division algebras and the Brauer group, Hopf algebras and quantum groups, and it connects to group theory, algebraic geometry, operator algebras and mathematical physics.

example.title: The quaternions
example.text: Hamilton's quaternions are the expressions \(a+bi+cj+dk\) with real \(a,b,c,d\), multiplied using \(i^2=j^2=k^2=-1\) and \(ij=k\), \(ji=-k\). So the order of the factors matters. Still, every nonzero quaternion \(q\) has an inverse: with \(\bar q=a-bi-cj-dk\) one finds \(q\bar q=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2\), so \(q^{-1}=\bar q/(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)\). The quaternions form a division ring that is not a field.

objects.gloss: A set with addition and an associative multiplication that distributes over addition.
An abelian group on which a ring acts linearly, generalizing a vector space.
Additive subgroups closed under multiplication by ring elements on one side or on both.
A ring in which every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.
The set of elements that act as zero on every simple module.
A ring all of whose modules are direct sums of simple modules.
Two rings are Morita equivalent when their categories of modules are equivalent.

theorems.name: Frobenius's theorem on real division algebras
theorems.statement: Every finite-dimensional associative division algebra over the real numbers is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\mathbb{C}\) or the quaternions \(\mathbb{H}\).

theorems.name: Maschke's theorem
theorems.statement: If \(G\) is a finite group and \(k\) is a field whose characteristic does not divide the order of \(G\), then the group algebra \(k[G]\) is semisimple.

theorems.name: Wedderburn's little theorem
theorems.statement: Every finite division ring is commutative, hence a field.

theorems.name: Wedderburn-Artin theorem
theorems.statement: A ring \(R\) is semisimple, meaning that every left \(R\)-module is a direct sum of simple modules, if and only if \(R\) is isomorphic to a finite product of matrix rings \(M_{n_i}(D_i)\) over division rings \(D_i\). The numbers \(n_i\) and the rings \(D_i\) are determined up to order and isomorphism.

theorems.name: Skolem-Noether theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(A\) be a finite-dimensional central simple algebra over a field \(k\). Every \(k\)-algebra automorphism of \(A\) has the form \(x\mapsto uxu^{-1}\) for some invertible \(u\) in \(A\).

theorems.name: Jacobson density theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(M\) be a simple left module over a ring \(R\), and \(D\) the division ring of \(R\)-linear maps from \(M\) to itself. If \(x_1,\dots,x_n\in M\) are linearly independent over \(D\) and \(y_1,\dots,y_n\in M\) are arbitrary, then some \(r\in R\) satisfies \(rx_i=y_i\) for all \(i\).

open.name: Köthe conjecture
open.gloss: If a ring has no nonzero two-sided ideal consisting of nilpotent elements, then it has no nonzero one-sided ideal of that kind.

open.name: Kaplansky's zero divisor conjecture
open.gloss: The group algebra of a torsion-free group over a field has no zero divisors.

open.name: Dixmier conjecture
open.gloss: Every algebra endomorphism of a Weyl algebra over a field of characteristic 0 is an automorphism.

page.hook: What is left of algebra when \((ab)c\) need not equal \(a(bc)\)?
about: This area studies algebras whose multiplication is not assumed to be associative. The most studied are Lie algebras, in which the product is a bracket \([x,y]\) that changes sign when its arguments are swapped and satisfies the Jacobi identity. Other classes are Jordan algebras, alternative algebras such as the octonions, and super and infinite-dimensional versions of all of these.

Lie algebras arise as the infinitesimal form of continuous symmetry: the tangent space at the identity of a Lie group is a Lie algebra, and much of the group can be recovered from it. Classification proceeds through root systems and Dynkin diagrams, and representation theory through weights and characters. Infinite-dimensional examples such as Kac-Moody and Virasoro algebras, and quantum groups, are standard tools in mathematical physics.

example.title: The cross product
example.text: For vectors in space, the cross product satisfies \(a\times b=-b\times a\), and it is not associative. With the standard unit vectors, \((i\times i)\times j=0\) while \(i\times(i\times j)=i\times k=-j\). In place of associativity it obeys the Jacobi identity \(a\times(b\times c)+b\times(c\times a)+c\times(a\times b)=0\). This makes three-dimensional space a Lie algebra, the one that belongs to the group of rotations.

objects.gloss: A vector space with a bilinear bracket satisfying \([x,x]=0\) and the Jacobi identity.
The rule \([x,[y,z]]+[y,[z,x]]+[z,[x,y]]=0\), which replaces associativity.
A finite configuration of vectors, closed under certain reflections, that encodes a semisimple Lie algebra.
An associative algebra whose modules are the same as the representations of a given Lie algebra.
A commutative algebra satisfying \((xy)(xx)=x(y(xx))\), modeled on symmetric matrices.
An eight-dimensional real division algebra that is neither commutative nor associative.
A Lie algebra, usually infinite-dimensional, defined by generators and relations from a generalized Cartan matrix.

theorems.name: Classification of simple Lie algebras
theorems.statement: Every finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra over \(\mathbb{C}\) is isomorphic to exactly one of the classical algebras \(A_n\ (n\ge1)\), \(B_n\ (n\ge2)\), \(C_n\ (n\ge3)\), \(D_n\ (n\ge4)\) or one of the five exceptional algebras \(E_6,E_7,E_8,F_4,G_2\). The result is due to Killing, with gaps repaired in Cartan's thesis of 1894.

theorems.name: Hurwitz's theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(A\) be a finite-dimensional real algebra with identity, not assumed associative, with a positive definite quadratic form \(N\) such that \(N(xy)=N(x)N(y)\). Then \(A\) is isomorphic to the real numbers, the complex numbers, the quaternions or the octonions, so its dimension is 1, 2, 4 or 8.

theorems.name: Levi decomposition
theorems.statement: Every finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic 0 is the semidirect product of its largest solvable ideal and a semisimple subalgebra.

theorems.name: Weyl's theorem on complete reducibility
theorems.statement: Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over a field of characteristic 0 is a direct sum of irreducible representations.

theorems.name: Poincaré-Birkhoff-Witt theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(\mathfrak g\) be a Lie algebra over a field with a totally ordered basis \((x_i)\). Then the products \(x_{i_1}x_{i_2}\cdots x_{i_k}\) with \(i_1\le i_2\le\dots\le i_k\), including the empty product, form a basis of the universal enveloping algebra of \(\mathfrak g\).

theorems.name: Ado's theorem
theorems.statement: Every finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field of characteristic 0 is isomorphic to a Lie algebra of square matrices with the bracket \([X,Y]=XY-YX\).

open.name: Simple Lie algebras in small characteristic
open.gloss: The finite-dimensional simple Lie algebras over an algebraically closed field of characteristic \(p\) are classified for \(p>3\); the cases \(p=2\) and \(p=3\) are open.

subareas.name: General theory of categories and functors
Homological algebra in category theory, derived categories and functors

page.hook: What can you learn about a mathematical object from the maps going in and out of it alone?
about: Category theory studies mathematical structures through the maps between them. A category consists of objects, such as sets, groups or spaces, and morphisms, such as functions, homomorphisms or continuous maps, which can be composed. Functors carry one category to another, and natural transformations compare functors. Homological algebra, classified in the same area, studies chain complexes and the invariants derived from them.

The characteristic move is to define an object by a universal property, that is, by how it maps to or from everything else, and not by its internal makeup. Products, quotients, free objects and completions all arise this way, as limits, colimits or adjoint functors. The language organizes algebraic topology and algebraic geometry, and it is used in logic, computer science and mathematical physics.

example.title: One definition, many products
example.text: A product of objects \(A\) and \(B\) is an object \(P\) with maps to \(A\) and to \(B\) such that any object with maps to both factors through \(P\) in exactly one way. For sets this gives the set of pairs \((a,b)\). Now view the positive integers as a category with one arrow from \(m\) to \(n\) when \(m\) divides \(n\). The product of 4 and 6 is then 2, their greatest common divisor.

objects.gloss: A collection of objects and composable morphisms between them, with identities and associativity.
A map between categories that sends objects to objects and morphisms to morphisms, respecting composition.
A family of morphisms that compares two functors compatibly with every morphism.
Universal objects built from a diagram, such as products, pullbacks, sums and quotients.
A pair of functors \(F,G\) with a natural bijection between maps \(F(a)\to b\) and maps \(a\to G(b)\).
A category with kernels, cokernels and exact sequences, modeled on modules over a ring.
Functors, such as Ext and Tor, that measure how far a given functor is from being exact.

theorems.name: Yoneda lemma
theorems.statement: Let \(C\) be a locally small category, \(F\) a functor from \(C^{\mathrm{op}}\) to sets, and \(A\) an object of \(C\). Natural transformations from \(\operatorname{Hom}(-,A)\) to \(F\) correspond bijectively to elements of \(F(A)\), by sending \(\alpha\) to \(\alpha_A(\mathrm{id}_A)\).

theorems.name: Right adjoints preserve limits
theorems.statement: If a functor \(G\colon D\to C\) has a left adjoint, then \(G\) preserves every limit that exists in \(D\). Dually, a functor with a right adjoint preserves colimits.

theorems.name: General adjoint functor theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(D\) be a complete, locally small category. A functor \(G\colon D\to C\) has a left adjoint if and only if it preserves all small limits and satisfies the solution set condition: for each object \(c\) of \(C\) there is a set of morphisms \(f_i\colon c\to G(d_i)\) such that every morphism \(c\to G(d)\) equals \(G(h)\circ f_i\) for some \(i\) and some \(h\colon d_i\to d\).

theorems.name: Long exact sequence in homology
theorems.statement: A short exact sequence \(0\to A\to B\to C\to 0\) of chain complexes in an abelian category induces a long exact sequence \(\cdots\to H_n(A)\to H_n(B)\to H_n(C)\to H_{n-1}(A)\to\cdots\) of homology objects.

theorems.name: Mac Lane's coherence theorem
theorems.statement: Every monoidal category is monoidally equivalent to a strict monoidal category, one in which the associativity and unit isomorphisms are identities.

theorems.name: Freyd-Mitchell embedding theorem
theorems.statement: For every small abelian category \(\mathcal A\) there are a ring \(R\) and a full, faithful, exact functor from \(\mathcal A\) to the category of left \(R\)-modules.

open.name: Finitistic dimension conjecture
open.gloss: For a finite-dimensional algebra over a field, is there a finite bound on the projective dimensions of those finitely generated modules whose projective dimension is finite?

open.name: Comparing definitions of higher categories
open.gloss: Several definitions of weak \(n\)-category are in use, and it is not known in general that they are all equivalent.

page.hook: A Möbius band is twisted, yet two of them combine into something untwisted. How do you keep the books?
about: K-theory attaches abelian groups to a ring, a space or an algebraic variety by formally adding and subtracting the vector bundles or projective modules that live on it. The group \(K_0\) records these objects up to a stable form of equivalence, the group \(K_1\) records invertible matrices up to elementary operations, and higher groups continue the pattern.

There are several versions. Topological K-theory is a cohomology theory for spaces, governed by Bott periodicity. Algebraic K-theory of rings and schemes is much harder to compute and carries arithmetic information, such as class groups and special values of zeta functions. Operator K-theory applies to C*-algebras. The subject grew out of the Riemann-Roch theorem and remains tied to index theory, the topology of manifolds and motivic cohomology.

example.title: Two Möbius bands
example.text: Over the circle there are two real line bundles: the trivial one, a cylinder, and the Möbius band \(M\). They are not isomorphic. Yet the direct sum \(M\oplus M\) is isomorphic to the trivial plane bundle over the circle. In K-theory the class \([M]-[1]\) is therefore not zero, but twice it is zero. In fact the reduced real K-group of the circle is \(\mathbb{Z}/2\), generated by this class.

objects.gloss: A family of vector spaces that varies continuously over the points of a space.
A direct summand of a free module; the algebraic counterpart of a vector bundle.
The abelian group obtained from a commutative monoid by adjoining formal differences.
The Grothendieck group of finitely generated projective modules, or of vector bundles, under direct sum.
The group of invertible matrices of all sizes over a ring, made abelian.
Homotopy groups of a space built from the category of projective modules, as defined by Quillen.
A ring homomorphism from K-theory to rational cohomology; for finite complexes an isomorphism after tensoring with the rationals.

theorems.name: Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(f\colon X\to Y\) be a proper morphism of smooth quasi-projective varieties over a field. For every class \(x\) in \(K_0(X)\), \(\mathrm{ch}(f_*x)\,\mathrm{td}(T_Y)=f_*\bigl(\mathrm{ch}(x)\,\mathrm{td}(T_X)\bigr)\) in the rational Chow ring of \(Y\), where \(f_*x\) is defined as the alternating sum of the higher direct images.

theorems.name: Bott periodicity
theorems.statement: For a compact Hausdorff space \(X\), complex K-theory satisfies \(\tilde K(\Sigma^2X)\cong\tilde K(X)\), where \(\Sigma\) denotes reduced suspension. Equivalently, the homotopy groups of the infinite unitary group repeat with period 2. For real K-theory the period is 8.

theorems.name: Hopf invariant one theorem
theorems.statement: For \(n\ge 2\), a continuous map \(S^{2n-1}\to S^n\) of Hopf invariant one exists only when \(n\) is 2, 4 or 8. Adams proved this with cohomology operations; K-theory later gave a short proof.

theorems.name: Serre-Swan theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(X\) be a compact Hausdorff space. Sending a complex vector bundle to its module of continuous sections is an equivalence between the category of vector bundles over \(X\) and the category of finitely generated projective modules over the ring of continuous complex functions on \(X\).

theorems.name: K-theory of finite fields
theorems.statement: For the field \(\mathbb{F}_q\) with \(q\) elements and every \(i\ge 1\), Quillen's K-groups are \(K_{2i}(\mathbb{F}_q)=0\) and \(K_{2i-1}(\mathbb{F}_q)\cong\mathbb{Z}/(q^i-1)\).

theorems.name: Norm residue isomorphism theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(k\) be a field and \(\ell\) a prime different from the characteristic of \(k\). For every \(n\ge 0\), the norm residue map from Milnor K-theory \(K^M_n(k)/\ell\) to the Galois cohomology group \(H^n(k,\mu_\ell^{\otimes n})\) is an isomorphism.

open.name: Farrell-Jones conjecture
open.gloss: Predicts that the algebraic K-theory of a group ring can be computed from the virtually cyclic subgroups of the group; proved for many classes of groups, open in general.

open.name: Baum-Connes conjecture
open.gloss: Predicts that an assembly map computes the K-theory of the reduced C*-algebra of a group from the proper actions of the group; open in general.

open.name: K-groups of the integers
open.gloss: Whether \(K_{4i}(\mathbb{Z})=0\) for every \(i\ge 1\); this is equivalent to Vandiver's conjecture in number theory.

uses: Charges of D-branes in string theory

subareas.name: Structure and classification of infinite or finite groups
Special aspects of infinite or finite groups
Linear algebraic groups and related topics
Connections of group theory with homological algebra and category theory
Groupoids (i.e. small categories in which all morphisms are isomorphisms)

page.hook: What do the symmetries of a square, a shuffled deck of cards and a Rubik's cube have in common?
about: Group theory is the mathematics of symmetry. A group is a set with one operation that is associative, has an identity element and has inverses. The rotations and reflections of a square, the permutations of a list, and the integers under addition are examples. The area also covers looser structures such as semigroups, where inverses need not exist.

Finite groups are studied through their subgroups, their actions on sets and their representations by matrices, and the finite simple groups, the building blocks, have been classified. Infinite groups are often studied geometrically, by viewing a group as a space through its Cayley graph, or through presentations by generators and relations. Groups appear throughout mathematics and science, from Galois theory and topology to crystallography and particle physics.

example.title: Symmetries of a square
example.text: A square has eight symmetries: rotations by 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees, and four reflections. Performing one after another gives a symmetry again, so they form a group. Order matters: rotating by 90 degrees and then reflecting in the vertical axis gives a different result from reflecting first and then rotating. The four rotations form a subgroup, and 4 divides 8, as Lagrange's theorem requires.

objects.gloss: A set with an associative operation, an identity element and an inverse for every element.
A subset of a group that is itself a group under the same operation.
A map between groups that respects the operation.
A subgroup stable under conjugation, so that its cosets form a quotient group.
A rule by which each group element permutes a set, compatibly with the operation.
A group with more than one element whose only normal subgroups are itself and the trivial subgroup.
A description of a group by generators and the relations they satisfy.

theorems.name: Lagrange's theorem
theorems.statement: If \(H\) is a subgroup of a finite group \(G\), then the order of \(H\) divides the order of \(G\).

theorems.name: Sylow theorems
theorems.statement: Let \(G\) be a finite group and \(p^k\) the largest power of a prime \(p\) dividing \(|G|\). Then \(G\) has a subgroup of order \(p^k\), all such subgroups are conjugate, and their number is congruent to 1 modulo \(p\) and divides \(|G|/p^k\).

theorems.name: Structure of finitely generated abelian groups
theorems.statement: Every finitely generated abelian group is isomorphic to \(\mathbb{Z}^r\oplus\mathbb{Z}/n_1\oplus\dots\oplus\mathbb{Z}/n_s\) with \(r\ge 0\), each \(n_i>1\), and \(n_i\) dividing \(n_{i+1}\). The numbers \(r,n_1,\dots,n_s\) are uniquely determined.

theorems.name: Nielsen-Schreier theorem
theorems.statement: Every subgroup of a free group is free.

theorems.name: Feit-Thompson theorem
theorems.statement: Every finite group of odd order is solvable.

theorems.name: Classification of finite simple groups
theorems.statement: Every finite simple group is isomorphic to a cyclic group of prime order, an alternating group \(A_n\) with \(n\ge 5\), a simple group of Lie type, or one of 26 sporadic groups, where the Tits group is counted with the groups of Lie type. The proof fills thousands of pages by many authors; its last major part was published in 2004.

open.name: Amenability of Thompson's group F
open.gloss: It is not known whether Thompson's group \(F\) of piecewise linear maps of the interval is amenable.

open.name: Residual finiteness of hyperbolic groups
open.gloss: Is every hyperbolic group residually finite, that is, can each nontrivial element be detected in some finite quotient?

open.name: Finitely presented torsion groups
open.gloss: Is there an infinite group with finitely many generators and relations in which every element has finite order?

subareas.name: Locally compact groups and their algebras

page.hook: How do you do algebra and calculus at once on symmetries that vary smoothly, like rotations of a sphere?
about: A topological group is a group that is also a space, with continuous multiplication and inversion. A Lie group is one that is a smooth manifold with smooth operations, such as the rotations of space or the invertible \(n\times n\) real matrices. These groups describe continuous symmetry: symmetries that can be varied gradually, unlike the finitely many symmetries of a square.

A Lie group is studied through its Lie algebra, the tangent space at the identity, which turns many questions into linear algebra. Integration against Haar measure allows averaging over a group. Representation theory decomposes functions on the group, or on spaces on which it acts, in a way that generalizes Fourier series. The area connects to differential geometry, harmonic analysis, number theory through automorphic forms, and quantum physics.

example.title: Rotations of the plane
example.text: Rotations of the plane about the origin form a group: rotating by \(\theta\) and then by \(\varphi\) is rotating by \(\theta+\varphi\). Each is given by the matrix \(R(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\), which depends smoothly on \(\theta\), so the group is a Lie group shaped like a circle. Its velocity at \(\theta=0\) is \(J=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\), and every rotation is recovered as a matrix exponential, \(R(\theta)=\exp(\theta J)\).

objects.gloss: A group with a topology for which multiplication and inversion are continuous.
A group that is a smooth manifold, with smooth multiplication and inversion.
The tangent space at the identity with the bracket induced by the group law.
The map from the Lie algebra to the group that follows one-parameter subgroups for unit time.
A measure on a locally compact group that is unchanged by left translation.
A continuous action of the group on a Hilbert space by unitary operators.
A space on which the group acts transitively, such as a sphere under rotations.

theorems.name: Lie's third theorem
theorems.statement: Every finite-dimensional real Lie algebra is isomorphic to the Lie algebra of a simply connected Lie group, and that group is unique up to isomorphism. The global form stated here is due to Cartan.

theorems.name: Peter-Weyl theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(G\) be a compact Hausdorff group. The matrix coefficients of its finite-dimensional irreducible unitary representations span a dense subspace of the continuous functions on \(G\) with the uniform norm, and every irreducible unitary representation of \(G\) is finite-dimensional.

theorems.name: Closed subgroup theorem
theorems.statement: Every closed subgroup of a Lie group is an embedded submanifold, and hence is itself a Lie group.

theorems.name: Existence of Haar measure
theorems.statement: Every locally compact Hausdorff group carries a nonzero Radon measure invariant under left translation, and it is unique up to a positive constant factor. Haar proved existence in 1933 for second countable groups; the general case and uniqueness followed within a few years.

theorems.name: Pontryagin duality
theorems.statement: Let \(G\) be a locally compact abelian Hausdorff group and \(\hat G\) the group of continuous homomorphisms from \(G\) to the circle group, with the compact-open topology. Then the evaluation map from \(G\) to the dual of \(\hat G\) is an isomorphism of topological groups.

theorems.name: Solution of Hilbert's fifth problem
theorems.statement: If a topological group is locally Euclidean, meaning that it is a topological manifold, then it has a smooth structure making it a Lie group. This follows from work of Gleason and of Montgomery and Zippin.

open.name: Hilbert-Smith conjecture
open.gloss: A locally compact group that acts faithfully on a connected manifold is a Lie group; known for manifolds of dimension at most 3.

open.name: Unitary dual problem
open.gloss: Describe all irreducible unitary representations of a real reductive Lie group; an algorithm is known, but an explicit description is not.

subareas.name: Polynomials, rational functions in real analysis

page.hook: Can a curve be unbroken yet have no tangent anywhere, and when does integrating undo differentiating?
about: This area is the rigorous study of functions of one or several real variables: continuity, differentiation, integration, and the many ways in which these properties can hold or fail. It contains the theory behind calculus, together with finer topics such as monotone and convex functions, functions of bounded variation, classical inequalities, and generalized derivatives and integrals.

Arguments rest on the completeness of the real line and on careful estimates with inequalities, the method of epsilon and delta. A large part of the tradition consists of examples that mark the limits of theorems, such as a continuous function that has a derivative nowhere. The area is the base for measure theory, functional analysis, differential equations, approximation theory and optimization.

example.title: The devil's staircase
example.text: Define \(f\) on \([0,1]\) to be \(\tfrac12\) on the middle third \([\tfrac13,\tfrac23]\), then \(\tfrac14\) on \([\tfrac19,\tfrac29]\) and \(\tfrac34\) on \([\tfrac79,\tfrac89]\), and so on in the remaining gaps. The result extends to a continuous function that never decreases and climbs from 0 to 1. Its derivative is 0 on every interval where it is constant, and these intervals have total length 1. So integrating \(f'\) gives 0, not \(f(1)-f(0)=1\).

objects.gloss: A function whose values change by as little as desired when the input changes little enough.
The limit of the slopes of secant lines; the instantaneous rate of change.
The limit of sums of function values times lengths of small intervals.
A function that never decreases, or never increases, as its input increases.
A function whose graph has finite total rise and fall; a difference of two monotone functions.
A function that is the integral of its derivative; stronger than continuity.
A function whose graph lies on or below each chord joining two of its points.

theorems.name: Intermediate value theorem
theorems.statement: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and \(y\) lies between \(f(a)\) and \(f(b)\), then \(f(c)=y\) for some \(c\) in \([a,b]\).

theorems.name: Mean value theorem
theorems.statement: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) with \(a<b\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\), then there is a point \(c\) in \((a,b)\) with \(f'(c)=\frac{f(b)-f(a)}{b-a}\).

theorems.name: Fundamental theorem of calculus
theorems.statement: If \(f\) is continuous on \([a,b]\), then \(F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\) is differentiable on \([a,b]\) with \(F'=f\). Consequently, if \(G\) is any function with \(G'=f\) on \([a,b]\), then \(\int_a^b f(t)\,dt=G(b)-G(a)\).

theorems.name: Inverse function theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(f\) be a continuously differentiable map from an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^n\) whose derivative at a point \(a\) is an invertible linear map. Then \(f\) maps some open neighborhood of \(a\) bijectively onto an open neighborhood of \(f(a)\), and the inverse map is continuously differentiable.

theorems.name: Lebesgue's theorem on monotone functions
theorems.statement: Every monotone real function on an interval is differentiable at every point outside a set of Lebesgue measure zero.

theorems.name: Jensen's inequality
theorems.statement: Let \(\varphi\) be a convex function on an interval, \(x_1,\dots,x_n\) points of the interval, and \(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n\ge 0\) with sum 1. Then \(\varphi\left(\sum_i\lambda_ix_i\right)\le\sum_i\lambda_i\varphi(x_i)\).

subareas.name: Set functions, measures and integrals with values in abstract spaces
Set functions and measures on spaces with additional structure

page.hook: What is the length of a set too scattered to draw, and which sets can be given a size at all?
about: Measure theory makes precise the idea of size: length, area, volume, mass and probability. A measure assigns a number to each set in a suitable family, so that the size of a union of countably many disjoint pieces is the sum of their sizes. On this base it builds the Lebesgue integral, which applies to far more functions than the Riemann integral of calculus.

The decisive feature is good behavior under limits: under mild conditions, the integral of a limit of functions is the limit of the integrals. This makes spaces of integrable functions complete, a property on which functional analysis, Fourier analysis and partial differential equations rely. Probability theory is measure theory with total mass one. Geometric measure theory extends the ideas to fractal sets and to surfaces with singularities.

example.title: The rationals take up no room
example.text: List the rational numbers in \([0,1]\) as \(q_1,q_2,q_3,\dots\) and cover \(q_n\) by an interval of length \(\varepsilon/2^n\). The total length used is at most \(\varepsilon\left(\tfrac12+\tfrac14+\tfrac18+\cdots\right)=\varepsilon\). Since \(\varepsilon\) can be as small as we like, the rationals have Lebesgue measure 0. So the function that is 1 at rational points and 0 elsewhere has Lebesgue integral 0, although it has no Riemann integral.

objects.gloss: A family of sets closed under complements and countable unions; the sets that get a size.
A countably additive assignment of nonnegative sizes to the sets of a sigma-algebra.
The standard measure on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), extending length, area and volume.
A function for which the preimage of every interval is a measurable set.
An integral defined by slicing the range of a function instead of its domain.
Said of a property that holds outside a set of measure zero.
A notion of dimension, possibly not an integer, that applies to arbitrary subsets of a metric space.

theorems.name: Carathéodory's extension theorem
theorems.statement: A countably additive function with values in \([0,\infty]\), zero on the empty set, defined on an algebra of subsets of a set \(X\) extends to a measure on the sigma-algebra generated by that algebra. If the function is sigma-finite, the extension is unique.

theorems.name: Monotone convergence theorem
theorems.statement: If \(0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots\) are measurable functions on a measure space and \(f\) is their pointwise limit, then \(\int f_n\,d\mu\) increases to \(\int f\,d\mu\).

theorems.name: Dominated convergence theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(f_n\) be measurable functions converging almost everywhere to \(f\), and suppose \(|f_n|\le g\) for all \(n\), where \(g\) is integrable. Then \(f\) is integrable and \(\int f_n\,d\mu\to\int f\,d\mu\).

theorems.statement:
Let \((X,\mu)\) and \((Y,
u)\) be sigma-finite measure spaces and \(f\) a function on \(X	imes Y\) that is integrable for the product measure. Then \(\int_{X	imes Y}f\,d(\mu	imes
