theorems.name: Lebesgue differentiation theorem
theorems.statement: If \(f\) is locally integrable on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), then for almost every \(x\) the average of \(f\) over the ball of radius \(r\) centered at \(x\) tends to \(f(x)\) as \(r\to 0\).

theorems.name: Radon-Nikodym theorem
theorems.statement:
Let \(\mu\) and \(
u\) be sigma-finite measures on the same measurable space such that \(
u(A)=0\) whenever \(\mu(A)=0\). Then there is a measurable function \(f\ge 0\) with \(
u(A)=\int_A f\,d\mu\) for every measurable set \(A\), and \(f\) is unique up to sets of \(\mu\)-measure zero.

open.name: Kakeya conjecture
open.gloss: A compact set in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) containing a unit segment in every direction has Hausdorff dimension \(n\). Proved in the plane; a proof for \(n=3\) was announced in 2025; open for \(n\ge 4\).

open.name: Falconer's distance conjecture
open.gloss: If a compact set in \(\mathbb{R}^d\), \(d\ge 2\), has Hausdorff dimension above \(d/2\), then its set of distances has positive Lebesgue measure.

open.name: Erdős similarity problem
open.gloss: Is there, for every infinite set of real numbers, a set of positive Lebesgue measure that contains no scaled and shifted copy of it?

subareas.name: General properties of functions of one complex variable
Series expansions of functions of one complex variable
Entire and meromorphic functions of one complex variable, and related topics
Miscellaneous topics of analysis in the complex plane
Spaces and algebras of analytic functions of one complex variable
Universal holomorphic functions of one complex variable

page.hook: Why is a function with a complex derivative fixed everywhere by its values on one small circle?
about: Complex analysis studies functions of one complex variable that have a derivative in the complex sense. Such functions are called holomorphic. The condition looks mild but is very strong: a holomorphic function is infinitely differentiable, equals its Taylor series near every point, and is fixed everywhere on a connected domain by its values on any small disk. The area also covers meromorphic functions, conformal maps and Riemann surfaces.

The main tools are contour integrals, power series and the geometry of conformal maps, which preserve angles. Results often trade analysis for geometry or topology: integrals are computed by locating poles, and zeros are counted by winding numbers. The subject feeds number theory through zeta and modular functions, and supplies methods to potential theory, fluid flow, differential equations and the theory of algebraic curves.

example.title: A real integral by residues
example.text: The function \(1/(1+z^2)\) has poles at \(i\) and \(-i\). Integrate it along the real segment from \(-R\) to \(R\) and back over the upper half circle of radius \(R>1\). The loop surrounds only the pole at \(i\), where the residue is \(1/(2i)\), so the loop integral is \(2\pi i\cdot\frac{1}{2i}=\pi\). As \(R\) grows the half circle contributes less and less, so \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=\pi\).

objects.gloss: A complex-valued function on an open set of the plane that is complex differentiable at every point.
A function that is holomorphic except at isolated poles.
The coefficient of \(1/(z-a)\) in the Laurent expansion of a function around an isolated singularity \(a\).
A holomorphic map with nowhere vanishing derivative; it preserves angles and orientation.
Extending a holomorphic function to a larger domain; the extension is unique when it exists.
A connected one-dimensional complex manifold, the natural home of multivalued functions such as the square root.
A function holomorphic on the whole complex plane.

theorems.name: Cauchy's integral theorem
theorems.statement: If \(f\) is holomorphic on a simply connected domain \(D\), then \(\oint_\gamma f(z)\,dz=0\) for every closed rectifiable curve \(\gamma\) in \(D\).

theorems.name: Residue theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(f\) be holomorphic on a simply connected domain \(D\) except at finitely many points \(a_1,\dots,a_m\), and let \(\gamma\) be a closed rectifiable curve in \(D\) avoiding them. Then \(\oint_\gamma f\,dz=2\pi i\sum_k n(\gamma,a_k)\,\mathrm{Res}(f,a_k)\), where \(n(\gamma,a_k)\) is the winding number of \(\gamma\) around \(a_k\).

theorems.name: Liouville's theorem
theorems.statement: Every bounded entire function is constant.

theorems.name: Riemann mapping theorem
theorems.statement: Every nonempty simply connected open subset of \(\mathbb{C}\) other than \(\mathbb{C}\) itself is biholomorphic to the open unit disk. Riemann stated the theorem in 1851; complete proofs came later.

theorems.name: Picard's little theorem
theorems.statement: A nonconstant entire function takes every complex value with at most one exception.

theorems.name: Uniformization theorem
theorems.statement: Every simply connected Riemann surface is biholomorphic to exactly one of the Riemann sphere, the complex plane and the open unit disk.

open.name: Bloch's constant
open.gloss: Every holomorphic \(f\) on the unit disk with \(f'(0)=1\) maps some subdomain bijectively onto a disk of a universal radius \(B\); the best value of \(B\) is unknown.

open.name: Sendov's conjecture
open.gloss: If all zeros of a polynomial of degree at least 2 lie in the closed unit disk, is every zero within distance 1 of a critical point? This is known for all sufficiently high degrees.

subareas.name: Potential theory on fractals and metric spaces

page.hook: What temperature settles inside a metal plate when the temperature along its edge is held fixed?
about: Potential theory began as the study of gravitational and electrostatic potentials, which in empty space satisfy Laplace's equation. Its central objects are harmonic functions, their relatives the subharmonic and superharmonic functions, and the potentials generated by distributions of mass or charge. It asks how such functions behave, how they are determined by boundary values, and how to measure the size of small sets by capacity.

Methods include the mean value property, maximum principles, Green functions, and the Perron method of taking upper envelopes of subharmonic functions. There is a close dictionary with probability: harmonic functions are averages over Brownian paths, and capacity measures how likely a path is to hit a set. The area connects complex analysis, elliptic partial differential equations, several complex variables through plurisubharmonic functions, and Markov processes.

example.title: Averages of a harmonic function
example.text: The function \(u(x,y)=x^2-y^2\) is harmonic, since \(u_{xx}+u_{yy}=2-2=0\). Take the circle of radius 1 around the point \((2,1)\). The mean value property says that the average of \(u\) over this circle equals \(u(2,1)=3\). Check: with \(x=2+\cos t\) and \(y=1+\sin t\), the average of \(x^2\) is \(4+\tfrac12\) and the average of \(y^2\) is \(1+\tfrac12\). The difference is 3.

objects.gloss: A twice differentiable function \(u\) with \(\Delta u=0\).
An upper semicontinuous function whose value at each point is at most its average over small surrounding spheres.
The convolution of a mass distribution with the fundamental solution of the Laplacian.
The potential of a unit point charge in a domain whose boundary is held at potential zero.
A measure of the size of a set by the charge it can hold at bounded potential.
The distribution of the point where Brownian motion started inside a domain first hits the boundary.
A set so small that Brownian motion almost surely never hits it at positive times.

theorems.name: Mean value property
theorems.statement: If \(u\) is harmonic on an open set containing a closed ball, then the value of \(u\) at the center equals the average of \(u\) over the bounding sphere. Conversely, a continuous function with this property for all such balls is harmonic.

theorems.name: Maximum principle
theorems.statement: A harmonic function on a connected open set that attains its maximum at some point of the set is constant.

theorems.name: Harnack's inequality
theorems.statement: For every compact subset \(K\) of a connected open set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) there is a constant \(C\) such that \(\sup_K u\le C\inf_K u\) for all positive harmonic functions \(u\) on \(\Omega\).

theorems.name: Perron's method
theorems.statement: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be bounded and open and \(f\) continuous on \(\partial\Omega\). The pointwise supremum of all subharmonic \(u\) on \(\Omega\) with \(\limsup_{x\to\xi}u(x)\le f(\xi)\) for every \(\xi\in\partial\Omega\) is harmonic in \(\Omega\), and it has boundary value \(f\) at every regular boundary point.

theorems.name: Wiener's criterion
theorems.statement: A boundary point \(x\) of a bounded open set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n\), \(n\ge3\), is regular for the Dirichlet problem if and only if \(\sum_k 2^{k(n-2)}\,\mathrm{cap}(A_k)=\infty\), where \(A_k\) is the set of points \(y\notin\Omega\) with \(2^{-k-1}\le|y-x|\le2^{-k}\) and cap is Newtonian capacity.

theorems.name: Riesz decomposition theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(u\) be subharmonic on an open set \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) and not identically \(-\infty\) on any component. Then the distribution \(\mu=\Delta u\) is a positive Radon measure, and on every open set with compact closure in \(\Omega\), \(u\) is the sum of a harmonic function and the potential \(\int E(x-y)\,d\mu(y)\), where \(E\) is the fundamental solution with \(\Delta E=\delta\).

open.name: Dimension of harmonic measure in space
open.gloss: In the plane, harmonic measure always sits on a set of Hausdorff dimension at most 1. For domains in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) the largest possible dimension is unknown; it is known to lie strictly between 2 and 3.

name: Several complex variables and analytic spaces

subareas.name: Holomorphic functions of several complex variables
Geometric convexity in several complex variables
Complex spaces with a group of automorphisms

page.hook: Why can a holomorphic function of two complex variables never have an isolated singularity?
about: This area studies holomorphic functions of two or more complex variables and the spaces on which they live: domains in \(\mathbb{C}^n\), complex manifolds, and analytic spaces, which are allowed to have singular points. New phenomena appear that have no counterpart in one variable. Some domains force every holomorphic function on them to extend to a larger domain, and no analog of the Riemann mapping theorem holds.

Methods mix analysis, geometry and algebra. Plurisubharmonic functions and the inhomogeneous Cauchy-Riemann equations \(\bar\partial u=f\), solved with \(L^2\) estimates, carry the analytic side. Sheaves and their cohomology organize the passage from local to global, a language that was largely developed here. The subject overlaps with algebraic geometry over the complex numbers, with differential geometry through Kähler metrics, and with partial differential equations.

example.title: A removable point
example.text: Let \(f(z,w)\) be holomorphic on the ball \(|z|^2+|w|^2<1\) minus the origin. For \(|z|<\tfrac12\) and \(|w|<\tfrac12\) set \(F(z,w)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{|\zeta|=1/2}\frac{f(\zeta,w)}{\zeta-z}\,d\zeta\). This is holomorphic, also at the origin. When \(w\ne0\), the function \(f(\cdot,w)\) is holomorphic on the whole disk \(|\zeta|\le\tfrac12\), so Cauchy's formula gives \(F=f\). Hence \(f\) extends over the origin. In one variable, \(1/z\) shows that this fails.

objects.gloss: A continuous function on an open set of complex n-space that is holomorphic in each variable separately.
A domain carrying a holomorphic function that cannot be extended holomorphically across any boundary point.
An upper semicontinuous function whose restriction to every complex line is subharmonic.
A domain in \(\mathbb{C}^n\) with a continuous plurisubharmonic exhaustion function.
A complex manifold that can be embedded as a closed complex submanifold of some \(\mathbb{C}^N\).
A set that is locally the common zero set of finitely many holomorphic functions.
A sheaf of modules locally presented by finitely many generators and relations over the holomorphic functions.

theorems.name: Hartogs extension theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{C}^n\) be open with \(n\ge2\), and let \(K\subset\Omega\) be compact with \(\Omega\setminus K\) connected. Then every holomorphic function on \(\Omega\setminus K\) extends to a holomorphic function on \(\Omega\).

theorems.name: Weierstrass preparation theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(f\) be holomorphic near \(0\in\mathbb{C}^n\) and suppose \(f(0,\dots,0,z_n)\) vanishes to exact order \(k\) at \(z_n=0\). Then near \(0\) there is a unique factorization \(f=u\,P\), where \(u\) is holomorphic and nonvanishing and \(P=z_n^k+a_1(z')z_n^{k-1}+\dots+a_k(z')\) with \(a_j\) holomorphic in \(z'=(z_1,\dots,z_{n-1})\) and \(a_j(0)=0\).

theorems.name: Solution of the Levi problem
theorems.statement: A domain in \(\mathbb{C}^n\) is a domain of holomorphy if and only if it is pseudoconvex. Oka proved this for \(n=2\) in 1942; the general case followed in the early 1950s.

theorems.name: Oka's coherence theorem
theorems.statement: The sheaf of germs of holomorphic functions on \(\mathbb{C}^n\) is coherent.

theorems.name: Cartan's Theorems A and B
theorems.statement: Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a coherent analytic sheaf on a Stein manifold \(X\). Then every stalk of \(\mathcal{F}\) is generated by global sections, and \(H^q(X,\mathcal{F})=0\) for all \(q\ge1\).

theorems.name: Hörmander's existence theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{C}^n\) be a bounded pseudoconvex domain and \(f\) a \((0,1)\)-form with coefficients in \(L^2(\Omega)\) and \(\bar\partial f=0\). Then there is \(u\in L^2(\Omega)\) with \(\bar\partial u=f\) and \(\|u\|_{L^2}\le C\|f\|_{L^2}\), where \(C\) depends only on the diameter of \(\Omega\).

open.name: Boundary regularity of biholomorphic maps
open.gloss: Does every biholomorphic map between bounded domains in \(\mathbb{C}^n\) with smooth boundary extend smoothly to the boundaries? This is known for strictly pseudoconvex domains.

open.name: Green-Griffiths-Lang conjecture
open.gloss: On a complex projective variety of general type, do all nonconstant entire holomorphic curves lie in one proper algebraic subvariety?

page.hook: Which functions beyond sine and logarithm turn up so often that they earned names of their own?
about: Special functions are the particular functions that arise again and again in mathematics and physics: the gamma function, Bessel functions, Legendre and other orthogonal polynomials, hypergeometric functions, elliptic functions and many more. Most appear as solutions of specific differential or difference equations, or as integrals that cannot be expressed through elementary functions. The area catalogs their properties and the relations among them.

Typical results are identities, integral representations, recurrence relations, asymptotic expansions and addition formulas. Much of the structure is explained by symmetry: many special functions are matrix entries of group representations or solutions singled out by separation of variables. The subject serves number theory, combinatorics, probability and mathematical physics, and its \(q\)-analogs link it to partitions and quantum groups.

example.title: The factorial between the integers
example.text: The gamma function is defined for \(x>0\) by the integral \(\Gamma(x)=\int_0^\infty t^{x-1}e^{-t}\,dt\). Integration by parts gives the rule \(\Gamma(x+1)=x\,\Gamma(x)\), and \(\Gamma(1)=1\), so \(\Gamma(5)=4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1=24\). In this way the gamma function extends the factorial to numbers that are not integers. Substituting \(t=s^2\) turns the integral for \(x=\tfrac12\) into the Gaussian integral, which gives \(\Gamma(\tfrac12)=\sqrt{\pi}\). The rule then yields \(\Gamma(\tfrac32)=\tfrac12\sqrt{\pi}\approx0.886\).

objects.gloss: The function \(\Gamma(x)=\int_0^\infty t^{x-1}e^{-t}\,dt\), which interpolates the factorial.
A power series in which the ratio of consecutive coefficients is a rational function of the index.
A solution of \(x^2y''+xy'+(x^2-\nu^2)y=0\), which arises from the Laplacian in cylindrical coordinates.
A sequence of polynomials, one of each degree, mutually orthogonal for a given weight or measure.
A meromorphic function on the complex plane with two independent periods.
A rapidly converging series in exponentials of quadratic terms, from which elliptic functions can be built.
A \(q\)-analog of a hypergeometric series: the coefficient ratio is rational in \(q^n\).

theorems.name: Euler's reflection formula
theorems.statement: For every complex \(z\) that is not an integer, \(\Gamma(z)\,\Gamma(1-z)=\dfrac{\pi}{\sin \pi z}\).

theorems.name: Stirling's formula
theorems.statement: As \(x\to+\infty\), \(\Gamma(x+1)\sim\sqrt{2\pi x}\,(x/e)^x\), meaning that the ratio of the two sides tends to 1.

theorems.name: Euler's beta integral
theorems.statement: For complex \(a,b\) with positive real parts, \(\int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt=\dfrac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}\).

theorems.name: Gauss's summation theorem
theorems.statement: If \(\mathrm{Re}(c-a-b)>0\) and \(c\) is not a nonpositive integer, then \({}_2F_1(a,b;c;1)=\dfrac{\Gamma(c)\,\Gamma(c-a-b)}{\Gamma(c-a)\,\Gamma(c-b)}\).

theorems.name: Jacobi triple product identity
theorems.statement: For complex \(q,z\) with \(|q|<1\) and \(z\ne0\), \(\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}q^{n^2}z^n=\prod_{m=1}^{\infty}(1-q^{2m})(1+q^{2m-1}z)(1+q^{2m-1}z^{-1})\).

theorems.name: Favard's theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(p_{-1}=0\), \(p_0=1\) and \(p_{n+1}(x)=(x-b_n)p_n(x)-c_n\,p_{n-1}(x)\) with real \(b_n\) and \(c_n>0\). Then there is a positive measure on the real line with respect to which the polynomials \(p_n\) are mutually orthogonal.

open.name: Irrationality of Euler's constant
open.gloss: It is not known whether \(\gamma=-\Gamma'(1)\approx0.5772\) is irrational.

open.name: Painlevé transcendents
open.gloss: The six Painlevé equations define nonlinear special functions; their asymptotics and connection formulas are still being worked out in full.

Dynamic equations on time scales or measure chains

page.hook: If you know the rule for how a quantity changes at each instant, can you predict its whole future?
about: An ordinary differential equation relates an unknown function of one variable, usually time, to its derivatives. Newton's laws, population models and electrical circuits all take this form. The area asks when solutions exist and are unique, how they depend on initial data and parameters, how they behave as time goes to infinity, and what happens when conditions are imposed at the two ends of an interval.

Few equations can be solved in closed form, so the emphasis is on qualitative and asymptotic methods: phase portraits, stability analysis by linearization and Lyapunov functions, bifurcation theory, perturbation expansions and spectral theory of boundary value problems. Linear equations in the complex domain bring in monodromy and special functions. The field merges into dynamical systems, control theory and numerical analysis.

example.title: One solution or many
example.text: The equation \(y'=y\) with \(y(0)=1\) has the single solution \(y=e^t\). By contrast, \(y'=2\sqrt{|y|}\) with \(y(0)=0\) has many solutions for \(t\ge0\): the constant \(y=0\), or \(y=t^2\), or zero until any chosen time \(c\) and then \((t-c)^2\). The right side \(2\sqrt{|y|}\) is continuous but not Lipschitz at \(y=0\), and a Lipschitz condition is what the uniqueness theorem asks for.

objects.gloss: A differential equation together with the value of the solution at one starting time.
The picture of all solution curves of a system in the space of states.
A state at which the vector field vanishes, so the constant function is a solution.
A function that does not increase along solutions, used to prove stability without solving the equation.
A periodic orbit that is isolated among periodic orbits.
A differential equation with conditions imposed at both ends of an interval.
A matrix whose columns form a basis of the solutions of a linear system.

theorems.name: Picard-Lindelöf theorem
theorems.statement: If \(f(t,y)\) is continuous near \((t_0,y_0)\) and Lipschitz in \(y\), then the problem \(y'=f(t,y)\), \(y(t_0)=y_0\) has exactly one solution on some interval around \(t_0\).

theorems.name: Peano existence theorem
theorems.statement: If \(f(t,y)\) is continuous near \((t_0,y_0)\), then \(y'=f(t,y)\), \(y(t_0)=y_0\) has at least one solution on some interval around \(t_0\).

theorems.name: Lyapunov's linearization theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(x'=f(x)\) with \(f\) continuously differentiable and \(f(x_0)=0\). If all eigenvalues of the Jacobian \(Df(x_0)\) have negative real part, then \(x_0\) is asymptotically stable. If some eigenvalue has positive real part, then \(x_0\) is unstable.

theorems.name: Floquet's theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(x'=A(t)x\) with \(A\) continuous and periodic of period \(T\). Then every fundamental matrix has the form \(\Phi(t)=P(t)e^{tB}\), where \(P(t)\) is invertible and \(T\)-periodic and \(B\) is a constant complex matrix.

theorems.name: Poincaré-Bendixson theorem
theorems.statement: Consider a continuously differentiable vector field on an open subset of the plane. If the \(\omega\)-limit set of an orbit is nonempty, compact and contains no equilibrium, then it is a periodic orbit.

theorems.name: Sturm-Liouville theorem
theorems.statement: Consider \(-(py')'+qy=\lambda wy\) on \([a,b]\) with \(p,p',q,w\) continuous, \(p>0\), \(w>0\), and separated boundary conditions. The eigenvalues are real and simple and form a sequence \(\lambda_1<\lambda_2<\cdots\to\infty\). The \(n\)-th eigenfunction has exactly \(n-1\) zeros in \((a,b)\), and the eigenfunctions form an orthogonal basis of \(L^2([a,b],w\,dx)\).

open.name: Hilbert's 16th problem, second part
open.gloss: Is there a bound, depending only on \(n\), for the number of limit cycles of a planar polynomial vector field of degree \(n\)? This is open even for \(n=2\).

page.hook: How do heat, sound and water waves evolve, and can the equations that govern them ever break down?
about: A partial differential equation relates an unknown function of several variables to its partial derivatives. The Laplace, heat and wave equations are the classical models, standing for equilibrium, diffusion and vibration. They also represent the three main types: elliptic, parabolic and hyperbolic. The area asks whether solutions exist, whether they are unique, how smooth they are, and how they behave over long times or near singularities.

Modern work treats solutions as elements of function spaces such as Sobolev spaces and proves a priori estimates: bounds that any solution must satisfy. Tools include energy methods, maximum principles, Fourier analysis, variational methods and weak or distributional solutions. Nonlinear equations from fluid mechanics, geometry and relativity drive much of the research, and the field leans on functional analysis, harmonic analysis and differential geometry.

example.title: Heat smooths things out
example.text: The heat equation \(u_t=u_{xx}\) on a rod \(0\le x\le\pi\) with both ends kept at temperature 0 has the solutions \(e^{-n^2t}\sin(nx)\) for \(n=1,2,3,\dots\). Starting from \(u(x,0)=\sin x+\tfrac12\sin3x\), the solution is \(e^{-t}\sin x+\tfrac12e^{-9t}\sin3x\). The fine wiggle has decay rate 9 against 1 for the main term, so the profile quickly smooths to a single arch that slowly fades.

objects.gloss: The three main types of equation, modeled on the Laplace, heat and wave equations.
A function that satisfies the equation after integration against smooth test functions.
A space of functions whose weak derivatives up to a given order have finite integral norms.
A solution with a point source, from which other solutions are built by convolution.
A problem whose solution exists, is unique, and depends continuously on the data.
Curves or surfaces along which a hyperbolic equation carries signals and singularities.
A bound that every solution must satisfy, proved before solutions are known to exist.

theorems.name: Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem
theorems.statement: Consider an equation \(\partial_t^k u=F\), where \(F\) is an analytic function of \(t\), \(x\) and the derivatives of \(u\) of order at most \(k\) other than \(\partial_t^k u\), with analytic initial data \(u,\partial_tu,\dots,\partial_t^{k-1}u\) on \(t=0\). Then near each point of the initial surface there is exactly one analytic solution.

theorems.name: Maximum principle
theorems.statement: Let \(\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be bounded and open, and let \(u\) be twice continuously differentiable in \(\Omega\) and continuous on its closure. If \(\Delta u\ge0\) in \(\Omega\), then the maximum of \(u\) over the closure of \(\Omega\) is attained on the boundary.

theorems.name: Weyl's lemma
theorems.statement: If a distribution \(u\) on an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \(\Delta u=0\), then \(u\) is a smooth harmonic function.

theorems.name: Lax-Milgram theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(B\) be a bounded bilinear form on a real Hilbert space \(H\) with \(B(u,u)\ge c\|u\|^2\) for some \(c>0\). Then for every bounded linear functional \(f\) on \(H\) there is a unique \(u\in H\) with \(B(u,v)=f(v)\) for all \(v\in H\).

theorems.name: De Giorgi-Nash-Moser theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(A(x)\) be a matrix of bounded measurable coefficients that is uniformly elliptic. Then every weak solution \(u\in H^1_{\mathrm{loc}}\) of \(\mathrm{div}(A\nabla u)=0\) is locally Hölder continuous.

theorems.name: Leray's theorem on Navier-Stokes
theorems.statement: For every divergence-free initial velocity in \(L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)\), the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations have a weak solution defined for all positive times that satisfies the energy inequality.

open.name: Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness
open.gloss: Do smooth, rapidly decaying initial data for the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations always give a solution that stays smooth for all time?

open.name: Hot spots conjecture
open.gloss: For a convex planar domain, does the second Neumann eigenfunction of the Laplacian attain its maximum and minimum only on the boundary?

Approximation methods and numerical treatment of dynamical systems

page.hook: If you apply the same rule over and over, when is the long-run behavior predictable and when chaotic?
about: A dynamical system is a space of states together with a rule for how states evolve, either in discrete steps by iterating a map or continuously along a flow. The area studies long-term behavior: fixed and periodic points, attractors, stability, and sensitive dependence on initial conditions, popularly called chaos. Ergodic theory studies the same systems statistically, through invariant measures and time averages.

The subject classifies systems up to conjugacy, a change of coordinates that matches orbits, and looks for invariants such as entropy, rotation numbers and Lyapunov exponents. It draws on topology, measure theory, differential geometry and complex analysis, and it grew out of celestial mechanics. Ergodic methods have in turn solved problems in number theory and combinatorics, for example on arithmetic progressions and Diophantine approximation.

example.title: The doubling map
example.text: The doubling map sends a number \(x\) in \([0,1)\) to \(2x\) minus its integer part. In binary it deletes the first digit: \(0.1011\ldots\) goes to \(0.011\ldots\). The point \(\tfrac13=0.0101\ldots\) has period 2, since \(\tfrac13\to\tfrac23\to\tfrac13\). Two points that agree in their first 20 binary digits stay close for about 20 steps and then separate. Rational points are eventually periodic, while almost every point has a dense orbit.

objects.gloss: The sequence or curve of states visited from a given starting state.
A measure on the state space that is unchanged by the dynamics.
The property that every invariant set has measure zero or full measure.
A number measuring the exponential growth rate of distinguishable orbit segments.
The exponential rate at which nearby orbits separate or approach.
A closed invariant set that nearby orbits approach as time goes to infinity.
An invertible change of coordinates carrying one system to another.

theorems.name: Poincaré recurrence theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(T\) be a measure-preserving map of a finite measure space and \(A\) a measurable set. Then almost every point of \(A\) returns to \(A\) infinitely often under iteration of \(T\).

theorems.name: Birkhoff ergodic theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(T\) preserve a probability measure \(\mu\) and let \(f\) be integrable. Then the averages \(\frac1n\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}f(T^kx)\) converge for almost every \(x\). If \(T\) is ergodic, the limit is \(\int f\,d\mu\).

theorems.name: Denjoy's theorem
theorems.statement: An orientation-preserving \(C^2\) diffeomorphism of the circle with irrational rotation number \(\alpha\) is topologically conjugate to the rotation by \(\alpha\).

theorems.name: Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser theorem
theorems.statement: Take an analytic integrable Hamiltonian system satisfying a nondegeneracy condition and perturb it by a sufficiently small smooth Hamiltonian term. Then the invariant tori whose frequencies satisfy a Diophantine condition survive, slightly deformed. They fill a set of positive measure whose complement has measure tending to zero with the size of the perturbation.

theorems.name: Hartman-Grobman theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(p\) be a fixed point of a \(C^1\) diffeomorphism \(f\) of \(\mathbb{R}^n\) such that no eigenvalue of \(Df(p)\) has modulus 1. Then near \(p\) the map \(f\) is topologically conjugate to the linear map \(Df(p)\) near \(0\).

theorems.name: Sharkovskii's theorem
theorems.statement: Order the positive integers as \(3\triangleright5\triangleright7\triangleright\cdots\triangleright2\cdot3\triangleright2\cdot5\triangleright\cdots\triangleright4\cdot3\triangleright4\cdot5\triangleright\cdots\triangleright8\triangleright4\triangleright2\triangleright1\). If a continuous map of the real line to itself has a periodic point of least period \(m\) and \(m\triangleright n\), then it has a periodic point of least period \(n\). In particular, period 3 implies all periods.

open.name: Local connectivity of the Mandelbrot set
open.gloss: Is the Mandelbrot set locally connected? A positive answer would imply that hyperbolic maps are dense among complex quadratic polynomials.

open.name: Entropy of the standard map
open.gloss: Does the Chirikov standard map of the torus have positive metric entropy with respect to area for some parameter value?

open.name: Furstenberg's times 2, times 3 conjecture
open.gloss: Is Lebesgue measure the only non-atomic ergodic Borel probability measure on the circle invariant under both \(x\mapsto2x\) and \(x\mapsto3x\) modulo 1?

page.hook: Which functions satisfy f(x + y) = f(x) + f(y), and what does a rule linking each term to earlier ones force?
about: A difference equation relates the values of a sequence, or of a function, at shifted arguments, as in the Fibonacci rule \(a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}+a_n\). It is the discrete counterpart of a differential equation. A functional equation asks for all functions satisfying a given identity, such as \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\). The area studies the solutions of both kinds of equation, their growth, their stability and their oscillation.

Linear recurrences are handled with characteristic polynomials, generating functions and discrete analogs of calculus, with summation in place of integration. Functional equations need regularity arguments: a weak assumption such as measurability often forces the solutions to have a simple explicit form. The area borders dynamical systems, since iterating a map is a difference equation, and it touches combinatorics, special functions, numerical analysis and economics.

example.title: A formula for Fibonacci numbers
example.text: The Fibonacci numbers \(1,1,2,3,5,8,13,\dots\) obey \(a_{n+2}=a_{n+1}+a_n\). Trying \(a_n=r^n\) gives \(r^2=r+1\), with roots \(\varphi=\tfrac{1+\sqrt5}{2}\) and \(\psi=\tfrac{1-\sqrt5}{2}\). Matching the first two terms yields \(a_n=(\varphi^n-\psi^n)/\sqrt5\). For \(n=10\) this gives 55, the tenth Fibonacci number. Since \(|\psi|<1\), the number \(a_n\) is the integer nearest to \(\varphi^n/\sqrt5\).

objects.gloss: A rule expressing each term of a sequence through earlier terms.
The polynomial whose roots give the exponential solutions of a linear recurrence with constant coefficients.
The operator \(\Delta f(x)=f(x+1)-f(x)\), a discrete analog of the derivative.
The equation \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\), whose solutions are the additive functions.
The question whether every approximate solution of a functional equation lies near an exact one.
The equation \(f(g(x))=s\,f(x)\) for unknown \(f\), which linearizes iteration of \(g\).
A closed set of real numbers on which difference and differential equations are treated together.

theorems.name: Linear recurrences with constant coefficients
theorems.statement: Let \(c_k\ne0\). The complex sequences with \(a_{n+k}=c_1a_{n+k-1}+\dots+c_ka_n\) for all \(n\ge0\) are exactly \(a_n=\sum_i p_i(n)\,r_i^n\), where the \(r_i\) are the distinct roots of \(x^k-c_1x^{k-1}-\dots-c_k\) and each \(p_i\) is a polynomial of degree less than the multiplicity of \(r_i\).

theorems.name: Cauchy's theorem on additive functions
theorems.statement: Every continuous \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) with \(f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y)\) for all \(x,y\) has the form \(f(x)=cx\). The same conclusion holds if \(f\) is only assumed Lebesgue measurable.

theorems.name: Poincaré's theorem on recurrences
theorems.statement: Let \(a_{n+k}+p_1(n)a_{n+k-1}+\dots+p_k(n)a_n=0\) with \(p_i(n)\to c_i\) as \(n\to\infty\), and suppose the roots of \(x^k+c_1x^{k-1}+\dots+c_k\) have distinct absolute values. Then for every solution either \(a_n=0\) for all large \(n\), or \(a_{n+1}/a_n\) converges to one of these roots.

theorems.name: Bohr-Mollerup theorem
theorems.statement: The gamma function is the only function \(f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)\) with \(f(1)=1\), \(f(x+1)=x\,f(x)\) for all \(x>0\), and \(\log f\) convex.

theorems.name: Hyers's theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(f:E\to E'\) be a map between Banach spaces with \(\|f(x+y)-f(x)-f(y)\|\le\varepsilon\) for all \(x,y\). Then there is a unique additive map \(A:E\to E'\) with \(\|f(x)-A(x)\|\le\varepsilon\) for all \(x\).

theorems.name: Skolem-Mahler-Lech theorem
theorems.statement: For a sequence over a field of characteristic zero that satisfies a linear recurrence with constant coefficients, the set of indices where the sequence vanishes is the union of a finite set and finitely many arithmetic progressions.

open.name: Skolem problem
open.gloss: Is there an algorithm that decides whether a given integer linear recurrence sequence has a zero term? This is known only for recurrences of low order.

uses: Discrete-time models in biology and economics

subareas.name: Convergence and divergence of infinite limiting processes

page.hook: What does it mean to add infinitely many numbers, and can a divergent sum still be given a sensible value?
about: This area studies infinite sequences and series of numbers and functions: when they converge, how fast, and what can be done when they do not. Besides convergence tests it covers infinite products, continued fractions seen as limits, and multiple series. A large part is summability theory, which assigns generalized sums to divergent series through averaging procedures such as those of Cesàro and Abel.

Summability methods are usually given by infinite matrices or integral means, and the main questions are which methods are consistent with ordinary convergence and how they compare. Tauberian theorems run the other way, recovering convergence from summability under a side condition. These ideas began with Fourier series and with power series on the boundary of convergence, and they are used in number theory, approximation theory and functional analysis.

example.title: Averaging a divergent series
example.text: The series \(1-1+1-1+\cdots\) has partial sums \(1,0,1,0,\dots\) and does not converge. The averages of the first \(n\) partial sums are \(1,\tfrac12,\tfrac23,\tfrac12,\tfrac35,\dots\), which tend to \(\tfrac12\). So the series is Cesàro summable to \(\tfrac12\). Abel's method agrees: \(1-x+x^2-\cdots=\frac{1}{1+x}\) for \(|x|<1\), and this tends to \(\tfrac12\) as \(x\) increases to 1.

objects.gloss: A series whose partial sums approach a finite limit.
Convergence of the series of absolute values; it allows free rearrangement of terms.
Convergence that is not absolute, so the sum depends on the order of terms.
The average of the first n partial sums of a series.
Assigning to \(\sum a_n\) the limit of \(\sum a_nx^n\) as \(x\) increases to 1.
A method that gives every convergent series its ordinary sum.
A side condition on the terms under which summability implies convergence.

theorems.name: Riemann rearrangement theorem
theorems.statement: If a series of real numbers converges but not absolutely, then its terms can be rearranged so that the new series converges to any prescribed real number, or diverges to \(+\infty\) or to \(-\infty\).

theorems.name: Abel's theorem
theorems.statement: If \(\sum_{n\ge0}a_n\) converges with sum \(s\), then \(\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n\to s\) as \(x\) tends to 1 from below along the real axis.

theorems.name: Tauber's theorem
theorems.statement: If \(\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n\to s\) as \(x\to1^-\) and \(n\,a_n\to0\), then \(\sum a_n\) converges to \(s\).

theorems.name: Littlewood's Tauberian theorem
theorems.statement: If \(\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n\to s\) as \(x\to1^-\) and the sequence \(n\,a_n\) is bounded, then \(\sum a_n\) converges to \(s\).

theorems.name: Silverman-Toeplitz theorem
theorems.statement: An infinite matrix \((a_{nk})\) transforms every convergent sequence \((s_k)\) into a sequence \(t_n=\sum_k a_{nk}s_k\) with the same limit if and only if \(\sup_n\sum_k|a_{nk}|<\infty\), \(\lim_n a_{nk}=0\) for each \(k\), and \(\lim_n\sum_k a_{nk}=1\).

theorems.name: Wiener's Tauberian theorem
theorems.statement: If \(f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})\) has a Fourier transform with no real zero, then the translates of \(f\) span a dense subspace of \(L^1(\mathbb{R})\). As a consequence, if \(g\) is bounded and \((f*g)(x)\to A\int f\) as \(x\to\infty\), then \((h*g)(x)\to A\int h\) for every \(h\in L^1(\mathbb{R})\).

open.name: Flint Hills series
open.gloss: It is unknown whether \(\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{1}{n^3\sin^2n}\) converges. The answer depends on how well \(\pi\) can be approximated by rational numbers.

page.hook: How well can a complicated function be imitated by a polynomial of degree ten?
about: Approximation theory asks how well complicated functions can be replaced by simpler ones such as polynomials, rational functions, trigonometric sums, splines or wavelets. For a given function and a given family, it studies whether a best approximation exists, whether it is unique, how to recognize it, and how fast the error falls as the family grows. Asymptotic expansions, which approximate functions near a limit point, also belong here.

A recurring theme is that the speed of approximation mirrors smoothness: the smoother the function, the faster polynomials converge to it, and conversely. Proofs use explicit operators, moduli of continuity, extremal polynomials and duality from functional analysis. The area supplies the theoretical base for numerical analysis and has close ties to Fourier analysis, interpolation, and more recently to learning theory and compressed representations of data.

example.title: The best line for a parabola
example.text: Among all lines \(ax+b\), which stays closest to \(x^2\) on \([-1,1]\)? The answer is the constant \(\tfrac12\). The error \(x^2-\tfrac12\) equals \(\tfrac12,-\tfrac12,\tfrac12\) at \(x=-1,0,1\), so it reaches its largest size three times with alternating signs. Chebyshev's criterion says that this alternation marks the best choice. No line has maximum error below \(\tfrac12\).

objects.gloss: An element of a given family at the smallest possible distance from the target function.
The largest change of a function over any two points at most a given distance apart.
The polynomial \(T_n\) with \(T_n(\cos\theta)=\cos n\theta\); it has extremal properties on \([-1,1]\).
Choosing a simple function that matches the target at prescribed points.
A function made of polynomial pieces joined with a prescribed degree of smoothness.
A rational function whose power series agrees with a given series to the highest possible order.
A series, possibly divergent, whose partial sums approximate a function increasingly well near a limit point.

theorems.name: Weierstrass approximation theorem
theorems.statement: Every continuous real function on a closed bounded interval \([a,b]\) is a uniform limit of polynomials.

theorems.name: Chebyshev equioscillation theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(f\) be continuous and real on \([a,b]\). A polynomial \(p\) of degree at most \(n\) minimizes \(\max|f-p|\) among such polynomials if and only if there are \(n+2\) points \(x_0<\dots<x_{n+1}\) in \([a,b]\) where \(f-p\) takes the values \(\pm\max|f-p|\) with alternating signs. The minimizer is unique.

theorems.name: Jackson's theorem
theorems.statement: There is an absolute constant \(C\) such that every continuous \(2\pi\)-periodic function \(f\) can be approximated uniformly by a trigonometric polynomial of degree at most \(n\) with error at most \(C\,\omega(f,1/n)\), where \(\omega\) is the modulus of continuity of \(f\) and \(n\ge1\).

theorems.name: Bernstein's inverse theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(0<\alpha<1\) and let \(f\) be continuous and \(2\pi\)-periodic. If for every \(n\) the error of best uniform approximation of \(f\) by trigonometric polynomials of degree at most \(n\) is at most \(Cn^{-\alpha}\), then \(f\) is Hölder continuous of order \(\alpha\).

theorems.name: Müntz-Szász theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(0<\lambda_1<\lambda_2<\cdots\) be real numbers. The linear span of \(1,x^{\lambda_1},x^{\lambda_2},\dots\) is dense in the continuous functions on \([0,1]\) with the uniform norm if and only if \(\sum_k1/\lambda_k=\infty\).

theorems.name: Stone-Weierstrass theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(X\) be a compact Hausdorff space. Every subalgebra of the real continuous functions on \(X\) that contains the constants and separates the points of \(X\) is dense in the uniform norm.

open.name: Bernstein's constant
open.gloss: Let \(E_n\) be the error of best uniform approximation of \(|x|\) on \([-1,1]\) by polynomials of degree at most \(n\). The limit of \(2nE_{2n}\) exists and is about 0.2802; no closed form for it is known.

open.name: Approximation by neural networks
open.gloss: For which classes of functions of many variables do neural networks achieve approximation rates that avoid the curse of dimensionality? This is under active study.

page.hook: Can every signal be split into pure tones, and does adding the tones back always return the signal?
about: Harmonic analysis on Euclidean spaces studies how functions on the circle, the line or \(\mathbb{R}^n\) decompose into waves of pure frequency. Fourier series and the Fourier transform are the basic tools. The area asks in what sense a function equals the sum of its frequency components, how properties of a function such as smoothness and decay are reflected in its transform, and how operators act on these decompositions.

Much of the modern subject concerns bounds for operators: maximal functions, singular integrals such as the Hilbert transform, multipliers and oscillatory integrals. Standard techniques include interpolation, covering lemmas, decompositions into pieces localized in space and frequency, and wavelet or other time-frequency expansions. The results are basic working tools in partial differential equations, and they connect with number theory, geometric measure theory and signal processing.

example.title: The square wave
example.text: The square wave equal to \(1\) on \((0,\pi)\) and \(-1\) on \((-\pi,0)\) has Fourier series \(\frac{4}{\pi}\left(\sin x+\frac{\sin3x}{3}+\frac{\sin5x}{5}+\cdots\right)\). At \(x=\pi/2\) this gives \(1=\frac4\pi\left(1-\frac13+\frac15-\cdots\right)\), which is Leibniz's series for \(\pi/4\). Near the jump at \(0\) the partial sums overshoot by about 9 percent of the jump, however many terms are used. This is the Gibbs phenomenon.

objects.gloss: The expansion of a periodic function in sines and cosines, or complex exponentials, of integer frequencies.
The map sending \(f\) to \(\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,dx\), its amplitude at each frequency.
The product \((f*g)(x)=\int f(x-y)g(y)\,dy\), which the Fourier transform turns into multiplication.
The supremum of the averages of a function over all balls centered at a point.
An operator given by convolution with a kernel too singular to be integrable, such as the Hilbert transform.
An operator that multiplies the Fourier transform of a function by a fixed function.
A function whose translates and dilates form a basis localized in both position and scale.

theorems.name: Riemann-Lebesgue lemma
theorems.statement: If \(f\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\), then \(\hat f\) is continuous and \(\hat f(\xi)\to0\) as \(|\xi|\to\infty\).

theorems.name: Plancherel theorem
theorems.statement: With \(\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,dx\), one has \(\|\hat f\|_2=\|f\|_2\) for \(f\in L^1\cap L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)\), and the Fourier transform extends to a unitary operator on \(L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)\).

theorems.name: Hardy-Littlewood maximal theorem
theorems.statement: The maximal operator \(M\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) satisfies \(|\{Mf>\lambda\}|\le C_n\|f\|_1/\lambda\) for all \(\lambda>0\), and it is bounded on \(L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)\) for \(1<p\le\infty\).

theorems.name: M. Riesz's theorem
theorems.statement: The Hilbert transform is bounded on \(L^p(\mathbb{R})\) for every \(1<p<\infty\). The same holds for the conjugate function on the circle, and it follows that the partial sums of the Fourier series of any \(f\in L^p\) of the circle converge to \(f\) in \(L^p\) norm for these \(p\).

theorems.name: Calderón-Zygmund theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(Tf=K*f\) be bounded on \(L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)\), where \(K\) is differentiable away from the origin with \(|\nabla K(x)|\le C|x|^{-n-1}\). Then \(T\) is of weak type \((1,1)\) and extends to a bounded operator on \(L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)\) for \(1<p<\infty\).

theorems.name: Carleson's theorem
theorems.statement: The Fourier series of every square-integrable function on the circle converges to the function at almost every point.

open.name: Kakeya conjecture
open.gloss: Must a compact set in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) that contains a unit segment in every direction have Hausdorff dimension \(n\)? This holds in the plane, a proof for \(n=3\) was announced in 2025, and higher dimensions are open.

open.name: Fourier restriction conjecture
open.gloss: For which exponents does the Fourier transform of an \(L^p\) function on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) restrict to the unit sphere as an \(L^q\) function? The conjectured range is proved in the plane and open for \(n\ge3\).

page.hook: What becomes of Fourier analysis when the circle is replaced by an arbitrary group of symmetries?
about: Abstract harmonic analysis extends Fourier analysis from the circle and the line to general topological groups, chiefly the locally compact ones. Such a group carries a Haar measure, a notion of volume unchanged by translation, so functions can be integrated and convolved. The area studies the resulting function spaces and algebras, and how functions on the group, or on spaces it acts on, decompose into pieces governed by symmetry.

On abelian groups the building blocks are characters, and the theory centers on the dual group and Pontryagin duality. On nonabelian groups characters are replaced by irreducible unitary representations, which may be infinite dimensional. Methods come from functional analysis, Banach and operator algebras and measure theory. The area links representation theory, number theory through adelic groups, ergodic theory, and the study of group properties such as amenability.

example.title: Fourier analysis on four points
example.text: On the cyclic group \(\mathbb{Z}/4\) the characters are \(\chi_k(n)=i^{kn}\) for \(k=0,1,2,3\). Every function \(f\) on the group is a combination \(f=\sum_k\hat f(k)\chi_k\) with \(\hat f(k)=\frac14\sum_n f(n)\,i^{-kn}\). For \(f=(1,0,0,0)\) every coefficient is \(\tfrac14\). For \(f=(1,1,1,1)\) only \(\hat f(0)=1\) is nonzero. A function concentrated at one point is spread evenly over all frequencies, and conversely.

objects.gloss: A topological group, assumed Hausdorff, in which every point has a compact neighborhood.
A measure on a locally compact group that is invariant under left translation.
A continuous homomorphism from a group to the circle group of complex numbers of modulus 1.
The group of all characters of a locally compact abelian group, itself locally compact abelian.
A continuous action of a group on a Hilbert space by unitary operators.
The space \(L^1(G)\) with convolution as multiplication.
A group admitting a finitely additive, translation-invariant mean on its bounded functions.

theorems.name: Existence and uniqueness of Haar measure
theorems.statement: Every locally compact Hausdorff group has a nonzero left-invariant Radon measure, and any two such measures differ by a positive constant factor.

theorems.name: Peter-Weyl theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(G\) be a compact group. The matrix coefficients of its finite-dimensional irreducible unitary representations span a dense subspace of the continuous functions on \(G\) in the uniform norm, and \(L^2(G)\) is the Hilbert space direct sum of the spaces of matrix coefficients of the distinct irreducible representations.

theorems.name: Pontryagin duality
theorems.statement: For a locally compact abelian group \(G\), the natural map from \(G\) to the dual group of its dual group is an isomorphism of topological groups.

theorems.name: Plancherel theorem for abelian groups
theorems.statement: Let \(G\) be a locally compact abelian group with dual \(\hat G\). For a suitable normalization of Haar measure on \(\hat G\), the Fourier transform on \(L^1(G)\cap L^2(G)\) extends to a unitary operator from \(L^2(G)\) onto \(L^2(\hat G)\).

theorems.name: Bochner's theorem
theorems.statement: A continuous function on a locally compact abelian group \(G\) is positive definite if and only if it is the Fourier transform of a finite positive Radon measure on the dual group. Bochner proved the case \(G=\mathbb{R}\) in 1932.

theorems.name: Gelfand-Raikov theorem
theorems.statement: The irreducible unitary representations of a locally compact group separate its points: for every element other than the identity, some irreducible unitary representation sends it to an operator other than the identity.

open.name: Dixmier's unitarizability problem
open.gloss: A group is unitarizable if each of its uniformly bounded representations on Hilbert space is similar to a unitary one. Is every unitarizable group amenable?

uses: Fast Fourier transforms and signal processing

page.hook: How can a transform turn a differential equation into a problem of plain algebra?
about: An integral transform turns a function \(f\) into a new function by integrating it against a fixed kernel: \((Tf)(s)=\int K(s,t)f(t)\,dt\). The Laplace, Fourier, Mellin, Hankel, Hilbert and Radon transforms are the best known. The area studies which functions each transform accepts, how to invert it, and how it converts operations such as differentiation and convolution into simpler ones.

The guiding idea is to move a hard problem to a setting where it becomes easy, solve it there, and transform back. Differential equations become algebraic equations, and convolutions become products. Operational calculus makes this systematic by treating differentiation as an algebraic symbol. The subject also includes moment problems, which ask when a measure is determined by its moments. It supports differential equations, probability, signal processing and tomography.

example.title: Solving an equation with the Laplace transform
example.text: The Laplace transform \(F(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt\) sends \(f'\) to \(sF(s)-f(0)\). Apply it to \(y'+2y=0\) with \(y(0)=3\). The equation becomes \(sY-3+2Y=0\), so \(Y=\frac{3}{s+2}\). Since \(e^{-2t}\) has transform \(\frac{1}{s+2}\), the solution is \(y=3e^{-2t}\). The calculus has been replaced by solving one linear equation for \(Y\) and looking up a table of transforms.

objects.gloss: The fixed function of two variables against which the input is integrated.
The transform \(F(s)=\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt\), suited to initial value problems.
The transform \(\int_0^\infty x^{s-1}f(x)\,dx\), the Fourier transform on the multiplicative group of positive reals.
The collection of integrals of a function over all lines or hyperplanes.
A product of two functions that most classical transforms turn into ordinary multiplication.
A formula recovering a function from its transform.
The numbers \(\int x^n\,d\mu(x)\) attached to a measure \(\mu\).

theorems.name: Fourier inversion theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(\hat f(\xi)=\int f(x)e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,dx\). If \(f\) and \(\hat f\) both belong to \(L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\), then \(f(x)=\int\hat f(\xi)e^{2\pi ix\cdot\xi}\,d\xi\) for almost every \(x\).

theorems.name: Convolution theorem
theorems.statement: If \(f,g\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\), then \(f*g\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)\) and the Fourier transform of \(f*g\) is the product \(\hat f\,\hat g\). The analogous statement holds for the Laplace transform and convolution on \([0,\infty)\).

theorems.name: Lerch's uniqueness theorem
theorems.statement: If two continuous functions on \([0,\infty)\) of at most exponential growth have Laplace transforms that agree for all sufficiently large real \(s\), then the functions are equal.

theorems.name: Radon inversion
theorems.statement: A smooth rapidly decreasing function on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), \(n\ge2\), is determined by its integrals over all hyperplanes, and it can be recovered from them by an explicit formula. Radon treated the plane and three-space.

theorems.name: Hausdorff moment theorem
theorems.statement: A real sequence \((m_n)_{n\ge0}\) has the form \(m_n=\int_0^1x^n\,d\mu(x)\) for a positive Borel measure \(\mu\) on \([0,1]\) if and only if \((-1)^k\Delta^km_n\ge0\) for all \(n,k\ge0\), where \(\Delta m_n=m_{n+1}-m_n\). The measure is then unique.

theorems.name: Paley-Wiener theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(A>0\). An entire function \(F\) has the form \(F(z)=\int_{-A}^{A}f(t)e^{itz}\,dt\) with \(f\in L^2(-A,A)\) if and only if \(F\) is square integrable on the real axis and \(|F(z)|\le Ce^{A|z|}\) for all complex \(z\).

subareas.name: Integral equations with miscellaneous special kernels
Theoretical approximation of solutions to integral equations
Qualitative behavior of solutions to integral equations
Abstract integral equations, integral equations in abstract spaces

page.hook: What if the unknown in an equation is a function hidden inside an integral?
about: In an integral equation the unknown function appears under an integral sign. A Fredholm equation such as \(u(x)-\lambda\int_a^bK(x,t)u(t)\,dt=f(x)\) integrates over a fixed interval. A Volterra equation integrates only up to the current point \(x\), which suits processes with memory. The area studies existence and uniqueness of solutions, their dependence on the parameter \(\lambda\), and eigenvalue problems for the integral operator.

Many boundary value problems for differential equations can be recast as integral equations by means of Green functions or boundary layer potentials, often with better analytic and numerical behavior. Fredholm's study of these equations around 1900 led to Hilbert spaces, compact operators and spectral theory, so the subject is a parent of functional analysis. Singular kernels, as in the Cauchy and Wiener-Hopf equations, need methods from complex analysis.

example.title: A kernel that separates
example.text: Solve \(u(x)=x+\int_0^1x\,t\,u(t)\,dt\). The integral equals \(c\,x\) with the unknown number \(c=\int_0^1t\,u(t)\,dt\), so \(u(x)=(1+c)x\). Substituting back, \(c=\int_0^1(1+c)t^2\,dt=\frac{1+c}{3}\), hence \(c=\tfrac12\) and \(u(x)=\tfrac32x\). Because the kernel \(xt\) is a product of a function of \(x\) and a function of \(t\), the problem reduced to one linear equation for one number.

objects.gloss: The function \(K(x,t)\) that weights the unknown inside the integral.
An integral equation over a fixed domain; second kind means the unknown also appears outside the integral.
An integral equation whose upper limit of integration is the variable itself.
The series solution obtained by iterating the integral operator, analogous to a geometric series.
The kernel of the integral operator that expresses the solution in terms of the right-hand side.
An integral operator mapping bounded sets to sets with compact closure, as continuous kernels do.
An equation whose kernel is not integrable, so the integral is taken as a principal value.

theorems.name: Abel's integral equation
theorems.statement: If \(f\) is continuously differentiable on \([0,a]\) with \(f(0)=0\), then \(\int_0^x\frac{u(t)}{\sqrt{x-t}}\,dt=f(x)\) has the unique continuous solution \(u(x)=\frac1\pi\int_0^x\frac{f'(t)}{\sqrt{x-t}}\,dt\) on \((0,a]\).

theorems.name: Volterra's theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(K(x,t)\) be continuous for \(a\le t\le x\le b\). Then for every continuous \(f\) on \([a,b]\) and every complex \(\lambda\), the equation \(u(x)-\lambda\int_a^xK(x,t)u(t)\,dt=f(x)\) has exactly one continuous solution, given by the Neumann series.

theorems.name: Fredholm alternative
theorems.statement: Let \(K\) be continuous on \([a,b]^2\). Either \(u(x)-\lambda\int_a^bK(x,t)u(t)\,dt=f(x)\) has a unique continuous solution for every continuous \(f\), or the homogeneous equation has a nonzero solution. In the second case the solution space of the homogeneous equation is finite dimensional, and the equation is solvable exactly for those \(f\) with \(\int_a^bf\,v\,dx=0\) for every solution \(v\) of the transposed homogeneous equation.

theorems.name: Hilbert-Schmidt theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(K\) be a real square-integrable kernel on \([a,b]^2\) with \(K(x,t)=K(t,x)\). Then \(L^2[a,b]\) has an orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions of the operator \(u\mapsto\int_a^bK(\cdot,t)u(t)\,dt\). The eigenvalues are real, and the nonzero ones have finite multiplicity and can accumulate only at 0.

theorems.name: Mercer's theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(K\) be a continuous symmetric kernel on \([a,b]^2\) whose integral operator is positive semidefinite, with orthonormal eigenfunctions \(\varphi_n\) and eigenvalues \(\mu_n>0\). Then \(K(x,t)=\sum_n\mu_n\varphi_n(x)\varphi_n(t)\), with absolute and uniform convergence.

subareas.name: Topological linear spaces and related structures
Normed linear spaces and Banach spaces; Banach lattices
Inner product spaces and their generalizations, Hilbert spaces
Linear function spaces and their duals
Measures, integration, derivative, holomorphy (all involving infinite-dimensional spaces)
Topological algebras, normed rings and algebras, Banach algebras
Commutative Banach algebras and commutative topological algebras
Topological (rings and) algebras with an involution
Selfadjoint operator algebras (\(C^*\)-algebras, von Neumann (\(W^*\)-) algebras, etc.)
Methods of category theory in functional analysis

page.hook: What happens to linear algebra when the vectors are functions and the space has infinitely many dimensions?
about: Functional analysis studies vector spaces of infinite dimension that carry a notion of distance or convergence, and the linear maps between them. Typical examples are spaces of functions: continuous functions, square-integrable functions, or distributions. The main classes are Hilbert spaces, Banach spaces and more general topological vector spaces, together with algebras of operators and of functions built on them.

The subject takes geometric intuition from finite dimensions and tests where it survives. Completeness, convexity, duality and compactness in weak topologies replace finite-dimensional arguments. Its general theorems turn concrete problems about differential or integral equations into statements about linear operators. It is the common language of partial differential equations, quantum mechanics, probability and optimization, and it includes operator algebras with their links to topology and group theory.

example.title: A bounded sequence that will not settle
example.text: The space \(\ell^2\) consists of the real sequences \(x=(x_1,x_2,\dots)\) with \(\sum x_n^2<\infty\), and the length of \(x\) is \(\|x\|=\sqrt{\sum x_n^2}\). The unit vectors \(e_1=(1,0,0,\dots)\), \(e_2=(0,1,0,\dots)\) and so on all have length 1, and any two of them are at distance \(\sqrt2\). So this bounded sequence has no convergent subsequence, which cannot happen in finite dimensions. The closed unit ball of \(\ell^2\) is not compact.

objects.gloss: A normed vector space in which every Cauchy sequence converges.
A Banach space whose norm comes from an inner product, so angles and orthogonality make sense.
A linear map between normed spaces that is continuous.
The space of all continuous linear functionals on a given space.
The coarsest topology making all continuous linear functionals continuous; it has more compact sets than the norm topology.
A continuous linear functional on smooth compactly supported functions; a generalized function that can always be differentiated.
A norm-closed algebra of bounded operators on a Hilbert space that is closed under taking adjoints.

theorems.name: Riesz representation theorem
theorems.statement: Every bounded linear functional on a Hilbert space \(H\) has the form \(x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle\) for a unique \(y\in H\), and its norm equals \(\|y\|\).

theorems.name: Hahn-Banach theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(p\) be a sublinear functional on a real vector space \(X\) and \(f\) a linear functional on a subspace with \(f\le p\) there. Then \(f\) extends to a linear functional on \(X\) with \(f\le p\) everywhere. In particular, a bounded linear functional on a subspace of a normed space extends to the whole space with the same norm.

theorems.name: Uniform boundedness principle
theorems.statement: Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a family of bounded linear operators from a Banach space \(X\) to a normed space \(Y\). If \(\sup_{T\in\mathcal{F}}\|Tx\|<\infty\) for every \(x\in X\), then \(\sup_{T\in\mathcal{F}}\|T\|<\infty\).

theorems.name: Open mapping theorem
theorems.statement: A bounded linear map from a Banach space onto a Banach space sends open sets to open sets. In particular, a bounded linear bijection between Banach spaces has a bounded inverse.

theorems.name: Banach-Alaoglu theorem
theorems.statement: The closed unit ball of the dual of a normed space is compact in the weak-star topology.

theorems.name: Gelfand-Naimark theorem
theorems.statement: Every commutative unital C*-algebra is isometrically \(*\)-isomorphic to the algebra of continuous complex functions on a compact Hausdorff space. Every C*-algebra, defined abstractly, is isometrically \(*\)-isomorphic to a norm-closed \(*\)-subalgebra of the bounded operators on some Hilbert space.

open.name: Free group factor problem
open.gloss: Are the von Neumann algebras of the free groups on two and on three generators isomorphic?

open.name: Separable quotient problem
open.gloss: Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space have an infinite-dimensional separable quotient space?

subareas.name: Individual linear operators as elements of algebraic systems
Groups and semigroups of linear operators, their generalizations and applications
Equations and inequalities involving nonlinear operators
Linear spaces and algebras of operators

page.hook: Can an infinite matrix be diagonalized, and what plays the role of its eigenvalues?
about: Operator theory studies linear maps, called operators, on Banach and Hilbert spaces, along with some nonlinear ones. Differentiation, integration against a kernel and multiplication by a function are typical examples. The central concept is the spectrum, which generalizes the set of eigenvalues of a matrix. The area classifies operators by their spectral behavior and studies special classes: compact, self-adjoint, normal, Fredholm, and unbounded operators such as differential operators.

The aim is a structure theory comparable to diagonalization and Jordan form for matrices. Tools include the spectral theorem, functional calculus, resolvents, semigroups of operators that describe time evolution, and index theory. Fixed point theorems and monotone operators handle nonlinear problems. Quantum mechanics is built on self-adjoint operators, and the subject works closely with functional analysis, differential equations, complex function theory and operator algebras.

example.title: Two shifts
example.text: On the space \(\ell^2\) of square-summable sequences, the right shift \(S\) sends \((x_1,x_2,\dots)\) to \((0,x_1,x_2,\dots)\). It preserves length but has no eigenvalue: \(Sx=\lambda x\) forces \(x=0\). The left shift \(L(x_1,x_2,\dots)=(x_2,x_3,\dots)\) has the eigenvector \((1,\lambda,\lambda^2,\dots)\) for every \(|\lambda|<1\). Both operators have the closed unit disk as spectrum. A square matrix and its transpose share their eigenvalues; these two adjoint operators do not.

objects.gloss: A continuous linear map from a normed space to itself or to another normed space.
The set of scalars \(\lambda\) for which \(T-\lambda I\) has no bounded inverse.
The operator-valued function \(\lambda\mapsto(T-\lambda I)^{-1}\), defined off the spectrum.
An operator sending bounded sets to sets with compact closure; the closest relative of a matrix.
An operator on a Hilbert space equal to its own adjoint, the analog of a Hermitian matrix.
The dimension of the kernel minus the codimension of the range, when both are finite.
A family \(T(t)\), \(t\ge0\), with \(T(s+t)=T(s)T(t)\), describing evolution in time.

theorems.name: Riesz theory of compact operators
theorems.statement: Let \(K\) be a compact operator on a Banach space and \(\lambda\ne0\). Then \(K-\lambda I\) is injective if and only if it is surjective. Every nonzero point of the spectrum of \(K\) is an eigenvalue of finite multiplicity, and the nonzero eigenvalues can accumulate only at 0.

theorems.name: Banach fixed-point theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(f\) be a map of a nonempty complete metric space to itself with \(d(f(x),f(y))\le q\,d(x,y)\) for some \(q<1\). Then \(f\) has exactly one fixed point, and the iterates \(f^n(x)\) converge to it from every starting point \(x\).

theorems.name: Spectral theorem
theorems.statement: Every bounded self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space is unitarily equivalent to the operator of multiplication by a bounded real measurable function on \(L^2(\mu)\) for some measure space. The same holds for unbounded self-adjoint operators, with a real measurable function that need not be bounded.

theorems.name: Stone's theorem
theorems.statement: The strongly continuous one-parameter groups of unitary operators on a Hilbert space are exactly the groups \(U(t)=e^{itA}\) with \(A\) a self-adjoint operator, possibly unbounded. The operator \(A\) is determined by the group.

theorems.name: Hille-Yosida theorem
theorems.statement: A linear operator \(A\) on a Banach space generates a strongly continuous semigroup of contractions if and only if \(A\) is closed and densely defined and, for every \(\lambda>0\), the operator \(\lambda I-A\) has a bounded inverse of norm at most \(1/\lambda\).

theorems.name: Atkinson's theorem
theorems.statement: A bounded operator on a Hilbert space is Fredholm if and only if it is invertible modulo the compact operators.

open.name: Invariant subspace problem
open.gloss: Does every bounded operator on an infinite-dimensional separable complex Hilbert space have a closed invariant subspace other than zero and the whole space? Counterexamples exist on some Banach spaces.

name: Calculus of variations and optimal control; optimization

subareas.name: Existence theories in calculus of variations and optimal control
Miscellaneous topics in calculus of variations and optimal control
Variational methods for eigenvalues of operators

page.hook: Among all curves joining two points, which one lets a bead slide down in the least time?
about: The calculus of variations seeks functions, curves or surfaces that make a given quantity, such as length, area, energy or travel time, as small or as large as possible. The unknown is a whole function rather than a number. Optimal control is the version in which a system evolving in time is steered by chosen inputs so as to minimize a cost. The area also covers the general theory of optimality conditions.

A minimizer satisfies a differential equation, the Euler-Lagrange equation, much as an ordinary function has zero derivative at a minimum. The direct method instead proves existence by compactness and lower semicontinuity in suitable function spaces, after which regularity must be shown. Convexity, duality and geometric measure theory are standard tools. Many laws of physics are variational principles, which ties the area to mechanics, partial differential equations and geometry.

example.title: Why the straight line is shortest
example.text: Consider graphs \(y(x)\) from \((0,0)\) to \((1,1)\). The length is \(\int_0^1\sqrt{1+y'^2}\,dx\). The Euler-Lagrange equation for this integrand says that \(y'/\sqrt{1+y'^2}\) is constant, so \(y'\) is constant and \(y=x\), of length \(\sqrt2\approx1.414\). For comparison, the parabola \(y=x^2\) between the same points has length about \(1.479\).

objects.gloss: A rule assigning a number to each function, such as the length of its graph.
The differential equation that a smooth minimizer of an integral functional must satisfy.
Proving that a minimizer exists by taking a minimizing sequence and using compactness with lower semicontinuity.
An auxiliary variable that turns a constrained extremum problem into an unconstrained one.
The optimal cost as a function of the starting state; it satisfies the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation.
A surface with zero mean curvature, a critical point of the area functional.
A notion of convergence of functionals under which minimizers converge to minimizers.

theorems.name: Euler-Lagrange equation
theorems.statement: Let \(L(x,y,p)\) be twice continuously differentiable. If a twice continuously differentiable \(y\) minimizes \(\int_a^bL(x,y,y')\,dx\) among such functions with the same endpoint values, then \(\frac{d}{dx}L_p(x,y,y')=L_y(x,y,y')\) on \([a,b]\).

theorems.name: Noether's theorem
theorems.statement: If the action integral of a Lagrangian system is invariant under a one-parameter group of smooth transformations, then there is an explicitly given quantity that is constant along every solution of the Euler-Lagrange equations.

theorems.name: Tonelli's existence theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(L(x,y,p)\) be continuous, convex in \(p\), and satisfy \(L\ge c|p|^q-C\) for some \(c>0\) and \(q>1\). Then \(\int_a^bL(x,y,y')\,dx\) attains its minimum over all absolutely continuous functions \(y\) on \([a,b]\) with prescribed values at \(a\) and \(b\).

theorems.name: Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions
theorems.statement:
Let \(x^*\) be a local minimum of a smooth \(f\) subject to smooth constraints \(g_i\le0\) and \(h_j=0\), and suppose a constraint qualification holds at \(x^*\). Then there are multipliers \(\mu_i\ge0\) and \(\lambda_j\) with \(
abla f+\sum_i\mu_i
abla g_i+\sum_j\lambda_j
abla h_j=0\) at \(x^*\) and \(\mu_i\,g_i(x^*)=0\) for all \(i\).

theorems.name: Pontryagin maximum principle
theorems.statement: Let \(u^*\) be an optimal control for minimizing \(\int\ell(x,u)\,dt\) subject to \(x'=f(x,u)\). Then there are a constant \(p_0\ge0\) and a costate \(p(t)\), not both zero, with \(p'=-\partial H/\partial x\) for \(H=p\cdot f(x,u)-p_0\,\ell(x,u)\), such that at almost every time \(u^*(t)\) maximizes \(H\) over the admissible control values.

theorems.name: Douglas-Radó theorem
theorems.statement: Every rectifiable Jordan curve in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) bounds a surface of the type of the disk that has least area among all such surfaces. This solved Plateau's problem around 1930.

open.name: Morrey's conjecture in dimension two
open.gloss: For functions of \(2\times2\) matrices, does rank-one convexity imply quasiconvexity? In higher dimensions the answer is no.

open.name: Mumford-Shah conjecture
open.gloss: Is the edge set of every minimizer of the Mumford-Shah functional in the plane a finite union of smooth arcs?

subareas.name: Finite geometry and special incidence structures
Classical or axiomatic geometry and physics

page.hook: What can be said about points and lines if the parallel axiom is dropped or changed?
about: This area covers geometry in the classical and axiomatic sense: Euclidean, affine, projective, hyperbolic and elliptic geometry, and the abstract study of points, lines and incidence. It includes finite geometries with only finitely many points, geometries coordinatized by fields or rings, and metric geometry based on distance alone. Questions concern what follows from which axioms, which configurations exist, and which transformations preserve the structure.

Two methods run side by side. The synthetic one argues from axioms and figures. The analytic one introduces coordinates and uses algebra; a central insight is that geometric axioms correspond to algebraic laws of the coordinate system. Following Klein, a geometry is also studied through its group of symmetries. The area connects to group theory, to combinatorics through finite planes and designs, to algebraic geometry, and to differential geometry.

example.title: A plane with seven points
example.text: The smallest projective plane has 7 points and 7 lines. Label the points \(1\) to \(7\) and take as lines the triples \(124, 235, 346, 457, 561, 672, 713\). Every line holds 3 points, every point lies on 3 lines, any two points lie on exactly one line, and any two lines meet in exactly one point. No two lines are parallel. This is the Fano plane, coordinatized by the field with two elements.

objects.gloss: Sets of points and lines with a relation saying which points lie on which lines.
An incidence structure in which two points lie on one line and two lines meet in one point.
An incidence structure in which two points span one line and parallels exist and are unique.
The plane geometry in which through a point off a line there pass many lines missing it.
A map that preserves all distances.
A bijection of the points of a geometry that maps lines onto lines.
The quantity \(\frac{(a-c)(b-d)}{(a-d)(b-c)}\) of four points on a line, invariant under projective maps.

theorems.name: Pythagorean theorem
theorems.statement: In a right triangle of the Euclidean plane with legs \(a,b\) and hypotenuse \(c\), \(a^2+b^2=c^2\). Conversely, a triangle whose sides satisfy this relation has a right angle opposite \(c\).

theorems.name: Desargues's theorem
theorems.statement: In a projective space of dimension at least 3, and in any projective plane over a division ring, two triangles that are in perspective from a point are in perspective from a line. Some projective planes do not satisfy it.

theorems.name: Pappus's theorem
theorems.statement: In a projective plane over a field, let \(A,B,C\) lie on one line and \(A',B',C'\) on another. Then the points \(AB'\cap A'B\), \(AC'\cap A'C\) and \(BC'\cap B'C\) are collinear. A plane over a division ring has this property if and only if the ring is commutative.

theorems.name: Fundamental theorem of projective geometry
theorems.statement: Let \(K\) be a division ring and \(n\ge2\). Every collineation of the projective space of dimension \(n\) over \(K\) is induced by a semilinear bijection of \(K^{n+1}\).

theorems.name: Gauss-Wantzel theorem
theorems.statement: A regular polygon with \(n\) sides can be constructed with straightedge and compass if and only if \(n\) is a power of 2 times a product of distinct Fermat primes. Gauss proved sufficiency in 1796 and Wantzel proved necessity in 1837.

theorems.name: Consistency of hyperbolic geometry
theorems.statement: Beltrami constructed models of the hyperbolic plane within Euclidean geometry. Hence, if Euclidean geometry is consistent, the parallel postulate cannot be derived from the remaining axioms of Euclidean geometry.

open.name: Prime power conjecture
open.gloss: Is the order of every finite projective plane a power of a prime? Order 10 has been excluded by computer search; order 12 is undecided.

open.name: Planes of prime order
open.gloss: Is every projective plane of prime order isomorphic to the plane over the field with that many elements?

uses: Coding theory and design of experiments

page.hook: How densely can equal balls be packed, and what shapes can a polyhedron take?
about: Convex geometry studies convex sets, those containing the whole segment between any two of their points, along with their volumes, surface areas, sections and projections. Discrete geometry studies arrangements of finitely or countably many geometric objects: packings of balls, tilings of space, configurations of points and lines, and polytopes, the higher-dimensional versions of polygons and polyhedra. Typical questions are extremal: which arrangement is densest, smallest or most numerous?

The subject mixes geometric inequalities, combinatorial counting and linear algebra, with input from analysis, topology and probability, and in recent decades from computer-assisted proof. Convex bodies in high dimensions show behavior that links the field to functional analysis. Polytopes tie it to linear programming and algebraic geometry, lattices tie it to number theory, and its combinatorial side underlies computational geometry.

example.title: Counting on a polyhedron
example.text: A cube has \(V=8\) vertices, \(E=12\) edges and \(F=6\) faces, and \(V-E+F=2\). An octahedron gives \(6-12+8=2\) and a dodecahedron \(20-30+12=2\). Euler's formula says this holds for every convex polyhedron. A quick consequence: every face has at least three edges and every edge lies on two faces, so \(3F\le2E\), which gives \(E\le3V-6\). A convex polyhedron with 6 vertices has at most 12 edges.

objects.gloss: A set that contains the segment joining any two of its points.
The smallest convex set containing a given set.
The convex hull of finitely many points; in three dimensions, a convex polyhedron.
The set of all integer combinations of a basis of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
An arrangement of copies of a body whose interiors do not overlap.
A covering of space by bodies whose interiors do not overlap.
The coefficients of the polynomial giving the volume of a weighted sum of convex bodies.

theorems.name: Euler's polyhedron formula
theorems.statement: For every convex polyhedron in three-dimensional space with \(V\) vertices, \(E\) edges and \(F\) faces, \(V-E+F=2\).

theorems.name: Minkowski's convex body theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(\Lambda\) be a lattice in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(K\) a convex set symmetric about the origin with volume greater than \(2^n\det\Lambda\). Then \(K\) contains a point of \(\Lambda\) other than the origin.
