theorems.name: Brunn-Minkowski inequality
theorems.statement: For nonempty compact sets \(A,B\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(A+B=\{a+b\}\), \(\mathrm{vol}(A+B)^{1/n}\ge\mathrm{vol}(A)^{1/n}+\mathrm{vol}(B)^{1/n}\).

theorems.name: Helly's theorem
theorems.statement: Let a finite family of at least \(d+1\) convex sets in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) be given. If every \(d+1\) of them have a common point, then all of them have a common point.

theorems.name: Upper bound theorem
theorems.statement: Among all convex polytopes of dimension \(d\) with \(n\) vertices, the cyclic polytope has the largest number of faces of every dimension.

theorems.name: Kepler conjecture
theorems.statement: No packing of equal balls in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) has density greater than \(\pi/\sqrt{18}\approx0.7405\), the density of the face-centered cubic packing. The proof was announced in 1998 and published in 2005.

open.name: Densest sphere packings
open.gloss: The greatest density of a packing of equal balls is known only in dimensions 1, 2, 3, 8 and 24.

open.name: Mahler's conjecture
open.gloss: Among convex bodies symmetric about the origin, is the product of the volumes of the body and its polar smallest for the cube? This is proved up to dimension 3.

open.name: Hadwiger's covering conjecture
open.gloss: Can every convex body in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) be covered by \(2^n\) smaller homothetic copies of itself? This is open for \(n\ge3\).

subareas.name: Applications of differential geometry to sciences and engineering

page.hook: How can an ant living on a surface tell, without ever leaving it, whether the surface is curved?
about: Differential geometry applies calculus to curved spaces: curves, surfaces and their higher-dimensional versions, smooth manifolds. Its basic question is how to define and measure curvature, and what curvature implies about shape. A Riemannian metric gives lengths and angles on a manifold, and from it come geodesics, volume and curvature. The area also studies other structures on manifolds, such as symplectic, complex, contact and Lorentzian ones.

Methods combine tensor calculus, connections and differential forms with differential equations and topology. A recurring theme is the passage from local to global: bounds on curvature at each point constrain the topology and size of the whole space. Geometric flows deform a shape in order to improve it. General relativity models gravity as curvature of spacetime, and gauge theories in physics use connections on bundles, so exchange with physics is constant.

example.title: A triangle with three right angles
example.text: On a sphere of radius 1, draw a triangle with one corner at the north pole and two on the equator, a quarter turn apart. Its sides are arcs of great circles and all three angles are right angles, so they sum to \(270^\circ\), not \(180^\circ\). The excess, \(\pi/2\) in radians, equals the area of the triangle, which is one eighth of \(4\pi\). The excess measures the curvature enclosed: here the Gaussian curvature is 1.

objects.gloss: A space that near every point looks like Euclidean space, with smooth changes of coordinates.
A smoothly varying inner product on the tangent spaces, giving lengths and angles.
A curve with zero acceleration; short pieces of it are shortest paths.
A rule for differentiating vector fields, which defines parallel transport along curves.
The tensor recording how parallel transport around small loops fails to return vectors unchanged.
The product of the two principal curvatures of a surface at a point.
A closed nondegenerate differential 2-form, the geometric structure of classical mechanics.

theorems.name: Theorema Egregium
theorems.statement: The Gaussian curvature of a surface in \(\mathbb{R}^3\) is determined by the first fundamental form alone. Hence it is preserved by local isometries.

theorems.name: Gauss-Bonnet theorem
theorems.statement: For a compact oriented Riemannian surface \(M\) without boundary, with Gaussian curvature \(K\) and Euler characteristic \(\chi(M)\), \(\int_MK\,dA=2\pi\chi(M)\).

theorems.name: Fundamental theorem of Riemannian geometry
theorems.statement: On every Riemannian manifold there is exactly one connection that is torsion-free and compatible with the metric, the Levi-Civita connection.

theorems.name: Hopf-Rinow theorem
theorems.statement: For a connected Riemannian manifold the following are equivalent: it is complete as a metric space; every geodesic extends to all values of its parameter; closed bounded subsets are compact. When they hold, any two points are joined by a geodesic of least length.

theorems.name: Bonnet-Myers theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(M\) be a complete Riemannian manifold of dimension \(n\) whose Ricci curvature satisfies \(\mathrm{Ric}\ge(n-1)k\) for a constant \(k>0\). Then \(M\) is compact with diameter at most \(\pi/\sqrt{k}\), and its fundamental group is finite.

theorems.name: Nash embedding theorem
theorems.statement: Every smooth Riemannian manifold admits a smooth isometric embedding into a Euclidean space of sufficiently high dimension.

open.name: Hopf's product question
open.gloss: Does \(S^2\times S^2\) carry a Riemannian metric of positive sectional curvature?

open.name: Complex structure on the six-sphere
open.gloss: Is there an integrable complex structure on \(S^6\), making it a complex manifold?

subareas.name: Maps and general types of topological spaces defined by maps
Fairly general properties of topological spaces
Connections of general topology with other structures, applications

page.hook: What is left of the idea of nearness when you throw away distances and keep only open sets?
about: General topology, also called point-set topology, sets out the basic language of continuity. A topological space is a set with a chosen family of open sets, which is enough to define limits, continuous maps, connectedness and compactness without any notion of distance. The area studies these concepts and their relations, the separation and countability axioms, when a space can be given a metric, dimension, and constructions such as products and quotients.

Arguments are set-theoretic in character, and counterexamples play as large a role as theorems, since they mark the boundaries of each concept. Some questions turn out to be independent of the usual axioms of set theory. Nearly every part of analysis and geometry uses this framework, and specialized branches such as continuum theory, dimension theory and the study of function spaces remain active areas of research.

example.title: Compact or not
example.text: Take the real line with its usual open sets. The interval \([0,1]\) is compact: every cover by open sets has a finite subcover. The interval \((0,1)\) is not: the sets \((\tfrac1n,1)\) for \(n=2,3,\dots\) cover it, but any finitely many of them miss the points below the smallest \(\tfrac1n\) used. Yet \((0,1)\) is homeomorphic to the whole line, through \(x\mapsto\tan(\pi x-\tfrac{\pi}{2})\). So boundedness is not a topological property.

objects.gloss: A set with a family of open subsets closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections.
A map for which the preimage of every open set is open.
A continuous bijection whose inverse is continuous; the notion of sameness for spaces.
The property that every cover by open sets has a finite subcover.
The property that the space is not a union of two disjoint nonempty open sets.
A space in which any two distinct points have disjoint open neighborhoods.
A space whose topology comes from some distance function.

theorems.name: Urysohn's lemma
theorems.statement: Let \(A\) and \(B\) be disjoint closed subsets of a normal space \(X\). Then there is a continuous function \(f:X\to[0,1]\) with \(f=0\) on \(A\) and \(f=1\) on \(B\).

theorems.name: Tietze extension theorem
theorems.statement: Every continuous real-valued function on a closed subset of a normal space extends to a continuous real-valued function on the whole space.

theorems.name: Tychonoff's theorem
theorems.statement: The product of any family of compact spaces is compact in the product topology. Over the other axioms of set theory, this statement is equivalent to the axiom of choice.

theorems.name: Urysohn metrization theorem
theorems.statement: Every regular Hausdorff space with a countable base for its topology is metrizable.

theorems.name: Baire category theorem
theorems.statement: In a complete metric space, and in a locally compact Hausdorff space, the intersection of countably many dense open sets is dense.

theorems.name: Nagata-Smirnov metrization theorem
theorems.statement: A topological space is metrizable if and only if it is regular and Hausdorff and has a base that is a countable union of locally finite families of open sets.

open.name: Plane fixed point problem
open.gloss: Does every continuous map of a compact connected plane set that does not separate the plane to itself have a fixed point?

open.name: Efimov's problem
open.gloss: Can it be proved from the usual axioms that every infinite compact Hausdorff space contains a nontrivial convergent sequence or a copy of the Stone-Čech compactification of the natural numbers?

subareas.name: Homology and cohomology theories in algebraic topology
Fiber spaces and bundles in algebraic topology
Operations and obstructions in algebraic topology
Applied homological algebra and category theory in algebraic topology

page.hook: How can algebra prove that a doughnut surface can never be deformed into a sphere?
about: Algebraic topology attaches algebraic objects, such as numbers, groups and rings, to topological spaces in such a way that continuous deformations do not change them. If two spaces have different invariants, they cannot be deformed into each other. The main invariants are homotopy groups, which record maps of spheres into a space, and homology and cohomology groups, which detect holes of each dimension.

The invariants are functors: maps between spaces induce homomorphisms between groups, so topological problems become algebraic ones. Computation relies on exact sequences, spectral sequences, fibrations and cell decompositions. Homotopy theory studies spaces up to deformation and has grown into an abstract framework used across mathematics. The area gave rise to homological algebra and category theory, and it interacts with the geometry of manifolds, algebraic geometry and mathematical physics.

example.title: Counting turns around a hole
example.text: For a closed loop in the plane that avoids the origin, count how many times it winds around the origin, with counterclockwise turns positive. The loop \(t\mapsto(\cos2t,\sin2t)\), \(0\le t\le2\pi\), has winding number 2. Deforming a loop without crossing the origin never changes this integer, and two loops with the same number can be deformed into each other. So loops in the punctured plane are classified by integers: its fundamental group is \(\mathbb{Z}\).

objects.gloss: A continuous deformation of one map into another.
The group of loops at a base point, taken up to homotopy, under concatenation.
An abelian group measuring the holes of a given dimension in a space.
The dual counterpart of homology, which carries a product structure.
A space built by attaching cells of increasing dimension along their boundaries.
A map with the homotopy lifting property; over a path-connected base all fibers are homotopy equivalent.
A computational device that approximates a homology group through successive pages of simpler groups.

theorems.name: Brouwer fixed-point theorem
theorems.statement: Every continuous map from a closed ball in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to itself has a fixed point.

theorems.name: Seifert-van Kampen theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(X\) be the union of two open path-connected sets \(U\) and \(V\) whose intersection is path-connected and contains the base point. Then \(\pi_1(X)\) is the free product of \(\pi_1(U)\) and \(\pi_1(V)\) amalgamated over \(\pi_1(U\cap V)\).

theorems.name: Poincaré duality
theorems.statement: For a closed orientable manifold \(M\) of dimension \(n\), \(H^k(M;\mathbb{Z})\cong H_{n-k}(M;\mathbb{Z})\) for every \(k\).

theorems.name: Lefschetz fixed-point theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(f\) be a continuous map of a compact triangulable space \(X\) to itself. If the Lefschetz number \(\sum_k(-1)^k\,\mathrm{tr}\big(f_*\ \text{on}\ H_k(X;\mathbb{Q})\big)\) is not zero, then \(f\) has a fixed point.

theorems.name: Hurewicz theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(n\ge2\) and let \(X\) be a path-connected space with \(\pi_i(X)=0\) for \(0<i<n\). Then \(H_i(X;\mathbb{Z})=0\) for \(0<i<n\), and the Hurewicz map \(\pi_n(X)\to H_n(X;\mathbb{Z})\) is an isomorphism.

theorems.name: Whitehead's theorem
theorems.statement: A map between connected CW complexes that induces isomorphisms on all homotopy groups is a homotopy equivalence.

open.name: Homotopy groups of spheres
open.gloss: The groups of homotopy classes of maps between spheres are known only in a limited range; finding their general pattern is a long-running program.

open.name: Whitehead's asphericity question
open.gloss: Is every connected subcomplex of an aspherical two-dimensional CW complex itself aspherical?

subareas.name: Homology and homotopy of topological groups and related structures
Relations of manifolds and cell complexes with science and engineering

page.hook: Can you tell a knotted loop from an unknotted one, or a sphere from a doughnut, without cutting anything?
about: A manifold is a space that looks, near each of its points, like ordinary Euclidean space of some dimension. Curves and surfaces are the first examples, and there are analogs in every higher dimension. This area classifies manifolds and studies how they are assembled from simple pieces such as cells, simplices and handles. It includes knot theory and the topology of dimensions three and four.

The main tools are invariants such as the fundamental group, homology, intersection forms and knot polynomials, together with cut-and-paste techniques such as surgery and handle decompositions. In dimensions five and above, classification questions reduce largely to algebra. Dimensions three and four behave differently and draw on hyperbolic geometry, geometric flows and gauge theory from physics.

example.title: Counting on a surface
example.text: Divide a surface into polygons and compute \(V - E + F\), vertices minus edges plus faces. A cube gives \(8 - 12 + 6 = 2\), and so does every other division of a sphere. A torus cut into a 3 by 3 grid of squares has 9 vertices, 18 edges and 9 faces, giving \(9 - 18 + 9 = 0\). The number depends only on the surface, so a sphere cannot be deformed into a torus.

objects.gloss: A space that near every point looks like Euclidean space of a fixed dimension.
A closed loop in three-dimensional space, studied up to deformation that never passes the loop through itself.
A space built by attaching cells of increasing dimension along their boundaries.
A way of building a manifold by attaching thickened cells called handles, one at a time.
A manifold whose boundary consists of two given manifolds, relating one to the other.
A choice of coordinate charts on a manifold that makes differentiation meaningful.
The integer bilinear form on the middle homology of a 4-manifold that counts intersections of surfaces.

theorems.name: Classification of closed surfaces
theorems.statement: Every closed connected surface is homeomorphic to exactly one of the following: the sphere, a connected sum of \(g \ge 1\) tori, or a connected sum of \(k \ge 1\) real projective planes.

theorems.name: Milnor's exotic spheres
theorems.statement: There exist smooth manifolds that are homeomorphic to the 7-sphere \(S^7\) but not diffeomorphic to it.

theorems.name: h-cobordism theorem
theorems.statement: Let \(W\) be a compact smooth manifold of dimension at least 6 whose boundary is the disjoint union of \(M\) and \(N\), with \(W\), \(M\), \(N\) simply connected and both inclusions \(M \to W\), \(N \to W\) homotopy equivalences. Then \(W\) is diffeomorphic to \(M \times [0,1]\).

theorems.name: Freedman's classification theorem
theorems.statement: Two closed simply connected topological 4-manifolds are homeomorphic if and only if they have isomorphic intersection forms and equal Kirby-Siebenmann invariants. In particular, a closed 4-manifold homotopy equivalent to the 4-sphere is homeomorphic to it.

theorems.name: Donaldson's diagonalization theorem
theorems.statement: If the intersection form of a closed, simply connected, smooth 4-manifold is positive or negative definite, then it is diagonalizable over the integers.

theorems.name: Poincaré conjecture
theorems.statement: Every closed simply connected 3-manifold is homeomorphic to the 3-sphere.

open.name: Smooth 4-dimensional Poincaré conjecture
open.gloss: Is every smooth 4-manifold that is homeomorphic to the 4-sphere also diffeomorphic to it?

open.name: Slice-ribbon conjecture
open.gloss: Is every knot that bounds a smooth disk in the 4-ball a ribbon knot?

open.name: Jones polynomial and the unknot
open.gloss: Is the unknot the only knot whose Jones polynomial equals 1?

subareas.name: Spaces and manifolds of mappings (including nonlinear versions of 46Exx)
Pseudogroups, differentiable groupoids and general structures on manifolds
Partial differential equations on manifolds; differential operators
Theory of singularities and catastrophe theory
Applications of global analysis to the sciences

page.hook: What can the frequencies at which a drum vibrates tell you about its shape?
about: Global analysis studies calculus and differential equations on curved spaces, called manifolds, instead of on flat Euclidean space. Typical questions ask how the solutions of an equation on a manifold, or the critical points of a function on it, reflect the overall shape of the space. The area also covers infinite-dimensional manifolds, such as spaces of curves or maps, and the singularities of smooth maps.

The methods combine the analysis of elliptic operators, the calculus of variations and algebraic topology. Many results equate an analytic quantity, such as the number of independent solutions of an equation, with a topological one that can be computed without solving anything. The area is tied to differential geometry and partial differential equations, and to physics through gauge theory and spectral problems.

example.title: Critical points on a torus
example.text: Stand a torus upright like a tire and let \(h\) be the height of each point. The function \(h\) has four critical points: a minimum at the bottom, two saddles at the bottom and top of the hole, and a maximum at the top. The alternating count \(1 - 2 + 1 = 0\) is the Euler characteristic of the torus. On a sphere, height has one minimum and one maximum, and \(1 + 1 = 2\).

objects.gloss: A space with local coordinates in which functions can be differentiated.
An object that can be integrated over curves, surfaces or higher-dimensional pieces of a manifold.
A differential operator, like the Laplacian, whose highest-order part is invertible in every nonzero direction.
The generalization of the Laplacian to functions on a Riemannian manifold.
A smooth function all of whose critical points are nondegenerate.
A bounded linear operator with finite-dimensional kernel and cokernel; its index is their difference in dimension.
A point where the derivative of a smooth map fails to have maximal rank.

theorems.name: Stokes' theorem
theorems.statement: If \(M\) is a compact oriented smooth \(n\)-manifold with boundary and \(\omega\) is a smooth \((n-1)\)-form on \(M\), then \(\int_M d\omega = \int_{\partial M} \omega\).

theorems.name: De Rham's theorem
theorems.statement: For a smooth manifold \(M\), integration of differential forms over smooth chains induces an isomorphism between the de Rham cohomology of \(M\) and its singular cohomology with real coefficients.

theorems.name: Sard's theorem
theorems.statement: The set of critical values of a \(C^\infty\) map between smooth manifolds has measure zero.

theorems.name: Morse inequalities
theorems.statement: Let \(f\) be a Morse function on a closed manifold \(M\) with \(c_k\) critical points of index \(k\), and let \(b_k\) be the Betti numbers of \(M\). Then \(c_k \ge b_k\) for every \(k\), and \(\sum_k (-1)^k c_k = \chi(M)\).

theorems.name: Hodge theorem
theorems.statement: On a compact oriented Riemannian manifold, every de Rham cohomology class contains exactly one harmonic form.

theorems.name: Atiyah-Singer index theorem
theorems.statement: For an elliptic differential operator on a compact manifold without boundary, the analytic index, which is the dimension of the kernel minus the dimension of the cokernel, equals the topological index, which is computed from the symbol of the operator and characteristic classes of the manifold.

open.name: Hearing the shape of a convex drum
open.gloss: Is a smooth convex planar domain determined, up to rigid motion, by the Dirichlet eigenvalues of its Laplacian?

open.name: Pólya's conjecture
open.gloss: Is the \(k\)-th Dirichlet eigenvalue of every bounded Euclidean domain at least the leading term in Weyl's law? It is proved for tiling domains and for balls.

subareas.name: Probability theory on algebraic and topological structures

page.hook: Why do averages of many random outcomes settle down, and how large are the fluctuations that remain?
about: Probability theory is the mathematics of chance. It assigns numbers between 0 and 1 to events and works out the consequences, from coin tossing to the motion of a pollen grain in water. Stochastic processes, which are random quantities that evolve in time, form a large part of the area. Examples are random walks, Markov chains and Brownian motion.

Since the 1930s the subject has been built on measure theory, with probabilities treated as measures and random variables as measurable functions. A recurring theme is that large random systems show regular behavior: averages converge and fluctuations follow universal laws. Probability supplies the language for statistics, statistical physics and mathematical finance, and probabilistic arguments are used in analysis, combinatorics and number theory.

example.title: Shared birthdays
example.text: Put 23 people in a room and assume birthdays are independent and uniform over 365 days. The chance that all 23 birthdays differ is \(\frac{365}{365}\cdot\frac{364}{365}\cdots\frac{343}{365} \approx 0.493\). So the chance that at least two people share a birthday is about \(0.507\), a little more than one half. With 50 people it rises to about \(0.97\).

objects.gloss: A set of outcomes, a collection of events and a measure assigning each event a probability.
A measurable function that assigns a number to each outcome.
The probability-weighted average of a random variable.
Events or variables are independent when the probability of joint occurrences is the product of individual probabilities.
A random process whose next step depends only on its current state.
A continuous random path with independent, normally distributed increments.
A process whose expected future value, given the past, equals its present value.

theorems.name: Strong law of large numbers
theorems.statement: If \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) are independent and identically distributed with \(E|X_1| < \infty\) and mean \(\mu\), then \((X_1 + \cdots + X_n)/n \to \mu\) almost surely.

theorems.name: Central limit theorem
theorems.statement: If \(X_1, X_2, \dots\) are independent and identically distributed with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(0 < \sigma^2 < \infty\), then \((X_1 + \cdots + X_n - n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt{n})\) converges in distribution to the standard normal law.

theorems.name: Convergence theorem for Markov chains
theorems.statement: An irreducible aperiodic Markov chain on a finite state space has a unique stationary distribution \(\pi\), and from every starting state the distribution of the chain at time \(n\) converges to \(\pi\) as \(n \to \infty\).

theorems.name: Martingale convergence theorem
theorems.statement: A martingale \((M_n)\) with \(\sup_n E|M_n| < \infty\) converges almost surely to a limit with finite expectation.

theorems.name: Itô's formula
theorems.statement: If \(B\) is a standard Brownian motion and \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable, then almost surely \(f(B_t) = f(B_0) + \int_0^t f'(B_s)\,dB_s + \frac12\int_0^t f''(B_s)\,ds\) for all \(t \ge 0\).

theorems.name: Donsker's invariance principle
theorems.statement: Let \(S_n\) be a random walk whose steps are independent and identically distributed with mean 0 and variance 1. The rescaled, linearly interpolated paths \(t \mapsto S_{nt}/\sqrt{n}\) on \([0,1]\) converge in distribution, as random continuous functions, to Brownian motion.

open.name: Self-avoiding walk in the plane
open.gloss: Show that a uniformly random \(n\)-step self-avoiding walk on a planar lattice typically travels a distance of order \(n^{3/4}\).

open.name: Critical percolation in three dimensions
open.gloss: Prove that there is no infinite open cluster at the critical probability on the cubic lattice.

open.name: KPZ universality
open.gloss: Show that a wide class of random growth models share the fluctuation exponents and limit laws found in a few exactly solvable cases.

subareas.name: Statistical sampling theory and related topics
Statistics on algebraic and topological structures

page.hook: How much can a sample of a thousand people tell you about a population of millions?
about: Statistics is the study of how to learn from data in the presence of variation and uncertainty. Given observations, it asks which explanations are plausible, how to estimate unknown quantities and how sure one can be of the answers. It also covers how to collect data well, through the design of experiments and of sample surveys.

The mathematical side rests on probability: data are modeled as random draws from a distribution that is only partly known. Estimators and tests are then judged by their error rates, either for a fixed sample size or as the sample grows. Frequentist and Bayesian approaches differ in how they treat unknown parameters. Statistics draws on optimization, linear algebra and computation, and underlies much of machine learning.

example.title: Reading a poll
example.text: A poll asks 1000 randomly chosen voters and 520 favor a proposal, so the estimate is \(52\%\). The standard error is \(\sqrt{0.52 \cdot 0.48/1000} \approx 0.016\). An approximate 95 percent confidence interval is \(0.52 \pm 1.96 \cdot 0.016\), which runs from about \(48.9\%\) to \(55.1\%\). Since the interval contains \(50\%\), this poll alone does not settle whether a majority is in favor.

objects.gloss: A family of probability distributions, one of which is assumed to have produced the data.
A rule that turns data into a guess for an unknown quantity.
The probability or density of the observed data, viewed as a function of the unknown parameter.
A rule for deciding whether data are compatible with a stated hypothesis, with controlled error rates.
A data-dependent interval that covers the true parameter with a stated probability.
A summary of the data that retains all information about the parameter.
In Bayesian inference, the distribution of the parameter after combining a prior with the data.

theorems.name: Gauss-Markov theorem
theorems.statement: In the linear model \(y = X\beta + \varepsilon\), where \(X\) has full column rank and the errors have mean zero, equal finite variance and are uncorrelated, the least squares estimator has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators of \(\beta\).

theorems.name: Neyman-Pearson lemma
theorems.statement: For testing one fully specified distribution against another, a test that rejects when the likelihood ratio exceeds a threshold and accepts when it is below has the greatest probability of correctly rejecting among all tests whose level does not exceed its own.

theorems.name: Cramér-Rao bound
theorems.statement: Under regularity conditions, any unbiased estimator of a real parameter \(\theta\) has variance at least \(1/I(\theta)\), where \(I(\theta)\) is the Fisher information of the sample.

theorems.name: Rao-Blackwell theorem
theorems.statement: If an unbiased estimator with finite variance is replaced by its conditional expectation given a sufficient statistic, the result is an unbiased estimator whose variance is no larger.

theorems.name: Glivenko-Cantelli theorem
theorems.statement: For independent observations from a common distribution, the empirical distribution function converges uniformly to the true distribution function, almost surely.

theorems.name: Asymptotic normality of maximum likelihood
theorems.statement: For independent observations from a parametric family satisfying regularity conditions, with true parameter \(\theta_0\), a consistent maximum likelihood estimator \(\hat\theta_n\) satisfies that \(\sqrt{n}(\hat\theta_n - \theta_0)\) converges in distribution to a normal law with mean 0 and covariance \(I(\theta_0)^{-1}\), the inverse Fisher information of one observation.

open.name: High-dimensional inference
open.gloss: Finding reliable estimates and error statements when the number of unknown parameters is comparable to or exceeds the number of observations.

open.name: Statistical-computational gaps
open.gloss: For problems such as detecting a small planted structure in noise, can efficient algorithms reach the accuracy that is statistically possible?

open.name: Inference after model selection
open.gloss: Producing valid tests and intervals when the same data were used to choose the model.

Numerical approximation and computational geometry (primarily algorithms)
Numerical methods in complex analysis (potential theory, etc.)
Numerical methods for mathematical programming, optimization and variational techniques
Numerical methods for ordinary differential equations
Numerical methods for partial differential equations, initial value and time-dependent initial-boundary value problems
Numerical methods for partial differential equations, boundary value problems
Numerical methods for difference and functional equations, recurrence relations
Numerical methods for integral equations, integral transforms

page.hook: How do you solve an equation on a machine that keeps only about sixteen digits of each number?
about: Numerical analysis designs and studies algorithms that compute approximate answers to mathematical problems: solving equations, evaluating integrals, and following the solutions of differential equations. Most problems from science and engineering have no closed-form solution, so they are replaced by finite computations. The area asks how accurate the result is, how much work it takes and how errors grow along the way.

Typical arguments bound the error of a method in terms of a step size or the number of iterations, and check that rounding errors are not amplified. Linear algebra is at the center, since most methods end in large systems of linear equations or eigenvalue problems. The area draws on approximation theory and functional analysis, and it supplies the algorithms used in scientific computing.

example.title: Square root of 2 by Newton's method
example.text: To solve \(x^2 = 2\), start from \(x_0 = 1\) and repeat \(x_{n+1} = \frac12\left(x_n + \frac{2}{x_n}\right)\). The iterates are \(1.5\), \(1.41667\), \(1.4142157\), \(1.41421356237\). The true value is \(1.41421356237\ldots\), so the number of correct digits roughly doubles with each step. Four steps with only division, addition and halving already give eleven correct decimals.

objects.gloss: Computer arithmetic with a fixed number of significant digits, so each operation is rounded.
A measure of how much the answer to a problem changes when its data change slightly.
The property that an algorithm does not amplify rounding and approximation errors unduly.
Replacing a continuous problem by a finite one, for example on a grid or a mesh.
The rate at which the error shrinks as the step size decreases or iterations proceed.
A procedure that improves an approximate solution step by step.
A formula that approximates an integral by a weighted sum of function values.

theorems.name: Convergence of Newton's method
theorems.statement: If \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable near a root \(x^*\) with \(f'(x^*) \ne 0\), then for every starting point close enough to \(x^*\) the iteration \(x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n)\) converges to \(x^*\), and \(|x_{n+1} - x^*| \le C|x_n - x^*|^2\) for some constant \(C\).

theorems.name: Gaussian quadrature
theorems.statement: The \(n\)-point rule whose nodes are the zeros of the Legendre polynomial of degree \(n\) integrates every polynomial of degree at most \(2n-1\) exactly over \([-1,1]\). No rule with \(n\) nodes is exact for all polynomials of degree \(2n\).

theorems.name: Conjugate gradient method
theorems.statement: For a symmetric positive definite \(n \times n\) system \(Ax = b\), the method reaches the exact solution in at most \(n\) steps in exact arithmetic. After \(k\) steps the error in the \(A\)-norm is at most \(2\left(\frac{\sqrt\kappa - 1}{\sqrt\kappa + 1}\right)^k\) times the initial error, where \(\kappa\) is the ratio of the largest to the smallest eigenvalue of \(A\).

theorems.name: Lax equivalence theorem
theorems.statement: For a consistent finite difference scheme applied to a well-posed linear initial value problem, stability is necessary and sufficient for convergence.

theorems.name: Dahlquist equivalence theorem
theorems.statement: A linear multistep method for ordinary differential equations is convergent if and only if it is consistent and zero-stable.

theorems.name: Céa's lemma
theorems.statement: Let \(a\) be a bilinear form on a Hilbert space \(V\) with \(|a(u,v)| \le M\|u\|\|v\|\) and \(a(v,v) \ge \alpha\|v\|^2\), \(\alpha > 0\). If \(u\) solves \(a(u,v) = \ell(v)\) for all \(v \in V\) and \(u_h\) is the Galerkin solution in a closed subspace \(V_h\), then \(\|u - u_h\| \le \frac{M}{\alpha}\inf_{v \in V_h}\|u - v\|\).

open.name: Growth factor for complete pivoting
open.gloss: How large can the entries become during Gaussian elimination with complete pivoting on an \(n \times n\) real matrix? The true growth rate is unknown.

open.name: High-dimensional problems
open.gloss: Finding methods for differential equations in many variables whose cost does not grow exponentially with the dimension.

subareas.name: Discrete mathematics in relation to computer science
Computer science support for mathematical research and practice

page.hook: Are there problems whose answers are quick to check but hopelessly slow to find?
about: The mathematical side of computer science studies what can be computed and at what cost. It defines precise models of computation, designs algorithms and data structures, and proves limits on what any algorithm can achieve. It also covers the theory of programming languages and software, formal languages, databases, artificial intelligence and the use of computers in mathematical research.

Results come in two kinds. Upper bounds exhibit an algorithm and analyze its running time or memory use. Lower bounds and impossibility results show that no algorithm can do better, often by reducing one problem to another. The area borrows heavily from logic, combinatorics, probability and algebra, and it returns questions to them, such as the P versus NP problem.

example.title: How many comparisons to sort?
example.text: Eight distinct numbers can be arranged in \(8 \cdot 7 \cdots 2 \cdot 1 = 40320\) orders. A sorting method that only compares pairs learns one yes or no answer per comparison, so \(k\) comparisons can tell apart at most \(2^k\) orders. Since \(2^{15} = 32768 < 40320\), every such method needs at least 16 comparisons on some input. Merge sort needs at most 17 on eight numbers.

objects.gloss: A finite, precise procedure that transforms an input into an output.
A simple abstract computer with a tape and a finite set of rules, used to define computability.
A set of problems solvable within a given resource bound, such as P or NP.
A way of transforming one problem into another, showing the second is at least as hard.
A way of organizing data so that chosen operations are fast.
A set of strings over a finite alphabet, often described by a grammar or an automaton.
A network of AND, OR and NOT gates computing a function of input bits.

theorems.name: Undecidability of the halting problem
theorems.statement: There is no algorithm that takes as input a Turing machine and an input string and correctly decides, in every case, whether the machine eventually halts on that input.

theorems.name: Kleene's theorem
theorems.statement: A language is accepted by some finite automaton if and only if it is described by some regular expression.

theorems.name: Time hierarchy theorem
theorems.statement: If \(f\) and \(g\) are time-constructible functions with \(f(n)\log f(n) = o(g(n))\), then some language is decidable by a deterministic Turing machine in time \(O(g(n))\) but not in time \(O(f(n))\). In particular, P is strictly contained in EXP.

theorems.name: Cook-Levin theorem
theorems.statement: Boolean satisfiability is NP-complete: it lies in NP, and every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time.

theorems.name: PCP theorem
theorems.statement: Every language in NP has a verifier that uses \(O(\log n)\) random bits, reads only a constant number of bits of a proposed proof, always accepts a correct proof of a true statement, and rejects every proposed proof of a false statement with probability at least \(1/2\).

theorems.name: AKS primality theorem
theorems.statement: There is a deterministic algorithm that decides whether a given integer is prime in time polynomial in the number of its digits.

open.name: P versus NP
open.gloss: Can every problem whose solutions can be verified in polynomial time also be solved in polynomial time?

open.name: Exponent of matrix multiplication
open.gloss: Can two \(n \times n\) matrices be multiplied using \(O(n^{2+\varepsilon})\) arithmetic operations for every \(\varepsilon > 0\)?

open.name: Complexity of integer factoring
open.gloss: Is there a polynomial-time algorithm on a classical computer that factors integers?

subareas.name: Dynamics of a rigid body and of multibody systems
Dynamics of a system of particles, including celestial mechanics
General models, approaches, and methods in mechanics of particles and systems
Random and stochastic aspects of the mechanics of particles and systems

page.hook: Given where the planets are tonight, where will they be a thousand years from now?
about: This area is classical mechanics: the motion of point masses, rigid bodies and systems built from them, under forces such as gravity, springs and constraints. It includes the motion of planets and satellites, spinning tops, pendulums, vibrating systems and machines with linked parts. Bodies that deform, such as elastic solids and fluids, are treated in neighboring areas.

Newton's laws turn a mechanical problem into ordinary differential equations. The Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations rewrite these equations in terms of a single function, the energy or a close relative, and make symmetries and conserved quantities visible. Hamiltonian mechanics is the origin of symplectic geometry, and questions about long-term behavior of orbits led to the modern theory of dynamical systems.

example.title: The period of a pendulum
example.text: A small weight hangs on a string of length \(L\). For small swings, the angle \(\theta\) satisfies \(\ddot\theta = -(g/L)\theta\), so the motion is a sine wave with period \(T = 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}\). With \(L = 1\) m and \(g = 9.81\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\) this gives \(T \approx 2.01\) seconds. The mass does not appear, and for small swings neither does the amplitude. Quadrupling the length doubles the period.

objects.gloss: The set of all positions a system can take; its dimension is the number of degrees of freedom.
The space of all positions together with momenta; a point determines the future motion.
Kinetic minus potential energy, as a function of positions and velocities.
The total energy expressed as a function of positions and momenta.
A function of the state, such as energy or angular momentum, that stays constant along every motion.
An idealized body whose points keep fixed distances from each other.
A restriction on the possible positions or velocities, such as a bead forced to stay on a wire.

theorems.name: Newton's second law
theorems.statement: In an inertial frame, a particle of constant mass \(m\) at position \(x(t)\) acted on by a force \(F\) moves according to \(m\ddot{x} = F\).

theorems.name: Euler-Lagrange equations
theorems.statement: The motions of a system with Lagrangian \(L(q, \dot q, t)\) are the paths that make the action \(\int L\,dt\) stationary among paths with fixed endpoints. Equivalently, \(\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}\) for each coordinate \(q_i\).

theorems.name: Hamilton's equations
theorems.statement: With momenta \(p_i = \partial L/\partial \dot q_i\) and Hamiltonian \(H(q,p,t)\), the motion satisfies \(\dot q_i = \partial H/\partial p_i\) and \(\dot p_i = -\partial H/\partial q_i\).

theorems.name: Liouville's theorem
theorems.statement: The flow of a Hamiltonian system preserves volume in phase space.

theorems.name: Noether's theorem
theorems.statement: If the Lagrangian \(L(q,\dot q)\) is unchanged by a smooth one-parameter family of transformations \(q \mapsto \phi_s(q)\) with \(\phi_0\) the identity, then \(\sum_i \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i}\,\frac{d\phi_s^i}{ds}\Big|_{s=0}\) is constant along every solution of the Euler-Lagrange equations.

theorems.name: Kolmogorov-Arnold-Moser theorem
theorems.statement: Under a sufficiently small and sufficiently smooth perturbation of a nondegenerate integrable Hamiltonian system, the invariant tori whose frequencies satisfy a Diophantine condition survive in slightly deformed form. They fill a set of positive measure, and the measure of its complement tends to zero with the size of the perturbation.

open.name: Finiteness of central configurations
open.gloss: For \(n\) point masses under Newtonian gravity, is the number of relative equilibria finite up to symmetry? This is known for \(n \le 4\) and, for generic masses, \(n = 5\).

open.name: Long-term stability of planetary systems
open.gloss: In the \(n\)-body problem with one large mass and several small ones, how common are orbits that eventually leave the neighborhood of the stable quasi-periodic motions?

subareas.name: Generalities, axiomatics, foundations of continuum mechanics of solids
Plastic materials, materials of stress-rate and internal-variable type
Materials of strain-rate type and history type, other materials with memory (including elastic materials with viscous damping, various viscoelastic materials)
Coupling of solid mechanics with other effects
Special kinds of problems in solid mechanics
Homogenization, determination of effective properties in solid mechanics
Numerical and other methods in solid mechanics

page.hook: How much load can a slender column carry before it suddenly bows sideways?
about: Solid mechanics describes how solid bodies deform, vibrate and break under loads. The body is modeled as a continuum, and the unknowns are the displacement of each point and the internal forces, called stresses. The area covers elastic materials that spring back, plastic materials that deform permanently, materials with memory, thin structures such as beams, plates and shells, and the growth of cracks.

The governing equations combine a balance law for momentum with a constitutive law that describes the material. They are systems of partial differential equations, linear for small elastic deformations and nonlinear otherwise. Equilibrium states are often found as minimizers of an energy, which links the area to the calculus of variations. Practical computation relies mostly on the finite element method.

example.title: Buckling of a steel rod
example.text: A straight rod of length \(L\), hinged at both ends and compressed along its axis, buckles at the Euler load \(P = \pi^2 EI/L^2\). For a steel rod with \(E = 200\) GPa, diameter 1 cm and length 1 m, the second moment of area is \(I = \pi d^4/64 \approx 4.9 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m^4}\), so \(P \approx 970\) N, about the weight of 99 kg. Doubling the length divides the load by four.

objects.gloss: The vector by which each point of the body has moved from its reference position.
A symmetric tensor measuring local stretching and shearing.
A tensor giving the force per unit area across any small surface inside the body.
The relation between stress and strain that characterizes a particular material.
A material constant, such as Young's modulus, relating stress to strain in the elastic range.
The elastic energy per unit volume as a function of the deformation gradient.
A surface inside the body across which the displacement may jump.

theorems.name: Cauchy's stress theorem
theorems.statement: The traction \(t\) acting on a surface element with unit normal \(n\) depends linearly on \(n\): there is a tensor field \(\sigma\) with \(t = \sigma n\).

theorems.name: Cauchy's equations of motion
theorems.statement: Balance of linear momentum gives \(\rho\,\ddot u = \operatorname{div}\sigma + f\), where \(\rho\) is the density, \(u\) the displacement and \(f\) the body force per unit volume. In the absence of body couples, balance of angular momentum makes \(\sigma\) symmetric.

theorems.name: Hooke's law for isotropic materials
theorems.statement: In linear elasticity of an isotropic material, \(\sigma = \lambda\,(\operatorname{tr}\varepsilon)\,I + 2\mu\,\varepsilon\), where \(\varepsilon = \frac12(\nabla u + \nabla u^{T})\) is the strain and \(\lambda\), \(\mu\) are the Lamé constants.

theorems.name: Korn's inequality
theorems.statement: Let \(\Omega\) be a bounded open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^n\). For every \(u\) in \(H^1_0(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^n)\), \(\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,dx \le 2\int_\Omega |\varepsilon(u)|^2\,dx\). Together with the Lax-Milgram lemma this yields existence and uniqueness of solutions in linear elasticity with fixed boundary.

theorems.name: Griffith's criterion
theorems.statement: A crack in a brittle material advances when the elastic energy released per unit of new crack area reaches a critical value characteristic of the material. For a crack of length \(2a\) in a large thin plate under tension, this gives the failure stress \(\sqrt{2E\gamma/(\pi a)}\), with \(\gamma\) the surface energy.

theorems.name: Ball's existence theorem
theorems.statement: If the stored energy function is polyconvex and satisfies suitable growth conditions, then the total elastic energy attains its minimum among admissible deformations with prescribed boundary values.

open.name: Regularity of energy minimizers
open.gloss: Are the energy minimizers of nonlinear elasticity smooth, and do they satisfy the equilibrium equations in the weak sense?

open.name: Dynamics in nonlinear elasticity
open.gloss: Do the equations of motion of nonlinear elasticity in three dimensions have global weak solutions for general initial data?

open.name: Prediction of crack paths
open.gloss: Finding mathematically justified models that predict when cracks start, where they go and how they branch.

uses: Design of buildings, bridges and aircraft

subareas.name: Foundations, constitutive equations, rheology, hydrodynamical models of non-fluid phenomena
Shock waves and blast waves in fluid mechanics
Rarefied gas flows, Boltzmann equation in fluid mechanics
Flows in porous media; filtration; seepage
Ionized gas flow in electromagnetic fields; plasmic flow

page.hook: Why does smoke rise in a smooth column and then suddenly break up into swirls?
about: Fluid mechanics describes the motion of liquids and gases: water in pipes and oceans, air around wings, blood in arteries, plasma in stars. The fluid is modeled as a continuum with a velocity, pressure and density at every point. The area covers viscous and inviscid flow, compressible gases and shock waves, waves, stability, turbulence, flow in porous media and electrically conducting fluids.

The basic equations are nonlinear partial differential equations expressing conservation of mass, momentum and energy. Exact solutions are rare, so the area relies on scaling arguments, asymptotic approximations such as boundary layer theory, stability analysis and numerical simulation. Whether the equations always have smooth solutions is itself a major open question in the theory of partial differential equations.

example.title: Smooth or turbulent?
example.text:
The Reynolds number \(Re = UL/
u\) compares inertia with viscosity, using a speed \(U\), a length \(L\) and the kinematic viscosity \(
u\). Water, with \(
u \approx 10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m^2/s}\), flowing at 1 m/s through a pipe 2 cm wide has \(Re = 20000\), and the flow is turbulent. A syrup ten thousand times more viscous gives \(Re = 2\), and the flow is smooth. Pipe flow typically turns turbulent at \(Re\) of a few thousand.

objects.gloss: The velocity of the fluid at each point of space and each time.
The force per unit area that the fluid exerts equally in all directions.
A measure of internal friction, the resistance of a fluid to shearing.
The curl of the velocity field, measuring local rotation.
A dimensionless ratio of inertial to viscous effects.
A thin region near a solid wall where viscosity matters even when it is negligible elsewhere.
A thin surface across which pressure, density and velocity of a gas change abruptly.

theorems.name: Bernoulli's principle
theorems.statement: In steady flow of an inviscid fluid of constant density \(\rho\) under gravity, \(p + \frac12\rho|u|^2 + \rho g z\) is constant along each streamline.
