theorems.name: Kelvin's circulation theorem
theorems.statement: In an inviscid fluid whose density depends only on pressure, acted on by conservative body forces, the circulation of the velocity around any closed curve that moves with the fluid is constant in time.

theorems.name: Leray's theorem
theorems.statement: For every divergence-free initial velocity in \(L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)\), the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations have a weak solution defined for all time that satisfies the energy inequality.

theorems.name: Kolmogorov's 1941 scaling law
theorems.statement: For turbulence at very high Reynolds number, Kolmogorov's similarity hypotheses predict an energy spectrum \(E(k) = C\varepsilon^{2/3}k^{-5/3}\) over the inertial range of wavenumbers \(k\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the mean rate of energy dissipation per unit mass. This is a physical prediction, not a theorem derived from the equations.

open.name: Navier-Stokes regularity
open.gloss: Do smooth, finite-energy initial data in three dimensions always give a solution of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations that stays smooth for all time?

open.name: Blow-up for the Euler equations
open.gloss: Can a smooth, finite-energy solution of the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations in the whole space become singular in finite time?

open.name: Theory of turbulence
open.gloss: Derive the observed statistical laws of turbulent flow, such as Kolmogorov's spectrum and its corrections, from the Navier-Stokes equations.

subareas.name: General topics in optics and electromagnetic theory
Basic methods for problems in optics and electromagnetic theory

page.hook: Why does a straw look bent in a glass of water, and what is light made of?
about: This area covers the mathematics of electric and magnetic fields and of light. Charges and currents create fields, changing fields create each other, and the resulting waves include radio, visible light and X-rays. Topics include electrostatics and magnetostatics, wave propagation, antennas and waveguides, scattering and diffraction, geometric optics with its rays and lenses, and the behavior of fields in materials.

Everything rests on Maxwell's equations, a system of linear partial differential equations for the fields, together with laws describing the material. Methods include potential theory, Fourier analysis, integral equations, asymptotic approximations for short wavelengths and numerical simulation. Inverse problems, where one infers an object from the waves it scatters, form a large modern part. The theory led to special relativity and to quantum electrodynamics.

example.title: Bending of light at a water surface
example.text: Snell's law says \(n_1\sin\theta_1 = n_2\sin\theta_2\), with angles measured from the perpendicular. For light going from air, \(n_1 = 1\), into water, \(n_2 = 1.33\), at \(45^\circ\), we get \(\sin\theta_2 = 0.707/1.33 = 0.532\), so \(\theta_2 \approx 32^\circ\). Going from water to air, no refracted ray exists beyond the critical angle \(\arcsin(1/1.33) \approx 48.8^\circ\), and all the light is reflected.

objects.gloss: Vector fields \(E\) and \(B\) that determine the force on a moving charge.
A self-sustaining oscillation of electric and magnetic fields that travels through space.
The ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in a material.
The direction in which the electric field of a wave oscillates.
The spreading and interference of waves that pass an obstacle or an opening.
Auxiliary fields from which the electric and magnetic fields are obtained by differentiation.
A structure, such as a metal tube or an optical fiber, that guides waves along its length.

theorems.name: Maxwell's equations
theorems.statement:
In SI units, \(
abla\cdot E = ho/\varepsilon_0\), \(
abla\cdot B = 0\), \(
abla	imes E = -\partial_t B\) and \(
abla	imes B = \mu_0 J + \mu_0\varepsilon_0\,\partial_t E\), where \(ho\) is the charge density and \(J\) the current density.

theorems.name: Lorentz force law
theorems.statement: A particle with charge \(q\) and velocity \(v\) experiences the force \(F = q(E + v\times B)\).

theorems.name: Electromagnetic wave equation
theorems.statement: In vacuum with no charges or currents, Maxwell's equations imply that every component of \(E\) and \(B\) satisfies the wave equation with speed \(c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_0\varepsilon_0}\).

theorems.name: Poynting's theorem
theorems.statement: With energy density \(u = \frac12(\varepsilon_0|E|^2 + |B|^2/\mu_0)\) and energy flux \(S = E\times B/\mu_0\), the fields in vacuum satisfy \(\partial_t u + \nabla\cdot S = -J\cdot E\).

theorems.name: Fermat's principle
theorems.statement: Among nearby paths between two points, a light ray follows one for which the optical length \(\int n\,ds\) is stationary. The laws of reflection and Snell's law of refraction follow.

theorems.name: Rayleigh scattering law
theorems.statement: Light scattered by particles much smaller than its wavelength \(\lambda\) has intensity proportional to \(\lambda^{-4}\), so blue light is scattered more strongly than red.

open.name: Radiation reaction
open.gloss: Find a fully consistent classical equation of motion for a point charge that includes the force from its own radiation; the standard candidate has unphysical runaway solutions.

open.name: Inverse scattering with limited data
open.gloss: Under what conditions do measurements of scattered waves from a few directions or frequencies determine the scattering object uniquely?

subareas.name: Basic methods in thermodynamics and heat transfer

page.hook: Why does heat flow from hot to cold and never the other way on its own?
about: Classical thermodynamics describes matter in bulk through a few quantities such as temperature, pressure, volume, energy and entropy, without reference to atoms. Its laws limit what any engine, refrigerator or chemical process can do. Heat transfer studies how thermal energy moves by conduction, convection and radiation, and includes melting and freezing, combustion and chemically reacting systems.

Mathematically, thermodynamics is a theory of state functions and inequalities, with convexity and Legendre transforms relating the different potentials. Heat conduction leads to the heat equation, the model parabolic partial differential equation, and phase change leads to free boundary problems in which the interface is part of the unknown. Statistical mechanics explains the laws from microscopic models, and continuum mechanics uses them as constraints.

example.title: The best possible engine
example.text: An engine takes heat from a hot source at \(T_h = 500\) K and rejects heat to surroundings at \(T_c = 300\) K. Carnot's theorem limits its efficiency to \(1 - T_c/T_h = 1 - 300/500 = 0.4\). So from every 1000 J of heat taken in, at most 400 J can become work, and at least 600 J must be discarded. No design can do better between these two temperatures.

objects.gloss: The quantity that is equal for two bodies in thermal equilibrium with each other.
The energy stored in a system, changed by heat flow and by work.
A state function that never decreases in an isolated system and measures irreversibility.
A relation among pressure, volume and temperature, such as the ideal gas law \(pV = nRT\).
A thermodynamic potential that is minimized at equilibrium under fixed temperature.
The rate of flow of thermal energy per unit area.
A moving interface, such as a melting front, whose position must be found along with the temperature.

theorems.name: First law of thermodynamics
theorems.statement: The change in internal energy of a closed system equals the heat supplied to it minus the work it does: \(dU = \delta Q - \delta W\).

theorems.name: Second law of thermodynamics
theorems.statement: No process has as its sole result the transfer of heat from a colder body to a hotter one. Equivalently, for any cyclic process \(\oint \delta Q/T \le 0\), with equality for reversible cycles, and the entropy of an isolated system never decreases.

theorems.name: Carnot's theorem
theorems.statement: No heat engine operating between reservoirs at absolute temperatures \(T_h > T_c\) is more efficient than a reversible one, and every reversible engine between them has efficiency \(1 - T_c/T_h\).

theorems.name: Fourier's law and the heat equation
theorems.statement: Heat flux is proportional to the temperature gradient, \(q = -k\nabla T\). With constant conductivity \(k\), density \(\rho\) and specific heat \(c\), and no heat sources, the temperature satisfies \(\partial_t T = \alpha\Delta T\) with \(\alpha = k/(\rho c)\).

theorems.name: Maximum principle for the heat equation
theorems.statement: A solution of \(\partial_t T = \alpha\Delta T\) on a bounded domain for \(0 \le t \le t_1\), continuous up to the boundary, attains its maximum either at time 0 or on the boundary of the domain.

theorems.name: Stefan condition
theorems.statement: At a melting or freezing front held at the melting temperature, the front moves with normal speed \(v\) such that \(\rho L v\) equals the difference between the conductive heat fluxes on its two sides, where \(L\) is the latent heat per unit mass.

open.name: Derivation of Fourier's law
open.gloss: Prove, starting from the deterministic motion of many interacting particles, that heat flux is proportional to the temperature gradient.

open.name: Thermodynamics far from equilibrium
open.gloss: Find general principles, comparable to the classical laws, that govern systems driven strongly away from equilibrium.

subareas.name: Foundations, quantum information and its processing, quantum axioms, and philosophy
General mathematical topics and methods in quantum theory
Groups and algebras in quantum theory
General quantum mechanics and problems of quantization
Quantum field theory; related classical field theories
Applications of quantum theory to specific physical systems

page.hook: Why can the position and the momentum of an electron never both be known exactly?
about: Quantum theory describes matter and light at the scale of atoms and below. A system is described by a state that assigns probabilities to the outcomes of measurements, and quantities such as energy often take only discrete values. The area covers quantum mechanics of particles, scattering, quantum field theory, which combines quantum mechanics with special relativity, and quantum information and computation.

States are vectors in a complex Hilbert space, observables are self-adjoint operators and time evolution is unitary. The mathematics therefore draws on functional analysis, spectral theory, representation theory of groups and partial differential equations. Quantum field theory has in turn produced ideas used in topology and geometry, although a large part of it still lacks rigorous mathematical foundations.

example.title: An electron in a box
example.text: An electron confined to a segment of length \(L\) has wave functions \(\sin(n\pi x/L)\) and energies \(E_n = n^2h^2/(8mL^2)\) for \(n = 1, 2, 3, \dots\). With \(L = 1\) nm this gives \(E_1 \approx 0.38\) eV, \(E_2 \approx 1.50\) eV and \(E_3 \approx 3.38\) eV. No energy in between is allowed. Dropping from level 2 to level 1 releases a photon of about \(1.13\) eV, in the near infrared.

objects.gloss: A unit vector in a complex Hilbert space, encoding all measurement probabilities of a system.
A self-adjoint operator; its spectrum is the set of possible measurement results.
The energy operator, which generates the time evolution of the state.
The state of a particle written as a complex function whose squared modulus is a probability density.
The operator \(AB - BA\), which measures the failure of two observables to be compatible.
A joint state of several systems that cannot be written as a product of states of the parts.
An operator-valued field on spacetime whose excitations are interpreted as particles.

theorems.name: Schrödinger equation
theorems.statement: The state \(\psi(t)\) of an isolated quantum system with Hamiltonian \(H\) evolves by \(i\hbar\,\partial_t\psi = H\psi\).

theorems.name: Uncertainty relation
theorems.statement: In every state, the standard deviations of position and momentum satisfy \(\sigma_x\sigma_p \ge \hbar/2\). More generally, for observables \(A\) and \(B\), \(\sigma_A\sigma_B \ge \frac12|\langle [A,B]\rangle|\).

theorems.name: Stone-von Neumann theorem
theorems.statement: For a system with finitely many degrees of freedom, any two irreducible strongly continuous unitary representations of the canonical commutation relations in Weyl form are unitarily equivalent. So the Schrödinger representation is essentially the only one.

theorems.name: Wigner's theorem
theorems.statement: Every bijection of the set of pure states of a Hilbert space onto itself that preserves transition probabilities is induced by a unitary or an antiunitary operator, unique up to a phase factor.

theorems.name: Bell's theorem
theorems.statement: No theory of local hidden variables can reproduce all predictions of quantum mechanics. In the later CHSH form, local hidden variables force a certain combination \(S\) of four correlations to satisfy \(|S| \le 2\), while quantum mechanics allows values up to \(2\sqrt2\).

theorems.name: No-cloning theorem
theorems.statement: There is no unitary operation that maps \(\lvert\psi\rangle\otimes\lvert 0\rangle\) to \(\lvert\psi\rangle\otimes\lvert\psi\rangle\) for every state \(\lvert\psi\rangle\).

open.name: Yang-Mills existence and mass gap
open.gloss: Construct quantum Yang-Mills theory on four-dimensional spacetime rigorously and show that its lightest particle has positive mass.

open.name: Quantum gravity
open.gloss: Find a consistent theory that combines quantum theory with general relativity.

open.name: Measurement problem
open.gloss: Explain how the definite outcomes seen in measurements arise from the linear, deterministic evolution of the quantum state.

subareas.name: Applications of statistical mechanics to specific types of physical systems

page.hook: How do countless jostling molecules add up to something as simple as temperature and pressure?
about: Statistical mechanics explains the behavior of matter in bulk from the laws governing its microscopic parts. Because a glass of water contains far too many molecules to follow one by one, the theory works with probability distributions over microscopic states. It derives thermodynamic quantities, explains phase transitions such as boiling and magnetization, and describes how systems approach equilibrium.

In equilibrium the central object is the partition function, a sum over all states weighted by their energies, and the main questions concern its behavior as the system grows. Lattice models, such as the Ising model of a magnet, serve as test cases. The area uses probability, combinatorics, analysis and operator algebras, and its ideas, notably the renormalization group and Monte Carlo sampling, are now used well outside physics.

example.title: A system with two levels
example.text: A particle can sit in a state of energy 0 or a state of energy \(\varepsilon\). At temperature \(T\), the two states have weights \(1\) and \(e^{-\varepsilon/kT}\), so the upper state has probability \(e^{-\varepsilon/kT}/(1 + e^{-\varepsilon/kT})\). When \(kT = \varepsilon\) this is \(0.269\). As \(T \to 0\) the probability tends to 0, and as \(T \to \infty\) it tends to \(\frac12\), never beyond.

objects.gloss: A complete specification of the state of every particle in the system.
The sum \(Z = \sum e^{-E/kT}\) over all microstates, from which thermodynamic quantities are computed.
The probability distribution on microstates describing a system in thermal equilibrium.
The quantity \(-kT\log Z\), minimized at equilibrium for fixed temperature.
An abrupt change in bulk behavior, such as melting, as a parameter like temperature varies.
A lattice of spins taking values plus or minus one, with neighboring spins favoring agreement.
A number describing how a quantity diverges or vanishes near a continuous phase transition.

theorems.name: Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution
theorems.statement: In equilibrium at temperature \(T\), a system in contact with a heat bath is in a microstate of energy \(E\) with probability \(e^{-E/kT}/Z\), where \(Z\) is the sum of \(e^{-E/kT}\) over all microstates. The free energy is \(F = -kT\log Z\).

theorems.name: Boltzmann's H-theorem
theorems.statement: For a solution \(f(t,x,v)\) of the Boltzmann equation for a dilute gas, the quantity \(H = \iint f\log f\,dx\,dv\) never increases in time.

theorems.name: Peierls argument
theorems.statement: The nearest-neighbor ferromagnetic Ising model on the square lattice with zero external field has spontaneous magnetization at all sufficiently low temperatures.

theorems.name: Onsager's solution
theorems.statement: The free energy of the Ising model on the square lattice with zero field and coupling \(J\) can be computed exactly. It is singular at the critical temperature given by \(\sinh(2J/kT_c) = 1\), that is \(kT_c/J = 2/\ln(1+\sqrt2) \approx 2.269\).

theorems.name: Lee-Yang circle theorem
theorems.statement: For the ferromagnetic Ising model on any finite graph with external field \(h\), the partition function is, up to a nonvanishing factor, a polynomial in \(z = e^{-2h/kT}\) all of whose zeros lie on the unit circle \(|z| = 1\).

theorems.name: Mermin-Wagner theorem
theorems.statement: In one and two dimensions, the quantum Heisenberg model with short-range interactions has no spontaneous magnetization at any positive temperature. More generally, a continuous symmetry cannot be spontaneously broken in such systems.

open.name: Three-dimensional Ising model
open.gloss: Determine rigorously the critical exponents of the Ising model in three dimensions; no exact solution is known.

open.name: Spin glasses in finite dimension
open.gloss: Describe the low-temperature phase of the Edwards-Anderson spin glass, including how many equilibrium states it has.

open.name: Heisenberg ferromagnet
open.gloss: Prove that the quantum Heisenberg ferromagnet in three dimensions has long-range order at low positive temperature.

subareas.name: Observational and experimental questions in relativity and gravitational theory
Relativistic gravitational theories other than Einstein's, including asymmetric field theories
Unified, higher-dimensional and super field theories

page.hook: Why do clocks on satellites tick at a different rate from clocks on the ground?
about: Relativity is the theory of space, time and gravity. Special relativity describes observers in uniform motion and shows that time and length depend on the observer while the speed of light does not. General relativity describes gravity as the curvature of a four-dimensional spacetime produced by matter and energy. The area includes black holes, gravitational waves, cosmological models and alternative theories of gravity.

The setting is a manifold with a Lorentzian metric, so the area is a branch of differential geometry in which one direction, time, is distinguished. The Einstein equations are nonlinear partial differential equations of hyperbolic type for the metric. Research combines geometric methods, such as the study of geodesics and causal structure, with the analysis of these equations and with numerical simulation.

example.title: Clocks on navigation satellites
example.text: A navigation satellite moves at about 3.9 km/s, and special relativity makes its clock run slow by about 7 microseconds per day. It also sits high in the Earth's gravitational field, and general relativity makes its clock run fast by about 45 microseconds per day. The net gain is about 38 microseconds per day. Light travels 11 km in that time, so positions would drift by kilometers per day without the correction.

objects.gloss: A four-dimensional manifold whose points are events, with time and space combined.
A rule for measuring intervals between nearby events, with one time direction and three space directions.
The path of a freely falling particle or a light ray; the analog of a straight line.
The quantity measuring how the geometry of spacetime departs from flatness; it encodes tidal forces.
The density and flow of energy and momentum of matter, the source of gravity.
A region of spacetime from which no signal can escape to distant observers.
A ripple in the geometry of spacetime that travels at the speed of light.

theorems.name: Lorentz transformation
theorems.statement: Two inertial frames in relative motion with speed \(v\) along the \(x\)-axis have coordinates related by \(t' = \gamma(t - vx/c^2)\), \(x' = \gamma(x - vt)\), \(y' = y\), \(z' = z\), where \(\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}\).

theorems.name: Einstein field equations
theorems.statement:
The metric \(g\) of spacetime satisfies \(R_{\mu
u} -  rac12 R\,g_{\mu
u} + \Lambda g_{\mu
u} =  rac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_{\mu
u}\), where \(R_{\mu
u}\) is the Ricci tensor, \(R\) the scalar curvature, \(\Lambda\) the cosmological constant and \(T_{\mu
u}\) the stress-energy tensor.

theorems.name: Birkhoff's theorem
theorems.statement: Every spherically symmetric solution of the vacuum Einstein equations with zero cosmological constant is locally isometric to a part of the Schwarzschild solution.

theorems.name: Choquet-Bruhat's theorem
theorems.statement: Smooth initial data for the vacuum Einstein equations that satisfy the constraint equations have a development into a solution for a short time, and any two such developments agree locally up to a diffeomorphism.

theorems.name: Penrose singularity theorem
theorems.statement: If a spacetime satisfies the null energy condition, has a non-compact Cauchy hypersurface and contains a closed trapped surface, then it has a future-directed null geodesic that cannot be extended to all values of its affine parameter.

theorems.name: Positive mass theorem
theorems.statement: A complete asymptotically flat Riemannian 3-manifold with nonnegative scalar curvature has nonnegative total mass, and the mass is zero only if the manifold is flat \(\mathbb{R}^3\).

open.name: Cosmic censorship
open.gloss: Do singularities that form from generic, physically reasonable initial data always stay hidden inside black holes, and is the evolution always uniquely determined?

open.name: Final state conjecture
open.gloss: Does every generic solution describing gravitational collapse settle down to a member of the Kerr family of rotating black holes?

open.name: Penrose inequality
open.gloss: Is the total mass of a spacetime bounded below in terms of the area of its black hole horizons in general, beyond the time-symmetric case that is proved?

page.hook: How can we weigh a star or a galaxy that we can never visit?
about: This area contains the mathematics used to describe the universe beyond the Earth: the orbits of planets, moons and spacecraft, the structure and evolution of stars, the dynamics of galaxies and clusters, and the expansion of the universe as a whole. It also covers the passage of light through stellar matter and the methods used to turn observations into measurements.

The models combine gravity with fluid dynamics, thermodynamics, nuclear and atomic physics and radiation. They lead to ordinary differential equations for orbits and stellar interiors, partial differential equations for gas and radiation, and large particle simulations for galaxies. Because experiments are impossible, statistical inference from observations carries much weight. General relativity is required for compact objects and for cosmology.

example.title: Weighing the Sun
example.text: For a small body in a circular orbit of radius \(a\) and period \(T\) around a mass \(M\), Newton's laws give \(M = 4\pi^2a^3/(GT^2)\). The Earth has \(a = 1.496\times10^{11}\) m and \(T = 3.156\times10^7\) s, and \(G = 6.674\times10^{-11}\) in SI units. This gives \(M \approx 1.99\times10^{30}\) kg for the Sun. The same formula, applied to stars orbiting a galaxy, weighs the galaxy.

objects.gloss: The path of a body moving under the gravitational pull of others.
A function whose gradient gives the gravitational force per unit mass.
The balance in a star between the inward pull of gravity and the outward pressure gradient.
The description of how light is emitted, absorbed and scattered on its way through matter.
The stretching of the wavelength of light from a receding or distant source.
A collection of masses, such as a star cluster, each moving under the gravity of all the others.
A solution of the equations of gravity describing the universe on the largest scales.

theorems.name: Kepler's laws
theorems.statement: A planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus. The line from the Sun to the planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis.

theorems.name: Newton's law of gravitation
theorems.statement: Two point masses \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) at distance \(r\) attract each other with a force of magnitude \(Gm_1m_2/r^2\) directed along the line joining them.

theorems.name: Virial theorem
theorems.statement: For a system of point masses interacting by Newtonian gravity whose positions and velocities stay bounded, the long-time averages of the kinetic energy \(K\) and potential energy \(U\) satisfy \(2\langle K\rangle + \langle U\rangle = 0\).

theorems.name: Lane-Emden equation
theorems.statement: A spherical star in hydrostatic equilibrium with pressure \(P = K\rho^{1+1/n}\) has density \(\rho = \rho_c\theta^n\), where \(\theta(\xi)\) solves \(\frac{1}{\xi^2}\frac{d}{d\xi}\left(\xi^2\frac{d\theta}{d\xi}\right) = -\theta^n\) with \(\theta(0) = 1\), \(\theta'(0) = 0\), and \(\xi\) is a rescaled radius.

theorems.name: Friedmann equation
theorems.statement: In a homogeneous and isotropic universe with scale factor \(a(t)\), mass density \(\rho\) and spatial curvature \(k\), general relativity gives \(\left(\frac{\dot a}{a}\right)^2 = \frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho - \frac{kc^2}{a^2} + \frac{\Lambda c^2}{3}\).

theorems.name: Chandrasekhar limit
theorems.statement: A non-rotating white dwarf supported by the pressure of degenerate electrons cannot exceed a maximum mass, about 1.4 solar masses for typical compositions.

open.name: Dark matter
open.gloss: What is the unseen matter whose gravity is inferred from the motion of galaxies and clusters?

open.name: Dark energy
open.gloss: What causes the observed acceleration of the expansion of the universe?

open.name: Hubble tension
open.gloss: Why do measurements of the present expansion rate from the nearby universe and from the early universe disagree?

page.hook: How do we know what the inside of the Earth looks like when nobody has ever been there?
about: Geophysics applies mathematics and physics to the Earth: its solid interior, oceans, atmosphere and magnetic field. Topics include earthquakes and the waves they send through the planet, the shape and gravity of the Earth, slow convection in the mantle that drives the plates, the generation of the magnetic field in the liquid core, and the circulation of air and water that makes weather and climate.

Almost nothing below the surface can be observed directly, so the area depends on inverse problems: inferring internal structure from measurements made at the surface or from satellites. The forward models come from elasticity and fluid dynamics on a rotating sphere. Data are noisy and incomplete, and the governing equations are often chaotic, so statistics, numerical simulation and data assimilation are central.

example.title: How far away was the earthquake?
example.text: An earthquake sends out fast P waves and slower S waves. Suppose they travel at 6 km/s and 3.5 km/s, and a station records the S wave 30 seconds after the P wave. The distance \(d\) satisfies \(d/3.5 - d/6 = 30\), so \(d = 252\) km. One station gives only a circle of possible locations. Circles from three stations meet in a single point, the epicenter.

objects.gloss: An elastic wave traveling through the Earth, generated by an earthquake or an explosion.
The surface of constant gravity potential that coincides with mean sea level.
The apparent force that deflects moving air and water on the rotating Earth.
The slow creeping flow of the solid mantle that carries heat outward and moves the plates.
The process by which flow of liquid iron in the outer core maintains the magnetic field.
Determining causes or internal structure from indirect measurements of their effects.
Combining a forecast model with new observations to estimate the current state of a system.

theorems.name: Clairaut's theorem
theorems.statement: For a slowly rotating body in hydrostatic equilibrium, gravity at latitude \(\varphi\) is, to first order, \(g = g_e\left[1 + \left(\frac52 m - f\right)\sin^2\varphi\right]\), where \(f\) is the flattening and \(m\) the ratio of centrifugal acceleration to gravity at the equator.

theorems.name: Speeds of elastic waves
theorems.statement: An isotropic elastic solid with Lamé constants \(\lambda\), \(\mu\) and density \(\rho\) carries compressional waves at speed \(\sqrt{(\lambda + 2\mu)/\rho}\) and shear waves at speed \(\sqrt{\mu/\rho}\). Shear waves do not propagate in a fluid, where \(\mu = 0\).

theorems.name: Herglotz-Wiechert inversion
theorems.statement: In a spherically symmetric Earth where \(r/v(r)\) decreases steadily with depth, the travel times of waves between surface points determine the wave speed \(v(r)\) uniquely, through an explicit formula of Abel type.

theorems.name: Geostrophic balance
theorems.statement: For large-scale, slowly changing flow away from the equator, the Coriolis force balances the horizontal pressure gradient: \(f\,\hat z\times u = -\nabla_h p/\rho\), with \(f = 2\Omega\sin\varphi\). The wind therefore blows along lines of constant pressure.

theorems.name: Cowling's theorem
theorems.statement: A magnetic field that is symmetric about an axis cannot be maintained by dynamo action.

theorems.name: Gutenberg-Richter law
theorems.statement: In a given region and time span, the number \(N\) of earthquakes of magnitude at least \(M\) follows \(\log_{10}N = a - bM\), with \(b\) close to 1. This is an empirical law.

open.name: Earthquake prediction
open.gloss: Can the time, place and size of individual large earthquakes be forecast with useful accuracy?

open.name: Reversals of the magnetic field
open.gloss: Explain and simulate, at realistic parameter values, why the geodynamo reverses polarity at irregular intervals.

open.name: Limits of climate prediction
open.gloss: How precisely can the response of the climate system to a given forcing be determined?

uses: Exploration for oil, gas and minerals

page.hook: What is the cheapest way to route a thousand deliveries, or the best mix of products to make?
about: Operations research uses mathematical models to make decisions about complex systems: how to schedule crews, route vehicles, manage inventories, or locate warehouses. Mathematical programming is its core. One seeks the values of decision variables that make an objective, such as cost or profit, as good as possible while satisfying a set of constraints.

Problems are sorted by structure. Linear programs can be solved at very large scale. Convex programs keep most of that tractability. Problems with integer variables or nonconvex functions are usually hard in the worst case and are attacked by branch-and-bound, cutting planes, relaxations and heuristics. Duality, which pairs each problem with a second one that bounds it, runs through the whole area. Uncertainty leads to stochastic and dynamic programming.

example.title: A small linear program
example.text: Maximize \(x + 2y\) subject to \(x + y \le 4\), \(x + 3y \le 6\), \(x \ge 0\), \(y \ge 0\). The feasible region is a quadrilateral with corners \((0,0)\), \((4,0)\), \((3,1)\) and \((0,2)\). The objective takes the values \(0\), \(4\), \(5\) and \(4\) there, so the maximum is \(5\) at \((3,1)\). A linear objective over such a region always attains its best value at a corner.

objects.gloss: The quantity to be minimized or maximized.
The set of all choices of the variables that satisfy the constraints.
An optimization problem with a linear objective and linear equality and inequality constraints.
A function whose graph lies below its chords, so that every local minimum is global.
A companion optimization problem whose value bounds that of the original.
An optimization problem in which some variables must take integer values.
An assignment of amounts to the edges of a graph that respects capacities and conserves flow at nodes.

theorems.name: Fundamental theorem of linear programming
theorems.statement: If the linear program of minimizing \(c^{T}x\) subject to \(Ax = b\), \(x \ge 0\) has an optimal solution, then it has an optimal solution that is a vertex of the feasible polyhedron.

theorems.name: Strong duality for linear programming
theorems.statement: If a linear program has an optimal solution, then so does its dual, and the two optimal values are equal.

theorems.name: Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions
theorems.statement:
Let \(x^*\) be a local minimizer of a smooth \(f\) subject to \(g_i(x) \le 0\) and \(h_j(x) = 0\), with smooth constraints satisfying a constraint qualification at \(x^*\). Then there are multipliers \(\lambda_i \ge 0\) and \(\mu_j\) with \(
abla f + \sum_i\lambda_i
abla g_i + \sum_j\mu_j
abla h_j = 0\) at \(x^*\) and \(\lambda_i g_i(x^*) = 0\) for all \(i\).

theorems.name: Max-flow min-cut theorem
theorems.statement: In a network with nonnegative edge capacities, the maximum value of a flow from the source to the sink equals the minimum total capacity of a set of edges whose removal separates the source from the sink.

theorems.name: Bellman equation
theorems.statement: In a Markov decision process with finitely many states and actions and discount factor \(0 \le \gamma < 1\), the optimal value function is the unique solution of \(V(s) = \max_a\left[r(s,a) + \gamma\sum_{s'}P(s'\mid s,a)V(s')\right]\), and choosing a maximizing action in each state is optimal.

theorems.name: Polynomial solvability of linear programming
theorems.statement: A linear program with rational data can be solved in time polynomial in the number of bits needed to write it down. The first proof used the ellipsoid method.

open.name: Strongly polynomial linear programming
open.gloss: Is there an algorithm for linear programming whose number of arithmetic operations is polynomial in the number of variables and constraints alone?

open.name: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
open.gloss: Is the diameter of the graph of every polytope bounded by a polynomial in its dimension and number of facets?

open.name: Four-thirds conjecture
open.gloss: Is the optimal traveling salesman tour in a metric space always at most 4/3 times the value of the subtour linear programming relaxation?

name: Game theory, economics, finance, and other social and behavioral sciences

subareas.name: Social and behavioral sciences: general topics
Other social and behavioral sciences (mathematical treatment)

page.hook: When everyone acts in their own interest, what outcome should we expect?
about: This area applies mathematics to human decisions and their interaction. Game theory studies situations where the result for each participant depends on the choices of all. Mathematical economics models markets, prices and the allocation of resources. Social choice theory studies voting and collective decisions. Mathematical finance and actuarial science price financial contracts and insurance and measure risk. Models in psychology and sociology also belong here.

The central notion is equilibrium: a state in which no participant can gain by changing course alone. Existence of equilibria is usually proved with fixed point theorems or convex analysis, and computing them leads to optimization and complexity theory. Finance relies on stochastic processes and partial differential equations. Much of the area consists of proving that a short list of desirable properties can or cannot be satisfied together.

example.title: The prisoner's dilemma
example.text: Two suspects are questioned separately. If both stay silent, each gets 1 year. If both confess, each gets 5 years. If only one confesses, that one goes free and the other gets 10 years. Whatever the other does, confessing is better: 0 years instead of 1, or 5 instead of 10. So both confess and serve 5 years, although both staying silent would have cost each only 1 year.

objects.gloss: A set of players, the strategies available to each, and the payoff each receives from every combination.
A choice of strategies from which no single player can gain by deviating alone.
A numerical representation of the preferences of an agent over outcomes.
Prices at which the amounts that agents wish to buy and sell balance in every market.
A procedure that turns individual preferences into a collective decision, such as a voting system.
The rules of an interaction, such as an auction, designed so that self-interested behavior gives a desired result.
A trading strategy that yields a riskless profit with no initial investment.

theorems.name: Minimax theorem
theorems.statement: For a finite two-player zero-sum game with payoff matrix \(A\), \(\max_x\min_y x^{T}Ay = \min_y\max_x x^{T}Ay\), where \(x\) and \(y\) range over the mixed strategies of the two players.

theorems.name: Nash's existence theorem
theorems.statement: Every game with finitely many players, each having finitely many pure strategies, has at least one Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies.

theorems.name: Arrow's impossibility theorem
theorems.statement: With at least three alternatives and finitely many voters, no rule that turns every profile of individual rankings into a collective ranking can satisfy all three of: respecting unanimous preferences, independence of irrelevant alternatives, and the absence of a dictator.

theorems.name: Arrow-Debreu theorem
theorems.statement: An economy with finitely many goods, consumers and producers has a competitive equilibrium, provided preferences are continuous and convex, production sets are closed and convex, and certain further technical conditions hold.

theorems.name: Gale-Shapley theorem
theorems.statement: Given two groups of equal size, each of whose members ranks all members of the other group, there is always a stable matching: a pairing in which no two unmatched individuals prefer each other to their assigned partners. The deferred acceptance algorithm finds one.

theorems.name: Black-Scholes formula
theorems.statement: If a stock paying no dividends follows geometric Brownian motion with constant volatility \(\sigma\) and the interest rate \(r\) is constant, then a European call with strike \(K\) and time \(T\) to expiry has price \(S\,N(d_1) - Ke^{-rT}N(d_2)\), where \(S\) is the stock price, \(N\) the standard normal distribution function, \(d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K) + (r + \sigma^2/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T}\) and \(d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt T\).

open.name: Complexity of Nash equilibrium
open.gloss: Finding a Nash equilibrium of a two-player game is complete for the class PPAD; whether a polynomial-time algorithm exists is unknown.

open.name: Optimal multi-item auctions
open.gloss: Describe the auction that maximizes the expected revenue of a seller with several different items; the answer is known in general only for one item.

open.name: Envy-freeness up to any good
open.gloss: For four or more agents with additive valuations, can indivisible goods always be divided so that no agent envies another after removing any single good from the other's share?

page.hook: How fast will an epidemic spread, and what share of people must be immune to stop it?
about: This area gathers the mathematics used in the life sciences and chemistry. It includes models of how populations grow and compete, how diseases spread, how genes change in frequency over generations, how nerve cells fire, how tissues take shape, and how molecules react. It also covers methods for biological data, such as comparing DNA sequences and reconstructing evolutionary trees.

Most models are dynamical systems. Ordinary differential equations describe well-mixed populations and chemical concentrations, partial differential equations add space, and stochastic processes handle small numbers and chance events. Graphs and combinatorics enter through networks and sequences. A model is judged by whether it explains data and predicts the result of an intervention, so parameter estimation and statistics are part of the work.

example.title: The herd immunity threshold
example.text: Suppose each infected person would infect \(R_0 = 3\) others in a fully susceptible population. If a fraction \(s\) of people is still susceptible, each case causes \(3s\) new ones on average. The outbreak shrinks once \(3s < 1\), which means more than \(1 - 1/3 \approx 67\%\) are immune. For measles, with \(R_0\) around 15, the threshold is \(1 - 1/15 \approx 93\%\).

objects.gloss: An equation describing how the size of one or more populations changes in time.
A model that divides a population into groups, such as susceptible, infected and recovered.
The average number of new infections caused by one case in a fully susceptible population.
A set of chemical species and the reactions that convert them into one another.
Equations for substances that react locally and spread through space.
The proportion of copies of a gene in a population that are of a given variant.
A branching diagram representing the evolutionary relationships among species or genes.

theorems.name: Logistic growth
theorems.statement: A population limited by a carrying capacity \(K\) is modeled by \(\dot N = rN(1 - N/K)\) with \(r > 0\). The solution with \(N(0) = N_0 > 0\) is \(N(t) = K/\left(1 + \frac{K - N_0}{N_0}e^{-rt}\right)\), which tends to \(K\).

theorems.name: Hardy-Weinberg law
theorems.statement: In a large randomly mating population with no selection, mutation or migration, the allele frequencies \(p\) and \(q = 1 - p\) at a gene with two alleles stay constant, and after one generation the genotype frequencies are \(p^2\), \(2pq\) and \(q^2\).

theorems.name: Lotka-Volterra equations
theorems.statement: The predator-prey model \(\dot x = x(\alpha - \beta y)\), \(\dot y = y(\delta x - \gamma)\) with positive constants has the equilibrium \((\gamma/\delta, \alpha/\beta)\), and every other solution with \(x, y > 0\) is a periodic orbit around it.

theorems.name: Kermack-McKendrick model
theorems.statement: With \(S\), \(I\), \(R\) the fractions susceptible, infected and recovered, \(\dot S = -\beta SI\), \(\dot I = \beta SI - \gamma I\), \(\dot R = \gamma I\). The number of infected initially grows if and only if \(R_0S(0) > 1\), where \(R_0 = \beta/\gamma\).

theorems.name: Hodgkin-Huxley model
theorems.statement: The membrane voltage \(V\) of a nerve axon satisfies \(C\dot V = I - g_{Na}m^3h(V - E_{Na}) - g_Kn^4(V - E_K) - g_L(V - E_L)\), where the gating variables \(m\), \(h\), \(n\) obey first-order kinetics with voltage-dependent rates. The model reproduces the action potential.

theorems.name: Turing instability
theorems.statement: A uniform steady state of two reacting chemicals that is stable without diffusion can become unstable when the two diffuse at sufficiently different rates. The instability produces a spatial pattern with a characteristic wavelength.

open.name: Global attractor conjecture
open.gloss: Does every complex-balanced mass-action reaction system converge to its positive equilibrium from every positive starting point with the same conserved quantities? A proof has been announced but is not yet generally accepted.

open.name: From genotype to phenotype
open.gloss: Predict the traits of an organism from its genome and environment.

open.name: Multiscale models of living systems
open.gloss: Link models of molecules, cells, tissues and whole organisms in a mathematically controlled way.

page.hook: How does cruise control hold a car at a steady speed on hills it cannot see coming?
about: Control theory studies systems that evolve in time and can be influenced through inputs. The goal is to choose the inputs so that the system behaves as desired: an aircraft holds its course, a chemical reactor keeps its temperature, a robot arm follows a path. The key idea is feedback, in which measurements of the current behavior are used continually to correct the input.

A system is described by differential or difference equations with input and output variables. For linear systems there is a complete theory based on linear algebra and complex analysis. Nonlinear, infinite-dimensional and stochastic systems require differential geometry, partial differential equations and probability. Typical questions are whether a state can be reached, whether it can be reconstructed from measurements, and whether a design remains stable under disturbances and modeling errors.

example.title: Stabilizing by feedback
example.text: Consider \(\dot x = x + u\), where \(u\) is an input we choose. With \(u = 0\) the state grows like \(e^{t}\): starting from \(x(0) = 1\), it reaches \(2.72\) after one second. Now measure \(x\) and set \(u = -3x\). The equation becomes \(\dot x = -2x\), with solution \(e^{-2t}\), which is \(0.135\) after one second and tends to zero. Feedback has turned an unstable system into a stable one.

objects.gloss: The set of variables that, with future inputs, determines the future behavior of the system.
A signal chosen by the controller, or imposed from outside, that drives the system.
Choosing the input as a function of measured outputs or states.
For a linear time-invariant system, the ratio of the Laplace transforms of output and input.
The property that inputs can steer the state from any point to any other in finite time.
The property that the state can be determined from the inputs and outputs over a time interval.
An energy-like function that decreases along trajectories and certifies stability.

theorems.name: Lyapunov's stability theorem
theorems.statement: If near an equilibrium of \(\dot x = f(x)\) there is a continuously differentiable positive definite function \(V\) whose derivative along solutions is nonpositive, the equilibrium is stable. If that derivative is negative definite, the equilibrium is asymptotically stable.

theorems.name: Nyquist stability criterion
theorems.statement: Let \(L(s)\) be a proper rational transfer function with \(P\) poles in the open right half-plane and none on the imaginary axis. The closed loop with unity negative feedback is stable if and only if the image of the imaginary axis under \(L\) does not pass through \(-1\) and encircles it exactly \(P\) times counterclockwise.

theorems.name: Kalman rank condition
theorems.statement: The system \(\dot x = Ax + Bu\) with state in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is controllable if and only if the matrix \([B, AB, \dots, A^{n-1}B]\) has rank \(n\).

theorems.name: Kalman filter
theorems.statement: For a linear system driven by Gaussian white noise and observed through linear measurements with Gaussian white noise, the conditional mean of the state given the measurements so far obeys a recursive linear update. It is the estimate with the smallest mean square error.

theorems.name: Pole placement theorem
theorems.statement: The pair \((A,B)\) is controllable if and only if for every monic real polynomial \(p\) of degree \(n\) there is a real matrix \(K\) such that \(A - BK\) has characteristic polynomial \(p\).

theorems.name: Linear-quadratic regulator
theorems.statement: For \(\dot x = Ax + Bu\) with cost \(\int_0^\infty (x^{T}Qx + u^{T}Ru)\,dt\), \(Q \succeq 0\), \(R \succ 0\), \((A,B)\) stabilizable and \((A,Q^{1/2})\) detectable, the optimal input is the feedback \(u = -R^{-1}B^{T}Px\), where \(P\) is the unique positive semidefinite solution of \(A^{T}P + PA - PBR^{-1}B^{T}P + Q = 0\).

open.name: Static output feedback
open.gloss: Given matrices \(A\), \(B\), \(C\), is there an efficient algorithm to decide whether some \(K\) makes \(A + BKC\) stable? The complexity of this problem is unknown.

open.name: Guarantees for learning-based control
open.gloss: Establish stability and safety guarantees for controllers that are learned from data.

page.hook: How can a scratched disc or a noisy phone line still deliver a message without a single error?
about: Information theory measures information and determines the limits of storing and transmitting it. It asks how far data can be compressed and how fast it can be sent reliably over a channel that introduces errors. Coding theory constructs the error-correcting codes that approach these limits. The area also includes cryptography, signal processing, and the theory of switching circuits and networks.

Shannon's theory is probabilistic: sources and channels are random, and the limits are expressed through entropy and mutual information. Constructing good codes, by contrast, uses algebra and combinatorics, including finite fields, polynomials, algebraic curves and sparse graphs. Cryptography adds number theory and computational complexity. Limits are usually proved by a counting or probabilistic argument, and the hard part is to reach them with efficient explicit schemes.

example.title: The information in a biased coin
example.text: A coin that lands heads with probability \(p\) has entropy \(H = -p\log_2p - (1-p)\log_2(1-p)\) bits per toss. A fair coin has \(H = 1\). A coin with \(p = 0.9\) has \(H \approx 0.9 \cdot 0.152 + 0.1 \cdot 3.322 \approx 0.469\). So a record of 1000 tosses of this coin can be compressed to about 469 bits on average, and no method can do better in the long run.

objects.gloss: The average number of bits needed per symbol to describe the output of a random source.
A model of a transmission medium, giving the probability of each output for each input.
The amount by which knowing one random variable reduces uncertainty about another.
The highest rate at which information can be sent over a channel with vanishing error probability.
A set of codewords chosen so that the original can be recovered after some symbols are corrupted.
The number of positions in which two words of equal length differ.
A method of scrambling a message with a key so that only key holders can read it.

theorems.name: Source coding theorem
theorems.statement: A source emitting independent identically distributed symbols with entropy \(H\) bits can be encoded at any rate above \(H\) bits per symbol with error probability tending to zero as the block length grows. At any rate below \(H\) this is impossible.

theorems.name: Noisy-channel coding theorem
theorems.statement: A discrete memoryless channel has a capacity \(C = \max_{p(x)} I(X;Y)\). For every rate \(R < C\) there are codes of rate \(R\) whose error probability tends to zero with the block length. For \(R > C\) the error probability stays bounded away from zero.

theorems.name: Sampling theorem
theorems.statement: If \(f\) is square-integrable and its Fourier transform vanishes outside the frequency band \([-W, W]\), then \(f\) is determined by its samples at spacing \(1/(2W)\): \(f(t) = \sum_{n} f\left(\frac{n}{2W}\right)\operatorname{sinc}(2Wt - n)\), where \(\operatorname{sinc}(x) = \sin(\pi x)/(\pi x)\).

theorems.name: Perfect secrecy
theorems.statement: A cipher is perfectly secret if the ciphertext is statistically independent of the message. This requires the entropy of the key to be at least the entropy of the message. The one-time pad, with a uniformly random key as long as the message and used once, achieves it.

theorems.name: Hamming bound
theorems.statement: A binary code of length \(n\) that corrects every pattern of up to \(t\) errors has at most \(2^n/\sum_{i=0}^{t}\binom{n}{i}\) codewords.

theorems.name: Singleton bound
theorems.statement: A code of length \(n\) and minimum distance \(d\) over an alphabet of \(q\) symbols has at most \(q^{n-d+1}\) codewords. Reed-Solomon codes attain the bound.

open.name: Capacity of networks
open.gloss: Determine the capacity of basic multi-user channels, such as the relay channel and the interference channel.

open.name: Best binary codes
open.gloss: What is the largest possible rate of binary codes with a given relative minimum distance as the length grows? It is unknown whether the Gilbert-Varshamov bound is optimal.

open.name: Shannon capacity of the 7-cycle
open.gloss: Determine the zero-error capacity of the channel whose confusion graph is a cycle of length 7.

page.hook: Why do so many students add fractions by adding the tops and the bottoms, and what teaching helps?
about: Mathematics education studies how people learn mathematics and how it can be taught well, from early counting to university courses. It examines what students understand and misunderstand, how curricula are designed, how teachers are prepared, how learning is assessed, and how tools such as textbooks, software and calculators affect what is learned. It also covers the history and social role of mathematics teaching.

Unlike the other areas, its methods are those of the social sciences: classroom experiments, interviews, large-scale assessments and statistical analysis, guided by theories from psychology. Its results are empirical findings and frameworks, not theorems. The work depends on a close knowledge of the mathematics involved, since one must know the many ways an idea can be understood in order to teach it.

example.title: A persistent error with fractions
example.text: Asked for \(\frac12 + \frac13\), many students write \(\frac25\), adding numerators and denominators. A quick check exposes the problem: \(\frac25\) is less than \(\frac12\), yet adding a positive amount should give more. The error comes from treating a fraction as two separate whole numbers. Teaching that presents fractions as single numbers, for example on a number line with common units \(\frac36 + \frac26 = \frac56\), addresses the cause.

objects.gloss: The planned sequence of topics and goals for mathematics teaching.
A systematic, reasoned but incorrect idea that leads students to predictable errors.
Understanding why methods work, and fluency in carrying them out.
Tackling tasks for which the learner has no ready-made method.
A way of showing a mathematical idea, such as a diagram, a graph, a table or symbols.
Methods for finding out what students know and can do.
The knowledge of a subject that is specific to teaching it, such as useful examples and typical difficulties.

theorems.name: Piaget's stages of development
theorems.statement: Piaget's theory holds that children's thinking develops through four stages: sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational. Abstract and hypothetical reasoning belongs to the last stage. Later research has questioned how sharp and universal the stages are.

theorems.name: Zone of proximal development
theorems.statement: Vygotsky's term for the range between what a learner can do alone and what the learner can do with guidance from a more capable person. Instruction is taken to be most effective when it targets this range.

theorems.name: Pólya's four phases of problem solving
theorems.statement: Pólya's book How to Solve It describes problem solving in four phases: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, and look back at the solution.

theorems.name: Bloom's taxonomy
theorems.statement: A classification of educational objectives in the cognitive domain into six levels of increasing complexity: knowledge, comprehension, application, analysis, synthesis and evaluation.

theorems.name: Van Hiele levels
theorems.statement: A model of how geometric thinking develops through five levels: visualization, analysis, informal deduction, formal deduction and rigor. According to the model the levels are passed in order, and teaching pitched above a learner's level is not understood.

theorems.name: Spacing and testing effects
theorems.statement: Practice that is spread over several sessions, and practice that requires recalling material from memory, lead to better long-term retention than the same time spent in one session or on rereading. These findings have been replicated in many laboratory and classroom studies.
